label: Chapter 4
title: The Thomistic Proof
tagline: From what things are to the One who simply is
oneSentence: Because everything we experience has an essence (what it is) really distinct from its existence (that it is), its existence must be imparted to it here and now by a cause, and the hierarchical series of such causes can only terminate in something whose very essence is existence itself — subsistent existence itself — which must be unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual, and therefore God.
bigPicture:
The Thomistic proof starts from the most basic fact about anything at all: not that it changes (chapter 1), not that it has parts (chapter 2), but simply that it *exists*. Feser draws the argument from Thomas Aquinas's early treatise *On Being and Essence* (*De Ente et Essentia*). Its engine is the famous Thomistic **real distinction** between a thing's **essence** — what it is — and its **existence** — the fact that it is. A lion's lion-ness does not contain or guarantee the lion's being there at all. Existence has to come to it from somewhere.

The chapter moves in two stages. **Stage 1** argues, in three independent ways, that essence and existence really are distinct in the things of experience; that nothing of this kind can give itself existence; that it therefore needs a cause of its existence *at every moment*, here and now; and that the resulting series of existence-imparting causes is **hierarchical**, so it must bottom out in a cause whose essence simply *is* existence — what Aquinas calls **subsistent existence itself** (*ipsum esse subsistens*). **Stage 2** shows that there can be only one such thing, that it causes everything else, that it exists necessarily and without a cause, and that — since essence relates to existence as potency to act — it is **purely actual**. That links it to the Aristotelian proof's purely actual actualizer and brings along all the divine attributes derived in chapter 1.

The chapter's second half defends the argument against serious critics: Hume's claim that an infinite series needs no first member, the charge of a fallacy of composition, Anthony Kenny's influential attack on the real distinction, the objection that the distinction is only conceptual (the aspirin case), and the doubt that things have real essences at all. What makes this proof distinctive is how deep it digs. It does not ask what keeps things *changing* or *holding together*, but what keeps them *in being at all* — and it answers that everything which merely *has* existence depends, right now, on the One who *is* existence.
objectives: Define essence and existence and explain, with an example, the difference between knowing what a thing is and knowing that it is.

State and defend Feser's three arguments for a real (not merely conceptual) distinction between essence and existence: from knowability, from contingency, and from the uniqueness of anything whose essence is existence.
Explain why a real distinction need not involve separability, using the circle's radius and circumference.

Explain why something whose essence is distinct from its existence can neither get existence from its own essence nor impart existence to itself, and so needs a cause of its existence at every moment.
Show why the series of existence-imparting causes is hierarchical, and why only something whose essence just is existence (subsistent existence itself) can be its first member.
Reconstruct the argument that there can be at most one thing whose essence is existence, and derive from that its uniqueness, necessity, uncausedness, and pure actuality.
Connect the Thomistic proof to the Aristotelian proof (essence and existence as potency and act) and the Neoplatonic proof (absolute simplicity), and explain how the divine attributes follow.
Answer Hume's ‘why need there be a first cause?’, the fallacy-of-composition charge, Kenny's objection, the ‘merely conceptual distinction’ objection, and conventionalism about essences.
Present the argument persuasively to a skeptic in a way that avoids the ‘everything has a cause’ caricature.

summary.heading: Stage 1: What a thing is versus that it is
summary.plain: About anything you know — a dog, a tree, a person — there are two different questions: what is it, and is there really one? The answer to the first is the thing's ‘essence’ (its nature); the answer to the second is its ‘existence’. The chapter starts by asking whether this difference is real, or just two ways of talking about the same thing.
summary.takeaway: Knowing what a thing is and knowing that it is are two different pieces of knowledge; the whole proof turns on whether that difference lies in things themselves or only in our minds.
summary.body:
Feser opens with an ordinary observation. When we know that there are stones, trees, dogs, and people, we actually know two different things about them. We know **what** they are — their **essence** or nature (for example, the traditional definition of a human being as a rational animal; Feser notes you may substitute another definition if you prefer). And we know **that** they are — that they really **exist** out there, independently of our minds.

So we can distinguish essence from existence. But not every distinction we draw marks a difference in reality. ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ differ only in wording; in the world they pick out exactly the same thing. The key question of Stage 1 is whether the essence/existence distinction is like that — merely verbal or conceptual — or whether it is a **real distinction**, reflecting something in things themselves apart from how we think or talk. Feser gives three reasons for thinking it is real.

Notice how modest this starting point is. Feser assumes nothing about God, cosmology, or the latest science; he asks only that we notice that knowing *what* something is and knowing *that* it is are two different pieces of knowledge. The difference is familiar from ordinary life. A police sketch artist can produce a detailed picture of what a suspect looks like while it remains entirely open whether anyone matching it exists. If the essence/existence distinction turns out to be merely verbal, nothing follows from it. But if it is real, a pressing question arises: where does a thing's existence come from, if it is not part of what the thing is? The rest of the chapter is the answer to that question.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is the very notion of a **real** as opposed to a **merely verbal** distinction, so go slowly. A distinction is merely verbal when two expressions pick out exactly one reality, so that nothing in the thing answers to the difference in wording. ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ are Feser's example: every fact about bachelors is a fact about unmarried men, and learning that someone is one tells you he is the other. A distinction is **real** when there is something in the thing corresponding to each side — two aspects of reality, not two labels for one aspect.

Try a thought experiment. Take the dodo. You can read a full description of what a dodo is — a large flightless bird of Mauritius, with such-and-such anatomy. Separately, you can learn that there are no dodos any more. These are two different discoveries. The first tells you about the bird's nature; the second tells you about its standing in reality. Is the difference between these discoveries only in your head, or does it mark something in dodos (and in lions, and in you)? That is the question Stage 1 sets.

Two nuances Feser adds. First, nothing depends on the traditional definition of a human as a rational animal; substitute any definition you like. The point is that things *have* an essence — whatever it is — and that knowing it differs from knowing they exist. Second, at this stage Feser claims only that we can **draw** the distinction. That is all that step 1 of the formal argument asserts. Whether the distinction is real is precisely what steps 2–11 go on to argue.

A common confusion: people picture existence as one more item on a thing's list of features — ‘big cat, maned, carnivorous, *exists*.’ The Thomist rejects that picture as firmly as any critic does. Existence isn't another feature alongside the others; it is what makes the whole list of features real rather than merely describable. Keep that in mind, because later objections (Kenny's especially) often assume that the Thomist must be treating existence as a property.

Why does this matter for the proof? Because if a thing's existence really were just part of what it is, the thing would carry its own existence with it and need no cause of its being. The possibility of a Thomistic proof opens only if what a thing is and that it is come apart in reality.

checks.q: What is Feser's example of a merely verbal distinction?
options: ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’
A circle's radius and circumference
Lions and unicorns
Essence and existence
checks.explanation: The two phrases pick out one and the same reality. Radius and circumference are Feser's example of a real but inseparable distinction; essence and existence are the pair whose status is in question.

checks.q: Does the argument depend on accepting ‘rational animal’ as the correct definition of a human being?
options: Yes — the whole proof rests on that definition
No — Feser says any other definition may be substituted, since the point concerns having an essence at all
Yes — only humans have essences
No — because humans have no essence
checks.explanation: Feser explicitly says it doesn't matter whether you accept the traditional definition. The argument needs only that things have some nature distinct from the fact that they exist.

checks.q: What question does Stage 1 set out to answer first?
options: Whether God exists
Whether the universe had a beginning
Whether everything has a cause
Whether the distinction between essence and existence is real or merely conceptual
checks.explanation: Stage 1 opens by asking whether the essence/existence distinction reflects mind-independent reality. God, and the need for a cause, come later.

summary.heading: First argument for the real distinction: we can know essence without knowing existence
summary.plain: You can know exactly what a lion, a pterodactyl, and a unicorn are, and still not be able to say which one is alive today, which died out, and which never existed. So knowing what something is doesn't tell you whether it's real. And if you wrongly think lions are extinct, you're wrong about the world, but you still understand perfectly well what a lion is — which shows that being real isn't part of what a lion is.
summary.takeaway: A thing's nature can be fully grasped without settling whether it exists, and denying its existence doesn't misconceive its nature, so existence is not part of its essence.
summary.body:
Imagine someone who has never heard of lions, pterodactyls, or unicorns. You describe the nature of each in detail, then tell him that one of the three exists, one once existed but is extinct, and one never existed at all — and ask him to say which is which from their essences alone. He cannot. Yet a thing's essence is part of its objective reality (the biology of lions would be the same whether or not anyone studied it), and so, if it exists, is its existence. If essence and existence were not distinct features of reality, knowing the one should give you the other. It doesn't. So they are really distinct.

**Objection:** this presupposes we grasp essences completely, which we usually don't; perhaps existence is hidden in the part we have not grasped. **Reply:** there is a telling disanalogy between genuine parts of an essence and existence. If you think a lion is an animal but haven't yet realized it is a cat, your conception is *incomplete* but not *mistaken*. If you judge that a lion is *not* a cat, you have *misconceived* what a lion is. But if you judge that lions do not exist (thinking them extinct or fictional), you have judged falsely without misconceiving what a lion is. If existence were part of the lion's essence, denying it would be a misconception on a par with denying that lions are cats. It isn't.

In the formal statement this first argument appears as steps 2 and 3. Feser returns to it near the end of the chapter, when he answers the objection that the distinction is merely conceptual. There, following Klima, he adds that knowing an essence gives *a priori* knowledge of what any member of the kind would have to be like, while whether any member exists can be known only *a posteriori*, through experience.
summary.deepDive:
The key tool in this section is the contrast between an **incomplete** conception and a **misconception**. Work through it with two imaginary students. Student A believes that lions are not cats. Student B believes that lions went extinct centuries ago. Ask a zoologist which of them misunderstands *what a lion is*. The answer is A. A is thinking of something that is not really a lion at all: denying a genuine part of the essence changes the subject. B, by contrast, is thinking of exactly the right animal; she is simply wrong about the world. That is why the zoologist can correct B by saying ‘No — lions are alive in Africa today.’ They can disagree about lions only because they share the same concept of a lion.

Now generalize. The features that belong to an essence are those whose denial distorts your idea of the thing. Existence fails this test every time: you can deny that pterodactyls or unicorns exist without misunderstanding what they are. So existence is not one of the ingredients of what a thing is, however much or little of the essence we have grasped. This is why Feser can admit — as he does — that our grasp of essences is usually incomplete, without weakening the argument.

Notice also the premise that a thing's essence belongs to its **objective reality**. The biology of lions would be the same whether or not anyone studied it. This premise blocks the reply that essence is ‘only in our concepts’. If both what a lion is and the lion's existence are features of mind-independent reality, then if they were one and the same feature, knowing the one would be knowing the other.

How does this feed the formal argument? Steps 2 and 3 record it: if the distinction were not real, knowing the essence would reveal the existence (2); it doesn't (3). Together with the other two arguments, this secures step 11.

A usual confusion: people think the argument is simply ‘I don't know whether X exists, so X's existence is distinct from its essence’ — a leap from our ignorance to a fact about things. Critics exploit this with the aspirin example (knowing aspirin without knowing it is acetylsalicylic acid). But the argument is subtler: it concerns what even a *complete* grasp of an essence would include, and it is backed by the misconception test. The chapter's later section on the ‘merely conceptual distinction’ objection develops exactly this point.

checks.q: Which of these judgments misconceives what a lion is?
options: Lions are extinct
Lions are fictional creatures
Lions are not cats
Lions live in Africa
checks.explanation: Denying that lions are cats denies part of their essence. Judging them extinct or fictional is false, but it does not distort the concept of a lion.

checks.q: Why does the argument insist that both a thing's essence and its existence belong to its objective reality?
options: Because if they were one and the same feature of reality, knowing one would amount to knowing the other
Because only objective things have causes
Because otherwise unicorns would exist
Because objective reality is always material
checks.explanation: The inference from ‘I can know the essence without the existence’ to ‘they are distinct in reality’ needs both to be features of the thing itself, not just of our concepts.

checks.q: Which steps of the formal argument record this first argument?
options: Steps 4–5
Steps 2–3
Steps 6–8
Steps 12–16
checks.explanation: Steps 2–3 are the knowability argument; 4–5 the contingency argument; 6–8 the uniqueness argument; 12–16 the need for an external cause.

summary.heading: Second argument: contingency
summary.plain: Lions exist, but they might never have existed and might someday die out. If being real were built into what a lion is, lions couldn't fail to exist. Since they can, being real must be something separate from what they are. The fact that lions need parents and can be killed doesn't replace this point; it's a sign of it.
summary.takeaway: Whatever had existence as part of its nature could not fail to exist; since the things around us can fail to exist, existence is not part of their nature.
summary.body:
The things of experience are **contingent**: they exist, but could have failed to. Had the history of life gone differently there would be no lions, and lions may one day go extinct. If a contingent thing's existence were not really distinct from its essence, it would exist simply by being what it is — by its very nature — and so it would be **necessary**, unable even in principle not to exist. Since it is not necessary, its essence and existence must be distinct.

**Objection:** we can explain contingency without any real distinction, just by noting that a lion needs a cause (earlier lions) and has potentialities for nonexistence (being killed, starving, disease). **Reply:** this misses the point. The question is *why* the lion needs, or even *could have*, a cause of its existence, and *why* it has any potential for nonexistence at all. If existence simply belonged to what it is, nothing else would have to supply it, and nothing in the thing could open the door to its ceasing to be. The causal dependence and the fragility are symptoms of the real distinction, not substitutes for it.

Notice the direction of explanation Feser insists on. The critic treats ‘has a cause’ and ‘can perish’ as basic facts that explain contingency. Feser treats them as consequences that themselves need explaining, and the real distinction is what explains them. In the formal statement this second argument appears as steps 4 and 5, and the principle behind it returns in step 28, where the absence of any real distinction in subsistent existence itself is what makes it exist necessarily.
summary.deepDive:
Start with what ‘necessary’ means here. It is not the necessity of a logical truth like ‘all bachelors are unmarried’. It is a feature of a *being*: something that exists necessarily could not, even in principle, fail to exist. Feser's claim is that if existence were part of a thing's essence, the thing would be necessary in exactly this sense.

Why? Compare triangles. Having three sides belongs to the essence of a triangle, which is why a four-sided triangle is impossible. If ‘exists’ belonged to the essence of a lion in the same way, a nonexistent lion would be as impossible as a four-sided triangle, and lions would exist necessarily. But a world without lions is perfectly possible — the history of life might have gone differently, and lions may yet go extinct. So existence is not part of what a lion is.

Now the objection. The critic says contingency is just a matter of having causes and potentialities for nonexistence: a lion needs parents, and it can be killed, starve, or fall ill. Feser's reply turns the tables. Ask *why* the lion needs, or even could have, a cause of its existence. A cause of existence gives existence; you can only receive what you don't have of yourself. And ask why the lion has any **potential** for nonexistence. A potential (in chapter 1's sense) is a real capacity in a thing; a thing that has existence by its very nature would have no capacity to lose it. So the lion's causal dependence and its fragility are *symptoms* of the real distinction. They presuppose it rather than replace it.

A nuance worth noting: contingency is not the same as having a beginning or being short-lived. Even a lion that had always existed and would never die would still be contingent, because its existence would still not follow from its being a lion. This is one reason the Thomistic proof has nothing to do with the age of the universe.

The usual confusion is to hear ‘contingent’ as ‘fragile’ or ‘caused in the past’. The Thomist means something deeper: *not existing by nature*. In the formal argument, this section secures steps 4 and 5, which feed step 11. Its principle — what lacks a real distinction exists necessarily — reappears in step 28, where it shows that subsistent existence itself exists necessarily.

checks.q: In Feser's sense, what would it mean for a lion to exist necessarily?
options: It would live for a very long time
It would have been caused by necessity
It would be needed by the ecosystem
It could not possibly fail to exist, even in principle
checks.explanation: Necessity here is the impossibility of nonexistence — what a thing would have if existence were part of its nature. Longevity or ecological importance are irrelevant.

checks.q: An objector says lions are contingent simply because they have causes and can be killed. What is Feser's reply?
options: That presupposes the real distinction: why would a lion need, or even be able to have, a cause of existence or a potential for nonexistence if existence were part of what it is?
Lions are actually necessary beings
Causes are illusions
Only God is contingent
checks.explanation: Feser says the objection misses the point. Dependence and fragility need explaining, and the real distinction explains them.

checks.q: Which later step of the formal argument reuses the principle behind the contingency argument?
options: Step 14
Step 21
Step 28
Step 35
checks.explanation: Step 28 says that whatever lacks a real distinction between essence and existence exists necessarily — the same principle applied to subsistent existence itself.

summary.heading: Third argument: there could be only one thing whose essence is existence
summary.plain: Suppose something's very nature were simply ‘to exist’. Could there be two of them? To be two, they'd need some difference — but anything added to make the difference would mean each is ‘existing plus something extra’, not just ‘existing’. So there could be only one such thing. Since there are many dogs, stones, and people, none of them is like that.
summary.takeaway: Anything that distinguished one ‘existence itself’ from another would make it ‘existence itself plus something’, so there can be at most one thing whose essence is existence — and since ordinary things come in many, theirs is not.
summary.body:
Suppose something's essence and existence are *not* really distinct. Then they are identical, and that thing's essence just **is existence itself**. Feser argues there could in principle be only one such thing. For two such things, A and B, to be two rather than one, something would have to differentiate them, and there are two standard ways things are differentiated:

- **As species within a genus.** Humans differ from other animals by a **specific difference**, rationality: a human is animality *plus* rationality. If A and B were two ‘species’ of the genus *that which is existence itself*, each would need its own specific difference — but then A would be existence itself *plus* something, and so not simply existence itself. Likewise B.
- **As members of one species.** Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle are all human; Fido, Rover, and Spot are all dogs. Such individuals are differentiated by being associated with different parcels of **matter** (differences like brain wiring or fur color presuppose different matter in which they inhere). Socrates is humanity *plus this matter*, which is why Socrates is not humanity itself. If A and B were differentiated this way, each would be existence itself *plus* a bit of matter — again, not existence itself.

In general, any differentiating feature would make each candidate ‘existence itself PLUS F’, so it would not really be existence itself. Hence anything whose essence is identical with its existence is unique. But stones, trees, dogs, and humans are not unique in this way: there is, or could be, more than one of each kind. So in each of them essence and existence are really distinct.
summary.deepDive:
This is one of the most important arguments in the book, so unpack it step by step. For two things to be *two* rather than one, there must be something by virtue of which they differ — something true of one and not of the other. Call it F. Suppose A has F and B lacks it. Then A is not simply ‘that which is existence itself’; it is existence itself *plus* F. But the whole idea of something whose essence just is existence is that nothing is added to existence. So A would not be what it was supposed to be. And B, to differ from A, would need its own differentiator too.

Feser checks the two standard ways of differentiating. **Species within a genus** differ by a specific difference: a human is animality plus rationality, which is why a human is not ‘animality itself’. **Members of a species** differ by matter: Socrates is humanity plus this bit of matter, which is why Socrates is not ‘humanity itself’. Either way, the differentiator is an *addition*, and additions are exactly what ‘existence itself’ cannot have. Step 6 adds ‘or in some other way’, so the argument covers any differentiator whatever; step 7 says none works.

A helpful analogy (not Feser's): imagine ‘redness itself’ — not a red apple or a red car, but pure redness with nothing else. Red things can be many because they differ in shape, size, and place. But what could make *two* instances of pure redness, with nothing but redness in them? Nothing. The same holds, even more strictly, for existence itself.

Two nuances. First, the argument is **conditional**: *if* there is anything whose essence is existence, it is unique. That is why Feser can use it in Stage 1, before he has shown that such a thing exists, without arguing in a circle. Second, step 10 says there *is, or could be*, more than one member of each kind we experience. This covers a kind reduced to a single member — the last of an endangered species still could have had company.

How it feeds the argument: steps 6–8 prove uniqueness; step 9 applies it; step 10 adds plurality; step 11 concludes, by modus tollens, that ordinary things have a real distinction. The same result is reused at step 24 to show the first cause is unique; it parallels chapter 2's argument for one simple cause.

The usual confusion is to picture ‘existence itself’ as the sum of all existing things, and then ask why there couldn't be several such sums. But existence itself is not a collection; it is that whose nature is simply to be.

checks.q: Why does step 10 say that there ‘is, or could be’ more than one of each kind of thing we experience?
options: To allow for kinds that don't exist
To cover kinds reduced to a single member, which still could have had others
To show that every kind is infinite
To prove that essences are conventional
checks.explanation: Feser notes that even where a class has been reduced to a single member, there could be more than one. That is enough to show the thing is not something whose essence is existence.

checks.q: What is the general principle behind the uniqueness argument?
options: Existence is a genus
Matter is the only possible differentiator
Two things can never be exactly alike
Any differentiating feature would make each candidate ‘existence itself PLUS F’, and so not existence itself
checks.explanation: Feser generalizes from the two standard cases: whatever made one instance differ from another would be an addition, which is incompatible with being simply existence itself.

checks.q: Is it circular to use the uniqueness argument in Stage 1, before God's existence has been shown?
options: No — the argument is conditional: if anything has existence as its essence, it is unique
Yes — it assumes God exists
Yes — it assumes the universe is unique
No — because Stage 1 does not mention uniqueness
checks.explanation: The uniqueness claim holds whether or not such a thing exists, so Stage 1 can use it to show ordinary things are not like that without presupposing God.

summary.heading: No middle ground: existence as a ‘part’ of an essence?
summary.plain: Someone might suggest that existence is just one ingredient in some things' natures, alongside other ingredients. Feser answers that if the whole thing's being real depended on that one ingredient, that ingredient would really be its whole nature. So there are only two options: a thing's nature is something other than existing, or its nature simply is existing.
summary.takeaway: Existence cannot be a mere component of an essence: a component on which the whole thing's existence depends would just be the real essence, so the only options are ‘distinct from existence’ or ‘identical with existence’.
summary.body:
One might try a middle option (Feser cites Peter Weigel's discussion): perhaps something's essence and existence are not distinct, not because its essence *is* existence, but because existence is one *part* of its essence, alongside others. Feser argues this makes no sense. Take the human essence, rational animality, whose parts are rationality and animality. If existence were another component, the existence of the whole human being would depend on that one component. That is as implausible as saying the whole human essence depends on animality alone — and if someone really insisted that the whole depended on animality alone, they would in effect be making animality the true essence. By the same logic, making the whole thing depend on its ‘existence component’ makes existence its true essence. That returns us to a thing whose essence just is existence — exactly what the objector wanted to avoid. So there are only two options: essence really distinct from existence, or essence identical with existence.

Why does this matter? The uniqueness argument (steps 6–11) and the identification of the first cause (steps 19 and 22) both assume a clean dichotomy: a thing's essence is either really distinct from its existence or simply is existence. If a third option were available, some being might escape both the need for a cause and the uniqueness result — a kind of ‘necessary being’ that was still one of many, or still limited. Closing the middle ground is what licenses step 19's ‘either…or’ and Stage 2's claim that the two categories exhaust all possibilities.
summary.deepDive:
The suggestion being rejected is tempting, so state it at its strongest. Maybe there is some being — call it a ‘necessary lion’ — whose essence is lion-ness *plus* existence. Its essence and existence would not be really distinct (existence is right there in the essence), yet its essence would not simply *be* existence (there is lion-ness too). Such a being would need no cause, but it would not fall under the uniqueness argument, and so there might be many such beings.

Feser's reply, drawing on Peter Weigel's discussion, focuses on the relation between a whole and its parts. Consider the human essence, rational animality, whose parts are rationality and animality. If existence were a third part, then the existence of the whole human being would depend on that one part. But no single part of an essence carries the whole in that way. If someone insisted that the whole human essence depended on animality alone, he would in effect be saying that animality is the *real* essence and rationality an extra. By parity, if the whole ‘necessary lion’ depends for its existence on its existence-part, then existence is its real essence — and we are back to something whose essence just is existence, which the uniqueness argument covers.

One way to feel the force of this (a tutor's gloss, not Feser's words): ask of the necessary lion whether its lion-ness is real *because of* the existence-part. If yes, the existence-part is doing all the work, and lion-ness is an addition to existence itself — ‘existence plus F’ again. If no, then lion-ness is real independently of the existence-part, and we must ask where *its* reality comes from — which reintroduces the need for a cause. Either way the middle position dissolves.

How it feeds the argument: this section supports step 9 (if a thing's essence and existence are not distinct, they are identical), step 19 (the cause is either a receiver of existence or existence itself — no third option), and step 25 (everything other than the unique cause has distinct essence and existence).

The usual confusion is to think that a ‘necessary being’ could be an ordinary sort of thing — a very durable particle, say — with ‘necessary existence’ attached as one feature among others. This section explains why that picture does not work. Necessity is not an add-on; the only thing that exists by its nature is the thing whose nature is existence.

checks.q: What does the ‘middle ground’ proposal claim?
options: Essence and existence are distinct in God
Existence is a property like any other
Some thing's existence is one part of its essence, alongside other parts, so its essence is neither distinct from existence nor identical with it
Essences exist separately from things
checks.explanation: The proposal tries to avoid both options: existence would be included in the essence without the essence being existence itself.

checks.q: What comparison does Feser use against the middle-ground proposal?
options: The circle's radius and circumference
Making the whole human essence depend on animality alone would make animality the true essence
The Lego wall
The aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid case
checks.explanation: By parity, if the whole thing depends on its existence-part, existence is the true essence, which returns us to a thing whose essence is existence.

checks.q: Which step's ‘either…or’ depends on closing the middle ground?
options: Step 3
Step 14
Step 36
Step 19
checks.explanation: Step 19 says the cause is either something with distinct essence and existence or subsistent existence itself. That is exhaustive only if there is no middle option.

summary.heading: Real distinction does not mean separability
summary.plain: Saying that what a thing is and that it is are ‘really different’ doesn't mean you could pull them apart. Every circle has both a radius and a circumference, and you never get one without the other, yet they aren't the same thing (one is about 6.28 times the other). In the same way, a real stone's nature and its being real are always together but still different.
summary.takeaway: Really distinct does not mean separable: like a circle's radius and circumference, a thing's essence and existence never occur apart, yet they are not the same.
summary.body:
Saying essence and existence are really distinct does not mean they are two objects that could exist apart, as two dogs, or a dog and its severed leg, can. Some real distinctions involve separability; some don't. Feser, drawing on David Oderberg, points to a circle: *having a radius* and *having a circumference* are really distinct properties (the circumference is 2π times the radius, so they are not the same thing), yet in a circle neither can occur without the other. The same holds for *triangularity* and *trilaterality* (having three angles versus having three sides). Likewise there is no such thing as a stone's essence floating around without its existence, or a free-floating existence without an essence. The two are inseparable in any real thing — and still really distinct.

This clarification heads off a picture that makes the Thomistic view look absurd: a warehouse of essences waiting to be ‘switched on’, or a stock of bare existence waiting to be poured into them. Feser's view is nothing like that. An essence is only ever the essence of some existing thing (or of a merely possible thing, as an object of thought), and existence is only ever the existence of something of a particular kind. The parallel with the circle is exact: having a radius and having a circumference are not two objects glued together but two really different aspects of one thing. The same clarification later disarms Kenny, who assumes that a real distinction must mean one item could exist without the other. And it sets up the next question: if essence and existence are distinct but always found together, what accounts for their being together?
summary.deepDive:
Why are radius and circumference really distinct? Because they stand in a definite relation to one another: the circumference is 2π times the radius. Things that are literally identical do not stand in a ratio of 2π to 1. So having a radius and having a circumference are two different features. Yet you will never find a circle with one and not the other. That shows that the test ‘can one exist without the other?’ is not the test for a real distinction. Separability is *sufficient* for a real distinction (two dogs, a dog and its severed leg), but it is not *necessary*.

Compare the verbal case. ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ do not stand in any relation like 2π; there is only one thing there, described twice. The radius/circumference case is different in kind: two aspects, inseparably united. Feser, quoting David Oderberg, adds triangularity and trilaterality — having three angles versus having three sides. In a triangle you can't have one without the other, yet an angle is not a side.

A further example (not Feser's, but traditional): the convex and concave sides of a curved line. Every curve has both, necessarily and inseparably, yet being convex from one side is not the same as being concave from the other.

Now apply this to essence and existence. The Thomist is not saying that a stone's essence is one object and its existence another, each of which could turn up alone. Feser is emphatic that there is no such thing in mind-independent reality as an essence existing apart from its existence (whatever that would mean) or existence existing apart from an essence. Essence and existence are what chapter 2 called **metaphysical parts** — principles of a thing, not pieces of it.

How this feeds the formal argument: it keeps step 11 coherent (a real distinction without absurd separable ‘essences’), it is essential to the reply to Kenny, and it sets up steps 12–16. If essence and existence are distinct but united, we must ask what unites them; that question drives the argument toward a cause.

The usual confusion is to think the Thomist believes in ghostly unrealized essences — possible lions waiting in limbo for existence. No: a possible lion is not a thing at all; its essence ‘exists’ only as an object of thought. What the real distinction says is that in every actual lion, what it is and that it is are two really different aspects of one reality.

checks.q: Which pair does Feser use as an example of a real but inseparable distinction?
options: A circle's radius and its circumference
A dog and its leg
Two dogs
‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’
checks.explanation: Radius and circumference are really distinct (one is 2π times the other) but inseparable. A dog and its leg, or two dogs, are separable; bachelor/unmarried man is merely verbal.

checks.q: Why is it important that a real distinction need not involve separability?
options: Because it proves that essences exist on their own
Because it shows that existence is a property
Because Kenny's objection assumes that a real distinction requires separability, and the Thomistic view would look absurd if essence and existence had to be separable things
Because it shows that circles are contingent
checks.explanation: The clarification blocks both the caricature of free-floating essences and Kenny's separability assumption.

checks.q: Which of the following does the Thomist NOT claim?
options: In every actual stone, what it is and that it is are distinct aspects
Essence and existence are inseparable in real things
Essence relates to existence as potency to act
A stone's essence could exist on its own, without the stone's existence
checks.explanation: Feser denies that there is any such thing as an essence existing apart from its existence. The distinction is real but not a matter of separable objects.

summary.heading: How do essence and existence come together? Not from within
summary.plain: If a lion's nature doesn't include being real, where does its being real come from? Not from its nature, the way a circle's circumference comes from being a circle. And not from the lion itself, because it would already have to exist in order to do anything, including giving itself existence. So it must come from something outside it.
summary.takeaway: Existence cannot come from a lion's own essence (the way a circle's properties do) or from the lion itself (it would have to exist first), so it must come from outside.
summary.body:
If essence and existence are really distinct, what unites them in an actual thing? Pointing to their inseparability is no answer; it only raises the question of *why* they are inseparable. With a circle, the answer is that radius and circumference both **follow from** the circle's essence: anything with that essence will have those properties. But existence cannot follow from the essence of a lion, pterodactyl, or unicorn in this way — otherwise knowing the essence would reveal the existence, and such things would be necessary rather than things that come to be and pass away. Only in something whose essence *is* existence would existence ‘follow’ from essence, and there can be only one such thing, whereas stones, dogs, and people come in many.

Nor can a thing impart existence to itself, adding it to its own essence. To do anything — including imparting existence — a thing must already exist. A thing whose essence and existence are distinct does not exist until existence is conferred; so to confer it on itself it would have to exist before it exists. Nothing can cause its own existence. Its existence must therefore come from a cause **outside** it.

In the formal statement this reasoning becomes steps 12–16: existence must be imparted either by the thing itself or by something distinct from it (12); imparting existence to oneself would be causing oneself (13); nothing can cause itself (14); so a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence must get its existence from a distinct cause (16). Notice that this is not the slogan ‘everything has a cause’. It applies only to things whose existence does not follow from their essence.
summary.deepDive:
Begin with the idea of something **following from** an essence. Some features belong to a thing simply because of what it is. Given the essence of a circle, having a radius and having a circumference come along automatically; given the essence of a triangle, trilaterality comes along. These features need no further explanation beyond the essence. So one might hope that a lion's existence could come along in the same way, given what a lion is.

It can't, and three lines of reasoning converge here. By the **knowability** argument, if existence followed from the lion's essence, knowing the essence would tell you lions exist, just as knowing a circle's essence tells you it has a circumference. By the **contingency** argument, if existence followed from the essence, lions would exist necessarily, not come and go. By the **uniqueness** argument, the only thing whose existence could follow from its essence is something whose essence *is* existence — and there is only one of those, while lions are many.

Then the second option: could the thing supply existence to itself? Here the key is a simple principle: **to act, a thing must already exist**. Imparting existence is an action. A thing that doesn't yet have existence can't do anything at all, so it can't give itself existence; it would have to exist before it exists. A course illustration: picture a bank account whose opening deposit is supposed to be paid from the account's own balance. There is no balance until the deposit is made, so the deposit must come from outside. Likewise, existence must come from a cause distinct from the thing.

A nuance worth getting right: the conclusion is not that God ‘causes himself’. Some philosophers have called God *causa sui*, self-caused. Feser's reasoning rules out self-causation for anything. The Thomistic God is not self-caused but **uncaused**. He needs no cause because his existence is not something added to a distinct essence (steps 29–30).

How this feeds the argument: this section is steps 12–16, turning the real distinction of step 11 into a need for an **external** cause. It also answers the earlier suggestion that inseparability explains the union of essence and existence: inseparability itself needs explaining, and for lions the explanation can't come from within.

The usual confusion is to think that because a lion is already there, it can ‘keep itself going’, as organisms maintain themselves by eating. But maintenance by eating is an existing organism acting on matter. It presupposes the organism's existence rather than supplying it.

checks.q: Why don't a circle's radius and circumference need an external cause to be united in a circle?
options: Because circles are abstract
Because both follow from the essence of a circle
Because they are separable
Because God creates circles directly
checks.explanation: Anything with the essence of a circle has both features. A lion's existence does not follow from its essence in that way, which is why its union with the essence needs a cause.

checks.q: Why can't a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence give itself existence?
options: Because it lacks enough energy
Because the laws of physics forbid it
Because only God is allowed to cause existence
Because to do anything it must already exist, so it would have to exist before it exists
checks.explanation: Feser's point is metaphysical: acting presupposes existing. Self-imparted existence is incoherent, not merely physically impossible.

checks.q: According to this reasoning, is God self-caused or uncaused?
options: Uncaused: nothing can cause itself, and what is existence itself neither needs nor could have a cause
Self-caused: God gives himself existence
Caused by the universe
Caused by a prior necessary being
checks.explanation: Step 14 rules out self-causation for anything. Subsistent existence itself is uncaused (steps 29–30), not a cause of itself.

summary.heading: Fido, here and now: the need for a conserving cause
summary.plain: This isn't only about how a dog got started. Right now, this second, being real still isn't part of what the dog is, and the dog still can't give itself existence. So something must be keeping it in existence right now — otherwise it would simply vanish.
summary.takeaway: Because Fido's essence never comes to include his existence, something must be imparting existence to him at every instant he exists, not just at his conception.
summary.body:
Everyday experience agrees that dogs and trees have causes — parents, seeds, and so on. But the dependence Feser has in mind is far more radical, because the reasoning applies not only before and when a thing comes into being but at **every moment** it exists. Take a dog, Fido. Right now, Fido's existence is still distinct from his essence, still does not follow from it, and still cannot be supplied by Fido himself. So right now something must be imparting existence to his essence; otherwise he would no more exist now than he did before he was conceived — he would ‘blink out’, be annihilated. And Fido cannot be doing this for himself even for an instant, because acting at an instant presupposes existing at that instant. Self-causation of existence is incoherent whether spread over time or confined to a single moment. So anything whose essence is distinct from its existence needs a cause of its existence **here and now**, not merely at some point in its past.

This is where the Thomistic proof parts company with popular ‘first cause’ arguments. Fido's parents, the sperm and egg, the evolutionary history of dogs — all of these belong to how Fido *came to be*. None of them explains why Fido, with his matter and his powers, is real at this very instant, because none of them is imparting existence to him now (his parents might even be dead). In the formal statement this point is captured by step 17. It is what makes the resulting series of causes hierarchical rather than linear (step 21), and every later step inherits the phrase ‘here and now’.
summary.deepDive:
The hardest idea here is why the dependence is **continuous**. The key is that the real distinction is not a temporary condition, like being hungry, that goes away once a need is met. It belongs to what Fido is. At every moment of his life, ‘dog’ still does not include ‘exists’. So every reason we had for saying Fido's existence must come from outside applies with full force at every moment, not only at the first.

Try a thought experiment. Freeze the universe at a single instant, say noon today. Ask: what accounts for Fido's being real *at noon*? Not something in the past. Past causes explain how Fido got started, but a past event can account for Fido's existing now only if something carries his existence forward — and that carrying-forward is exactly what's in question. Not Fido himself, since he would have to exist at noon in order to do anything at noon. So something must be imparting existence to Fido *at noon*, and likewise at every other instant.

A course analogy: compare a song on the radio with a house. When the builder leaves, the house stays up; its continued standing doesn't depend on the builder's continued activity. When the broadcast stops, the song is gone at once; its presence depends on the transmitter moment by moment. With respect to *existence itself*, the Thomist says, everything is like the song, not the house. (With respect to particular features like shape or position, many things are like the house — that is why everyday experience misses this deeper dependence.)

Feser's own nuances: common sense already agrees that dogs and stones have causes, but the dependence at issue is **more radical** than common sense notices. Without a present cause, Fido would ‘blink out’ — be annihilated. That doesn't mean decaying into dust, which is a change in something that still exists; it means lapsing into nothing. And the incoherence of self-causation holds at a single instant just as much as over a stretch of time.

How this feeds the argument: this section secures steps 17 and 18. It also sets up step 21's claim that the series is hierarchical: C imparts existence to Fido *while* B imparts existence to C.

People often think that things simply persist by default, so that only destruction needs a cause. But that assumes existence belongs to things by nature — precisely what the real distinction denies. Physical laws like inertia describe how existing things behave; they don't explain why there is anything there to behave.

checks.q: What does the Fido example chiefly show?
options: That dogs need parents
That the universe had a beginning
That a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence needs a cause of its existence at every moment it exists
That animals have immaterial souls
checks.explanation: The point is continuous dependence here and now. Parents explain Fido's beginning, and the argument is indifferent to the universe's beginning.

checks.q: Why can't Fido's parents be the cause the argument is looking for?
options: They explain his coming to be, not what imparts existence to him now; they might even have died
Because parents are material
Because Fido has no parents
Because parents are only accidental causes of color
checks.explanation: Generation (a linear cause) differs from conservation. The argument asks what is keeping Fido in existence at this moment.

checks.q: According to Feser, what would happen to Fido without a present cause of his existence?
options: He would gradually decay
He would keep existing by inertia
He would become a different species
He would blink out — be annihilated
checks.explanation: Feser says Fido would ‘blink out’ of existence, no more existent than before his conception. Decay is a change in something that still exists.

summary.heading: The regress and its first member: subsistent existence itself
summary.plain: Whatever keeps the dog in existence either just borrows its own existence too, or else is existence itself. A chain of borrowers passing along existence none of them has on its own can't explain anything, however long it is. So the chain must end in something whose very nature is to exist. Aquinas calls this ‘subsistent existence itself’ and says it is God.
summary.takeaway: A chain of causes that each only pass on existence they are receiving must be grounded in something that gives existence without receiving it — which only subsistent existence itself can do.
summary.body:
Call Fido's present cause of existence C. If C's own essence is distinct from its existence, then C too needs something imparting existence to it right now — call it B; and if B is the same way, it needs A; and so on. This is exactly the **hierarchical causal series** of chapter 1. What makes it hierarchical is not merely that the causes operate simultaneously but that none of them can act on its own: C gives existence to Fido only *insofar as* B is giving existence to C, and B only insofar as A is giving existence to B. As chapter 1 showed, such a series cannot regress infinitely; there must be a cause that is ‘first’ in the sense of *primary* — one that causes without, in the very act of causing, needing to be caused.

Here that means a cause that can impart existence without having to *receive* it. Nothing whose essence is distinct from its existence qualifies, since everything of that sort must receive existence. So the first cause can only be something whose very essence **is** existence — which need not, and indeed could not, derive existence from anything else, since its existence is, as it were, built in. It is not one more existing thing among others but what Aquinas calls **subsistent existence itself**. For Fido to exist at any moment, then, he must be caused to exist — directly or through intermediaries — by subsistent existence itself. And that, Feser says, means he is caused by God.
summary.deepDive:
The central notion is **instrumental** causation, so make it vivid. In chapter 1's example, a hand pushes a stick that pushes a stone. The stick really does move the stone, but only *insofar as* the hand is moving the stick. Its power to move the stone is borrowed at that very moment. Now apply this to existence. C imparts existence to Fido only insofar as B is, right then, imparting existence to C. C's ‘giving’ is really a passing-along of what it is itself receiving.

Why doesn't an infinite chain help? Because adding more instruments never adds a source. A course analogy: arrange mirrors so that each reflects light onto the next. However many mirrors you add — even infinitely many — the room stays dark unless something actually shines. Each mirror only passes on light. The chain needs something that is a source of light, not just a reflector. Feser's own analogy is the stack of IOUs, each backed by another IOU, which never amounts to real money without actual cash somewhere.

Now the crucial step: why must the source be something whose essence *is* existence? ‘First’ here means a cause that causes **without being caused in the very act of causing**. For existence, that means giving existence without receiving it. Anything whose essence is distinct from its existence has to receive existence (steps 12–16). So the first cause cannot be such a thing. And since there is no middle ground (section 4), it must be something whose essence just is existence. Its existence isn't on loan; it is, as Feser puts it, built in.

Two nuances. First, Feser says Fido is caused to exist by subsistent existence itself ‘directly or indirectly’. The argument doesn't deny that there may be real intermediate causes (C, B), nor does it need to identify them. The chain might be long, or subsistent existence itself might sustain Fido directly; either way, the ultimate source is the same. Second, the phrase ‘subsistent existence itself’ comes from Aquinas's *On Being and Essence*, chapter 4. It signals that this cause is not one more existing thing alongside the others.

How this feeds the argument: this section is steps 19–23 — the dichotomy (19), the regress (20), its hierarchical character and need for a first member (21), the identification of that member (22), and the conclusion for Fido and everything we experience (23).

The usual confusion is to picture the first cause as the *earliest* link, like the first domino. That picture belongs to linear series. Here ‘first’ means *primary*: the source on which every other link depends right now.

checks.q: What makes the series of existence-imparting causes hierarchical?
options: The causes are arranged by size
Each member imparts existence only insofar as it is simultaneously receiving existence from a prior member
The causes occurred in a temporal sequence
The causes are all material objects
checks.explanation: Feser says the more fundamental point, beyond simultaneity, is that none of the members can act independently of a prior cause.

checks.q: Why can't the first cause be something whose essence is distinct from its existence?
options: Because such things are too weak
Because such things are always material
Because such things came later in time
Because anything like that must itself receive existence, so it couldn't give existence without receiving it
checks.explanation: The first cause must impart existence without deriving it; anything with really distinct essence and existence derives it (step 16).

checks.q: Does the argument claim that God causes Fido's existence directly, with no intermediaries?
options: Not necessarily — directly or indirectly, through intermediate causes that themselves depend on subsistent existence itself
Yes — intermediate causes are impossible
No — God only started the chain long ago
Yes — Fido's parents play no role at all
checks.explanation: Feser's formulation is ‘directly or indirectly’. Intermediate causes are real but derivative.

terms: De Ente et Essentia (On Being and Essence)

summary.heading: Stage 2: Unique, the cause of all, necessary, uncaused
summary.plain: There can be only one thing whose nature is to exist, and everything else is a ‘borrower’ of existence that depends on it. So that one thing is the source of everything else's existence. It can't fail to exist, and nothing could have caused it, because there's nothing in it that needs to be given existence.
summary.takeaway: Because only one thing can have existence as its essence and the two categories are exhaustive, that one thing is the necessary, uncaused cause of absolutely everything else.
summary.body:
Why call subsistent existence itself God? First, what holds of Fido holds of every thing whose essence is distinct from its existence — stones, trees, lions, human beings, and even immaterial things such as angels or disembodied souls, if there are any. Second, there can in principle be only one thing whose essence is existence. Third, these two categories — things whose essence is distinct from their existence and a thing whose essence is identical with it — **exhaust** the possibilities. So everything other than subsistent existence itself belongs to the first category, and everything in that category depends on it. Therefore subsistent existence itself is **unique** and **the cause of everything other than itself**.

Moreover, since its essence just is existence, it cannot fail to exist: it exists **necessarily**. For the same reason it neither needs nor could receive existence from another: it is the **uncaused** cause of the existence of all other things.

It's worth seeing how little new is assumed here. Uniqueness comes from the argument already given in Stage 1 (step 8). Universal causality comes from uniqueness plus the dichotomy of steps 19 and 25: if only one thing can have existence as its essence, everything else is a receiver of existence and so depends, directly or indirectly, on that one thing (steps 24–27). Necessity and uncausedness come from the very idea of a thing whose essence is existence (steps 28–30). And the reasoning covers immaterial beings too: an angel or a disembodied soul, if there are such things, would lack matter but would still have an essence distinct from its existence, and so would still depend on subsistent existence itself.
summary.deepDive:
Think of Stage 2 as drawing a complete map of reality with only two regions. Region one holds everything whose essence is distinct from its existence: receivers of existence. Region two holds whatever has existence as its essence. The middle-ground argument shows there is no third region, and the uniqueness argument shows region two can hold at most one occupant. Stage 1 has shown it holds exactly one. So everything that exists is either that one thing, or a receiver that depends on it.

Test the map with candidates (a course exercise). A quark? It has a definite nature, can be many, and is contingent: region one. The multiverse? It has a nature (a structure governed by laws), could have been otherwise, and is composed of many things: region one. An angel? Immaterial, but its essence (what kind of spirit it is) is still distinct from its existence: region one, as Feser explicitly says. Zeus as mythology describes him? A bodily, changeable, limited being among other gods: region one. Only subsistent existence itself occupies region two. So only it is uncaused, and everything else depends on it.

Now the two attributes derived here. **Necessity**: since its essence is existence, it cannot fail to exist. This isn't a trick of definition. The argument first showed, starting from Fido, that such a cause must exist (step 23); necessity is a feature of what has been proved (step 28). **Uncausedness**: a cause of existence imparts existence to an essence that lacks it of itself. Subsistent existence itself contains nothing that lacks existence, so there is nothing for a cause to do (steps 29–30). That is why Feser insists God is not an arbitrary exception to a rule. The rule — whatever has distinct essence and existence needs a cause — simply doesn't apply.

A nuance: ‘cause of everything other than itself’ means cause of the *existence* of everything, including the very matter things are made of and their causal powers — not just the arranger of pre-existing stuff. This is creation understood as ongoing conservation, not merely a first event.

How this feeds the argument: steps 24–30.

The usual confusion is to hear ‘cause of everything’ as ‘the thing that started everything off’. The Thomistic claim is present-tense. Subsistent existence itself is the cause of everything *now*, and it would be even if the universe had no beginning.

checks.q: Why are the two categories — distinct essence and existence, and essence identical with existence — exhaustive?
options: Because Aquinas said so
Because every thing is either material or immaterial
Because the ‘middle ground’ of existence as merely part of an essence collapses into essence being existence
Because there are only two kinds of cause
checks.explanation: Feser's rebuttal of the middle-ground proposal is what guarantees there is no third category.

checks.q: Which things does Feser say depend on subsistent existence itself?
options: Only material things
Everything whose essence is distinct from its existence, including immaterial things like angels or souls if there are any
Only living things
Only the universe as a whole
checks.explanation: Feser explicitly extends the reasoning to immaterial beings. Being immaterial doesn't make something existence itself.

checks.q: Why is subsistent existence itself uncaused, rather than an arbitrary exception to a causal rule?
options: Because the rule is only a probability
Because it existed first in time
Because it is too powerful to be caused
Because the need for a cause comes from having an essence distinct from existence, and in it there is no such distinction, so there is nothing for a cause to do
checks.explanation: The causal principle applies only to receivers of existence. God isn't exempted from it; it never applied to him.

summary.heading: Stage 2: Pure actuality and the divine attributes
summary.plain: Aquinas compares a thing's nature to a possibility and its existence to that possibility being made real. So something that just is existence has no unrealized possibilities at all; it is completely ‘actual’. That links this argument to chapter 1: there can be only one completely actual being, so both arguments reach the same God, who must be changeless, timeless, non-physical, all-powerful, good, and all-knowing.
summary.takeaway: Since essence is to existence as potency to act, what just is existence is purely actual — the same unique being as chapter 1's unmoved mover, with all its attributes.
summary.body:
Feser now ties the argument to chapter 1's concepts of **potentiality** and **actuality**. As Aquinas stressed, in a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence, essence relates to existence as **potency to act**. Fido's essence by itself is only a *potential* dog; there is an *actual* dog only when existence is imparted to that essence. So if essence is a kind of potentiality and existence a kind of actuality, then that which simply *is* existence must be **purely actual**. It cannot have a potential for existence waiting to be actualized, for then it would be just one more thing that needs to receive existence.

And chapter 1 showed there can be only one purely actual thing. So the purely actual actualizer of the Aristotelian proof and the subsistent existence itself of the Thomistic proof are **one and the same cause of all things**, reached from different starting points. Chapter 1 also showed that whatever is purely actual must be **immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, and fully good**; and, adding the principle of proportionate causality, that the cause of all things must have **intellect** and **omniscience**. So subsistent existence itself is one, necessary, the uncaused cause of everything else, purely actual, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient — in short, God.

These last steps (31–33) are where the Thomistic proof borrows most heavily from chapter 1, and Feser is explicit that objections to the derivation of the divine attributes are addressed in the later chapter on the divine nature. What matters here is the bridge: once essence and existence are seen as potency and act, this chapter's conclusion and chapter 1's turn out to be the same being described from two angles.
summary.deepDive:
The bridge concept is Aquinas's claim that essence is to existence as **potency** is to **act**. Recall chapter 1: a potency is a real capacity to be some way one is not yet (the ice's capacity to be liquid); act is the realization of that capacity. Now think of Fido's essence *taken by itself*. It is a capacity to be a real dog — a possible dog. Existence realizes that capacity. So every receiver of existence is a composite of potency (its essence) and act (its existence).

Subsistent existence itself has no such composition. Its essence is not a capacity waiting to be realized; it is existence. So it has no potency for existence (step 32). Feser draws the conclusion that it exists ‘in a purely actual way’. One way to see why this rules out *all* potency, not just potency for existence (a tutor's gloss consistent with chapter 1): any unrealized potential would be something that must be actualized by a cause. But subsistent existence itself is uncaused (step 30), and chapter 1 shows that the ultimate source of all actualization must itself be purely actual.

With pure actuality in hand, chapter 1's derivations come along. Here is the short version of each:

- **Immutable**: change is actualizing a potential; no potential, no change.
- **Eternal**: time involves change; the changeless is outside time.
- **Immaterial, incorporeal**: matter is a principle of potentiality.
- **Perfect**: imperfection is unrealized potential; there is none.
- **Omnipotent**: as the source of all actuality it can actualize anything possible.
- **Fully good**: badness is a lack; pure act lacks nothing.
- **Intelligent, omniscient**: by the principle of proportionate causality, what is in an effect must be in its cause. The forms of all things must therefore pre-exist in their cause, and since it is immaterial, they exist there as in an intellect. As cause of all, it knows all.

Finally, **identity**: chapter 1 showed there can be only one purely actual being, since two would need a differentiating potential. So subsistent existence itself and the purely actual actualizer are one and the same.

How this feeds the argument: steps 31–34.

The usual confusion is to hear ‘pure actuality’ as maximal busyness, or to think the attributes are simply stipulated. Each attribute is a consequence of the absence of potency, argued for in chapter 1 and defended further in chapter 6.

checks.q: What relation does Aquinas see between a creature's essence and its existence?
options: Potency to act: the essence is a potential thing that existence actualizes
Cause to effect: the essence causes the existence
Part to whole: existence is one part of the essence
Matter to form
checks.explanation: Fido's essence by itself is only a potential dog; existence makes it actual. The essence doesn't cause the existence (steps 12–16).

checks.q: Why are the purely actual actualizer of chapter 1 and subsistent existence itself the same being?
options: Because both are material
Because both began the universe
Because subsistent existence itself is purely actual, and there can be only one purely actual being
Because Feser defines them as the same
checks.explanation: The identification follows from pure actuality plus chapter 1's uniqueness argument, not from a stipulation.

checks.q: How does Feser arrive at intellect and omniscience?
options: By appeal to religious experience
By adding the principle of proportionate causality to the fact that subsistent existence itself causes all things
By observing design in nature
By the ontological argument
checks.explanation: Feser says that when we factor in proportionate causality, the cause of all things must have intellect and omniscience.

summary.heading: The formal statement
summary.plain: Feser then lays out the whole argument as 36 short steps, so you can check each link. First he shows that what things are and that they are really differ; then that each thing needs a present cause of its existence; then that the chain of such causes must end in existence itself; then that this is one, the cause of everything, and has God's attributes.
summary.takeaway: The 36 steps move from the real distinction (1–11) to present dependence (12–18), to a first cause whose essence is existence (19–23), to its uniqueness and universality (24–27), to its attributes (28–33), and so to God (34–36).
summary.body:
Feser then restates the proof as a 36-step argument (reconstructed in full in the Argument section of this module). Its structure: steps 1–11 establish the real distinction in the things of experience by the three arguments above (knowability, contingency, uniqueness); steps 12–18 show that such things need an existence-imparting cause distinct from themselves at every moment, here and now; steps 19–23 show that the resulting hierarchical series must terminate in something whose essence and existence are identical; steps 24–27 show that this cause is unique and the cause of everything else; steps 28–33 derive necessity, uncausedness, pure actuality, and the attributes of pure actuality; and steps 34–36 conclude that God exists.

Several features of the structure are worth noticing. First, steps 1–11 are over-determined: three independent routes (2–3, 4–5, 6–10) converge on the real distinction, so a critic who rejects one argument must still face the other two. Second, the pivot of the whole proof is steps 12–16, which turn the real distinction into the need for an external cause, together with step 17, which makes that need continuous; the phrase ‘including here and now’ recurs from step 17 on. Third, the uniqueness result of step 8 is used twice: in step 9, to establish the real distinction in ordinary things, and in step 24, to show the first cause is unique and so the cause of all else. Finally, steps 33 and 35 are the only places where the proof leans on material outside the chapter. Step 33 imports chapter 1's derivation of the divine attributes, and step 35 identifies the result with what is meant by ‘God’.
summary.deepDive:
A good way to master a long formal argument is to follow one thing all the way through it. Take a single pebble.

**Steps 1–11.** The pebble has an essence — what a pebble of this mineral is — and existence. Its essence could be fully described in a geology textbook without settling whether this pebble is real (2–3). It is contingent: it formed, and it will erode (4–5). And there are many pebbles, whereas anything whose essence is existence would be unique (6–10). So its essence and existence are really distinct (11).

**Steps 12–18.** The pebble can't get existence from its essence, and it can't give itself existence (12–16). And that is true now, as you hold it (17–18).

**Steps 19–23.** Whatever is giving the pebble existence now is either another receiver of existence or existence itself (19). Receivers need givers (20), and the chain is hierarchical, so it needs a first member (21), which can only be existence itself (22). So the pebble is being kept in existence now, directly or indirectly, by subsistent existence itself (23).

**Steps 24–36.** That cause is unique (24), so everything else is a receiver (25) that depends on it (26–27). It is necessary (28), uncaused (29–30), and purely actual (31–32), with the attributes of pure actuality (33). That is God (34–36).

Now a map of where the objections attack. The Kenny objection, the aspirin objection, and doubts about real essences all target **steps 1–11**. Hume's ‘why a first cause?’ targets **step 21**. The fallacy-of-composition charge misreads **steps 25–27**. ‘What caused God?’ misreads **step 29**. ‘The first cause needn't be God’ targets **steps 33–35**. Knowing this map lets you respond precisely instead of generally.

A nuance on labels: some steps marked as premises are defended elsewhere. Step 21 comes from chapter 1's treatment of hierarchical series; step 33 comes from chapter 1 and is developed in chapter 6. The argument is meant as a **demonstration**, a deductive chain from evident starting points, not a probabilistic inference to the best explanation.

People often think a 36-step argument must be fragile, since ‘any one step could fail’. But much of the length comes from spelling out obvious inferences (15, 16, 18, 30, 36). The substantive premises are few: the real distinction, the impossibility of self-causation, the continuity of dependence, and the impossibility of an infinite hierarchical regress.

checks.q: Which steps turn the real distinction into the need for an external cause of existence?
options: Steps 1–3
Steps 24–27
Steps 31–33
Steps 12–16
checks.explanation: Steps 12–16: existence comes from self or other; not from self, since nothing causes itself; so from a distinct cause.

checks.q: Which objection targets step 21?
options: Kenny's objection
Hume's ‘why need there be a first cause?’
The aspirin objection
Conventionalism about essences
checks.explanation: Step 21 claims the hierarchical series must have a first member, which is exactly what Hume's objection questions. Kenny, aspirin, and conventionalism attack steps 1–11.

checks.q: Which step imports chapter 1's derivation of the divine attributes?
options: Step 11
Step 17
Step 33
Step 36
checks.explanation: Step 33 asserts that whatever is purely actual must be immutable, eternal, immaterial, and so on — established in chapter 1.

summary.heading: Objections shared with the Aristotelian proof
summary.plain: Some objections were already answered in chapter 1. The argument doesn't claim the universe had a beginning — it asks what keeps things in existence now, even if the universe is eternal. And it never claims ‘everything has a cause’, only that things whose nature doesn't include existence need a cause. So ‘What caused God?’ misses the point: God's nature is existence.
summary.takeaway: The Thomistic proof doesn't rely on a beginning of the universe or on ‘everything has a cause’, so the most common retorts simply miss it.
summary.body:
Several objections are the same as those already met in chapter 1. It is no good to say glibly that a first cause need not be *divine*: Stage 2 gives reasons why it must be (and the attributes will be defended further in the later chapters on God's nature). Nor does the argument assume the universe had a **beginning**: it traces Fido's existence not back into the past but down to what sustains it *here and now*. Even an eternal universe or eternal multiverse would leave the proof untouched.

Nor does the argument rest on the premise that **‘everything has a cause’**, so ‘What caused God?’ misfires. The actual premise is that whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence needs a cause. God is not an arbitrary exception to a general rule; in him there is no such distinction, so he not only needs no cause but could not have one. This is not a recent evasion — it was the Thomistic tradition's point from the start. Finally, appeals to Hume or to quantum mechanics against the causal principle fare no better here than they did against the Aristotelian proof in chapter 1.

Feser's handling of these objections shows a pattern that recurs throughout the book: many standard criticisms of ‘first cause’ arguments attack a version of the argument that its classical defenders never gave. The kalām argument, which does appeal to a beginning of the universe, is a respectable argument in its own right, but it is not this one. And the ‘everything has a cause’ premise is, as chapter 7 shows at length, a straw man that virtually no major defender of cosmological arguments has ever used.
summary.deepDive:
Take the ‘What caused God?’ retort slowly, because it is the one you will hear most. Its logic runs: your premise is that everything has a cause; God is something; so God has a cause; so either there's a regress or you're special-pleading. But the Thomistic premise is not ‘everything has a cause’. It is: **whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence** needs a cause of its existence. Subsistent existence itself has no such distinction. So the premise does not apply to it — not because it is exempted, but because it lacks the very feature that creates the need.

A course analogy shows why this isn't special pleading. Suppose a rule says: every rectangle that is not a square has two sides longer than the others. Nobody would accuse you of special pleading for saying squares don't. The rule was stated for a specific class, and squares aren't in it. Likewise, ‘needs a cause of existence’ was stated for receivers of existence, and God isn't one. Feser adds that this was the Thomistic position from the beginning, not an evasion invented to escape the retort.

Next, the ‘beginning of the universe’ worry. The argument traces Fido's existence not *backward* to a first moment but *downward* to what is sustaining him now.
