If the universe or a multiverse had always existed, every thing in it would still, at every moment, have an essence distinct from its existence, and so would still need existence imparted. (Historically, Aquinas himself held that reason alone cannot prove the world had a beginning; he accepted that on faith.)

Third, ‘a first cause needn't be divine’. Feser says it is no good to allege this glibly. Stage 2 has given reasons — uniqueness, necessity, pure actuality — why the first cause must have the divine attributes, and the attributes get a full defense in chapter 6.

Finally, Hume's conceivability argument and quantum mechanics. Feser simply refers back to chapter 1: conceiving of something without also conceiving its cause is not conceiving it as uncaused, and indeterministic causation is still causation.

How this connects to the formal argument: the here-and-now character is steps 17–18; uncausedness is steps 29–30; divinity is steps 33–35.

The usual confusion is to lump all ‘first cause’ arguments together with the kalām argument and the ‘everything has a cause’ caricature. Learning to separate them is half the work of defending the Thomistic proof.

checks.q: Would the Thomistic proof be refuted if the universe turned out to have always existed?
options: No — it concerns what imparts existence to things here and now, which an eternal universe would still need
Yes — it depends on a first moment of time
Yes — Feser concedes this
No — because the universe certainly had a beginning
checks.explanation: Feser says even an eternal universe or multiverse would not change the outcome in the slightest. Option D misses that the argument doesn't depend on the question either way.

checks.q: What is the argument's actual causal premise?
options: Everything has a cause
Everything that begins to exist has a cause
Whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence requires a cause
Only material things have causes
checks.explanation: Option B is the kalām premise; option A is the straw man. The Thomistic premise concerns the real distinction.

checks.q: What does Feser say about the charge that a first cause need not be divine?
options: He concedes that it might be impersonal
He says the question is unanswerable
He appeals to faith
He says it is no good to allege this glibly: Stage 2 gives reasons it must be divine, and the attributes are defended further in a later chapter
checks.explanation: Feser points to Stage 2's derivation (uniqueness, necessity, pure actuality, attributes) and to the later chapter on the divine nature.

summary.heading: Why need there be a first cause? (Hume)
summary.plain: The philosopher David Hume asked: if every link in a chain is explained by the one before, why do we need a first link? Feser agrees for chains stretching back in time, like parents and grandparents. But the chain he means is of things keeping one another in existence right now, each only passing on what it receives. That's like a stack of IOUs: however tall the stack, you get no real money unless something is backed by cash.
summary.takeaway: An infinite series of generators may need no first member, but an infinite series of conservers, each only passing on borrowed existence, explains nothing without a source that does not borrow.
summary.body:
Hume raised a separate challenge: if each member of a causal series is explained by an earlier member, why posit a first cause? Even an infinite series would leave no individual member unexplained. Feser grants this for **linear** series, as in chapter 1. But the Thomistic proof concerns a **hierarchical** series, in which every cause other than the first is merely **instrumental**, with no causal power of its own. Making such a series infinite changes nothing: if every member is causally inert of itself, something outside the series must supply the power to all of them — a cause ‘first’ not by standing at the head of a line but because every member depends on it.

The point is clearer still given the role of essence and existence. The series Hume rightly allows to be infinite is one of things *generated in time* from pre-existing materials: Fido from his parents, they from theirs, and so on. The Thomistic question is instead what **conserves** Fido — and his parents, and the very matter and powers involved — in existence at each moment rather than letting them lapse into nothing. Even if the line of dogs ran back forever, each dog would still need conserving at every moment, and so would any conserving cause whose essence is distinct from its existence. An infinite chain of such causes can no more produce a real dog than an infinite chain of IOUs can produce real money; the IOUs must be backed by actual cash somewhere, and the chain of existence-givers must terminate in something that does not need existence given to it.

Feser adds Barry Miller's analysis of the logical form of such explanations: A is caused to G by B *insofar as* B is caused to G by C *insofar as*… However many ‘insofar as’ clauses you add, the sentence can only be completed by naming a first member, M. With Fido as A and ‘exist’ as G, we are forced to stop with some M — and the only non-arbitrary place to stop is with something that is subsistent existence itself, since any other M would need a cause just as much as Fido does.
summary.deepDive:
Hume's objection has real force against some arguments, so understand why it fails here. Hume says: if A is explained by B, B by C, and so on forever, then every member has its explanation, so nothing is left over to require a first cause. The key question is **what kind of explanation** each member provides.

In a **linear** series of generation, the explanation is complete once given. Fido's parents produced him; once Fido exists, his parents' role in his origin is finished, and it doesn't matter whether they still exist. Each dog's origin is fully accounted for by its parents. Feser agrees with Hume that such a series could in principle regress forever.

In a **hierarchical** series of conservation, the explanation is only **conditional**. B accounts for C's existing now only *on the condition that* B itself is now being given existence. Every explanation in the chain is, so to speak, issued on credit, and an infinite series of conditional explanations never discharges the condition. That is the logical content of Feser's IOU analogy. Each IOU ‘explains’ the value of the one it backs only if it is itself backed; if nothing is ever actual money, none of them is worth anything.

Feser adds **Barry Miller's** point about logical form. Write the explanation out: ‘Fido is being caused to exist by B, insofar as B is being caused to exist by C, insofar as C is being caused to exist by…’. Every ‘insofar as’ opens a clause that must be closed. The sentence is incomplete — it has not yet said what explains Fido — until you name a first member M that is not itself caused to exist. And the only non-arbitrary M is something whose essence is existence, because any other M would need a cause as much as Fido does.

A subtle nuance: Feser even grants, for the sake of argument, an infinite hierarchical series. It would still require a cause **outside** the series imparting power to all its members — ‘first’ not as the head of the line, but as that on which every member depends. And the conserving question covers not only Fido and his parents but the very matter they're made of and their causal powers.

How this feeds the argument: it defends step 21 and supports step 22.

People often think this reply requires denying an infinite past. It doesn't. Aquinas and Feser can grant an infinite line of ancestors and still insist that each ancestor, at each moment it existed, needed existence imparted.

checks.q: About which kind of series does Feser agree with Hume that no first member is needed?
options: Hierarchical series of conservation
Linear series of things generated in time
Series of instrumental causes
Any series whatever
checks.explanation: Feser grants Hume's point for linear series like Fido's ancestry, but not for hierarchical ones.

checks.q: What is Barry Miller's point?
options: Infinite series are mathematically impossible
Hume misread Aquinas
Every cause must precede its effect in time
An explanation of the form ‘A is caused to G by B insofar as B is caused to G by C insofar as…’ can only be completed by naming a first member
checks.explanation: Miller analyzes the logical form of explanations by derived causality: the sentence cannot be completed without a term naming a first member.

checks.q: Suppose, for argument's sake, a hierarchical series were infinite. What does Feser say?
options: There would still need to be a cause outside the series imparting causal power to all its members
Then no first cause would be needed
Then the universe would have no beginning
Then each member would cause itself
checks.explanation: Since every member is purely instrumental, infinite extension changes nothing; a cause ‘first’ in the sense of that on which all depend is still required.

summary.heading: The fallacy of composition
summary.plain: Critics say it's a mistake to reason from ‘each part needs a cause’ to ‘the whole universe needs a cause’, just as a wall of one-pound bricks doesn't weigh one pound. Feser replies that such reasoning sometimes works (a wall of red Lego bricks is red), and anyway his argument doesn't need it: one single dog is enough to get to God.
summary.takeaway: The proof never argues from parts to whole — one dog is enough — and in any case some part-to-whole inferences, like the one about essence and existence, are valid.
summary.body:
Critics often charge first-cause arguments with the **fallacy of composition**: if each brick in a wall weighs a pound, the wall doesn't weigh a pound; so even if each thing in the universe needs a cause, the universe as a whole may not. Feser replies in two ways. First, part-to-whole reasoning is not always fallacious: if every brick in a Lego wall is red, the wall is red. Since what shows a material thing needs a cause is its real distinction between essence and existence, and the space-time universe is made of such things and has its own essence distinct from its existence, it is reasonable to conclude that it needs a cause too. Second, and more importantly, the Thomistic proof does not reason from parts to whole at all. It can start from any single thing — Fido, one stone, one tree — whose essence is distinct from its existence. The conclusion that subsistent existence itself causes the whole universe is a *consequence* of the argument (via uniqueness), not a premise.

The deeper lesson is about the argument's direction. Cosmological arguments are often pictured as starting with ‘the universe’ and asking for its cause. The Thomistic proof starts small — one dog, one stone — and asks what is imparting existence to that one thing now. Only after establishing a unique cause whose essence is existence does it follow, via steps 24–27, that everything else, and so the universe as a whole, depends on it. A critic who wants to resist the conclusion therefore has to deny something about the single dog, not complain about an illicit leap from parts to whole.
summary.deepDive:
When does part-to-whole reasoning work, and when does it fail? Compare weight and color. Weight is **summative**: a whole's weight is the *sum* of its parts' weights, so the whole doesn't have the same weight as each part. Color, for a wall built entirely of red bricks, is **homogeneous**: the whole has the very property each part has. So the question is never ‘is this a part-to-whole inference?’ but ‘is this property one that transfers?’

Which kind is ‘having an essence distinct from one's existence’? Feser argues it transfers: a whole made of things that are receivers of existence is itself a receiver of existence. But he goes further. The space-time universe **itself** has an essence distinct from its existence — not only because of its parts. A course example makes this concrete. Cosmologists routinely describe model universes with different constants, dimensions, or laws. Knowing everything about such a model does not tell you whether that universe exists; you would have to find out. The actual universe is no different: its nature, however fully described, doesn't include its existence. So the universe satisfies the conditions of the argument directly.

Now Feser's more important reply. The proof never needs any premise about the universe as a whole. Its first premise concerns ‘the things we know from experience’, taken one by one. Pick one: Fido. Steps 11–23 show that Fido, right now, is being given existence, directly or indirectly, by subsistent existence itself. The claim that subsistent existence itself causes *everything* — and so the universe — arrives only at step 27, and it arrives by way of **uniqueness**: since only one thing can have existence as its essence, everything else is a receiver and so depends on it. That's a consequence, not a premise.

How this feeds the argument: it clarifies steps 24–27 and shows why the proof is not vulnerable at step 1.

People often think every cosmological argument must say ‘each thing has a cause, therefore the universe has a cause’. Some popular versions do; the Thomistic proof doesn't. If a critic presses the composition charge, invite him to pick any single thing he likes and run the argument on it alone.

checks.q: Which is Feser's example of a valid part-to-whole inference?
options: A wall of one-pound bricks weighs one pound
Every citizen has a mother, so the human race has a mother
A wall built entirely of red Lego bricks is red
Each part of a machine is light, so the machine is light
checks.explanation: Color transfers from parts to whole in this case; weight does not. Option B is Russell's famous counterexample, not Feser's.

checks.q: Why is Feser's second reply more important than his first?
options: Because the proof doesn't reason from parts to whole at all: it can start from a single thing, and the claim about the universe is a consequence
Because the first reply is invalid
Because the universe has no parts
Because Hume accepted the second reply
checks.explanation: The first reply defends part-to-whole reasoning; the second shows the proof never relies on it.

checks.q: Cosmologists can fully describe model universes that may not exist. What does this suggest for the Thomistic proof?
options: That the universe is necessary
That essences are conventional
That cosmology refutes the proof
That the universe's essence can be known without knowing whether it exists, so the universe too has an essence distinct from its existence
checks.explanation: This parallels the lion/unicorn test at cosmic scale. Feser says the universe has an essence distinct from its existence.

summary.heading: Kenny's objection: two senses of ‘existence’
summary.plain: The philosopher Anthony Kenny argues that ‘existence’ has two meanings, and that on neither meaning can God's nature be existence while a dog's is not. Feser, drawing on other philosophers, replies that Kenny wrongly assumes that ‘really different’ means ‘separable’, and too quickly assumes his two meanings are the only ones. When we say ‘cats exist’, we can still ask what makes that true — and that is what the Thomist means by existence.
summary.takeaway: Kenny's dilemma assumes that real distinction means separability and that existence can only mean instantiation or ‘going on being what one is’; the Thomist rejects both assumptions and asks what makes a concept instantiated in the first place.
summary.body:
Anthony Kenny has attacked the real distinction by separating two notions of existence. **Specific existence** is what modern logic's existential quantifier expresses: ‘there is an x such that x is F.’ It concerns whether a *kind* or *concept* has instances, so it is a second-order predicate of concepts (the view associated with Frege). **Individual existence** is what the Great Pyramid still has and the Library of Alexandria lost when it was destroyed — something true of an individual (corresponding to what Frege called *Wirklichkeit*).

Kenny argues the Thomist fails on either reading. On specific existence, the only intelligible sense of ‘essence is distinct from existence’ is that we can know what a unicorn is without knowing whether there is any; but we can equally know what God is without knowing whether there is any God — so God is no different — and saying God's essence *is* specific existence would amount to the nonsense ‘God's essence is *there is an x such that…*’. On individual existence, for Fido to exist is just for Fido to go on being what he is, a dog; so if God's essence and existence are identical in the sense that God, if he exists, goes on being God, then essence and existence are identical in Fido and everything else too.

Feser, following Gyula Klima, replies. **First**, Kenny assumes that a real distinction requires that we could have one item without the other — that is, separability. But as the circle example showed, real distinction does not entail separability, and assuming otherwise begs the question. Fido's being what he is need not be identical to his individual existence even if you can't have one without the other. **Second**, and more deeply, Kenny assumes his two notions are the only respectable ones. The usual argument for that is Fregean: if existence were a first-level predicate of objects, ‘Martians do not exist’ would be self-contradictory, since it would seem to say that there *are* Martians who lack existence. But John Knasas argues this follows only if, in grasping the concept *Martian*, we already grasp it as applying to something existing. In fact we grasp the subjects of existential statements in an **existence-neutral** way; ‘Martians do not exist’ says that Martians, existentially neutral in themselves, are not in fact real. When the mind grasps an essence, it grasps it as distinct from its existence or nonexistence. (Feser notes that for the Thomist existence is not a property or accident either, since a thing must exist before it can have properties.) **Third**, specific existence leaves something out: when ‘cats exist’ is analyzed as ‘something falls under the concept *cat*’, we can still ask what *makes* it the case that something falls under it. That further fact — the act of existence that actualizes an essence which is otherwise merely potential — is precisely what the Thomist means.
summary.deepDive:
Start with the puzzle that motivates the Fregean view. Consider ‘Martians do not exist’. If ‘exist’ were an ordinary predicate applied to objects, like ‘are green’, the sentence would seem to be about some objects — Martians — and to deny that they have existence. But if there are objects there to be talked about, they exist. So the sentence would contradict itself. Frege's solution: ‘exists’ is not said of objects but of **concepts**. ‘Martians do not exist’ says that the concept *Martian* has no instances. That is ‘specific existence’, expressed by the existential quantifier.

Kenny then argues the Thomist is stuck. On this reading, God's essence and existence are as distinct as a unicorn's, since we can grasp the concept *God* without knowing if it has instances. And to say God's essence is ‘there is an x such that…’ is gibberish. If instead we use ‘individual existence’ — what the Great Pyramid still has and the Library of Alexandria lost — then existing is just going on being what you are, and that is as true of Fido as of God.

Now the replies. **First**, Kenny assumes that a real distinction means you can have one without the other. We've seen that it doesn't (radius and circumference). So Fido's being a dog need not be identical to his individual existence even though the two never come apart.

**Second**, Knasas defuses the Martian puzzle. The contradiction arises only if, in grasping ‘Martians’, we already grasp them *as existing*. But we don't. We grasp the subject in an **existence-neutral** way. Worked example: ‘The dodo is extinct.’ While understanding that sentence, you think of dodos neither as existing nor as nonexisting; the sentence then tells you which. So existence can be predicated of things without contradiction.

**Third**, the grounding question. Grant that ‘cats exist’ means that something falls under the concept *cat*. Why does something fall under it? Not because of anything in the concept, but because of how things are: a real cat is there. The quantifier *records* that fact; the Thomistic act of existence is an account of what the fact *is* — the actualizing of an essence that is otherwise merely potential.

A nuance from Feser's footnote: the Thomist does not treat existence as a property or accident either, since a thing must exist to have properties. Existence fits neither Frege's scheme nor the property scheme, and that shows the limits of those schemes.

How this feeds the argument: it defends steps 1–11.

People often assume the Thomist must hold that existence is a property like greenness. He doesn't — and seeing that dissolves much of Kenny's force.

checks.q: Which example does Kenny use for ‘individual existence’?
options: Unicorns and lions
The Great Pyramid still exists but the Library of Alexandria does not
Martians do not exist
Fido and Rover
checks.explanation: Individual existence is what the Pyramid still has and the Library lost. Martians feature in the Fregean argument about negative existentials.

checks.q: What does Klima identify as the first problem in Kenny's reasoning?
options: Kenny misreads Frege
Kenny ignores quantum mechanics
Kenny confuses genus and species
Kenny assumes a real distinction requires separability, which begs the question against the Thomist
checks.explanation: Kenny writes as if a real distinction means we can have one without the other; the radius/circumference case shows otherwise.

checks.q: What does ‘specific existence’ leave unexplained, according to Knasas and others?
options: What makes it the case that something falls under a given concept
Why concepts have definitions
Why logic is valid
Why unicorns are fictional
checks.explanation: The quantifier says that something falls under a concept; the further question of what makes it so is what the Thomist's act of existence addresses.

summary.heading: A real distinction or merely a conceptual one?
summary.plain: A critic says: you can know about aspirin without knowing it's acetylsalicylic acid, even though they're the same stuff; so knowing a lion without knowing it exists proves nothing. The reply: if you knew everything about aspirin's chemistry, you would know it's acetylsalicylic acid. But knowing everything about what a lion is would never tell you that lions exist — you'd still have to look.
summary.takeaway: The aspirin case fails as a parallel because fully grasping aspirin's essence would reveal that it is acetylsalicylic acid, whereas no grasp of a lion's essence, however complete, reveals that lions exist.
summary.body:
A critic might say the first argument for the real distinction is invalid, because the ‘substitutivity of identicals’ fails in intentional contexts (contexts of knowing, believing, and so on). Aspirin *is* acetylsalicylic acid, yet I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing that acetylsalicylic acid does. The *concepts* differ though the *thing* is one. Likewise, the critic says, I can know what a lion is without knowing whether it exists; that shows only that the *concept* of a lion differs from the *concept* of its existence, not that there are two distinct aspects in reality.

Klima replies that the lesson depends on whether the concepts are **logically independent**. The concept of aspirin is logically independent of *being currently less popular than acetaminophen*, so knowing one without the other is unsurprising. If I have only a vague idea of aspirin (a chemical sold for pain), I can fail to know it is acetylsalicylic acid; but with *complete* knowledge of aspirin's chemical essence I could not fail to know it — the fully grasped concept is not independent of the chemical one. Now if a lion's essence really were identical to its existence, a clear and complete knowledge of the essence would bring knowledge of the existence. But no complete knowledge of the essence of a lion, stone, or tree would tell you that it exists.

Is that begging the question? No — a circularity charge is answered when there is independent reason for the premise. Knowing the essence of a kind, I know *a priori* what attributes any member that exists, has existed, will exist, or could exist would have; but whether any member *does* exist I can know only *a posteriori*, through experience. That gives reason to think knowledge of essence doesn't entail knowledge of existence, whether or not I have ever considered the identity question. The earlier point supports this too: judging that aspirin is *not* acetylsalicylic acid misconceives aspirin, but judging that aspirin does not *exist* is merely a false judgment, not a misconception of what aspirin is.
summary.deepDive:
First, feel the objection's force. The principle that identical things can be swapped in any sentence without changing its truth — the **substitutivity of identicals** — fails in sentences about knowing and believing. A classic example (not in the book): Lois Lane knows Superman can fly but doesn't know Clark Kent can, though they are one man. So ‘I can know A without knowing B’ never, on its own, proves that A and B are distinct. The critic says Feser's first argument for the real distinction makes exactly this leap.

Klima's reply sharpens the question. **Why** does substitution fail in a given case? Sometimes because the concepts are **logically independent**: fully understanding aspirin tells you nothing about its current popularity compared with acetaminophen. Sometimes because the concept is **incomplete**: someone who knows only that aspirin is ‘a chemical sold for pain’ may not know it's acetylsalicylic acid. But with complete chemical knowledge the gap closes; the fully grasped concept of aspirin includes its identity with acetylsalicylic acid.

Now apply this test to lions. If a lion's essence were identical with its existence, the case would be like the second kind: complete knowledge of the essence would close the gap. But it never does. However completely you understand what a lion — or a stone, or a tree — is, you still have to look at the world to learn whether any exist.

The critic's rejoinder: ‘You're just assuming complete knowledge wouldn't reveal existence — that begs the question.’ Klima answers with independent evidence. When you know the essence of a kind, you know **a priori** what any member that does, did, will, or could exist must be like. Worked example: knowing what water is (H2O), you know in advance that any water, anywhere, ever, would be made of hydrogen and oxygen. But whether there *is* water on a given exoplanet you can only learn **a posteriori**, by observation. This pattern holds whether or not you've ever wondered about essence and existence. Feser adds the misconception test once more: judging that aspirin is not acetylsalicylic acid misconceives aspirin, but judging that aspirin doesn't exist doesn't.

How this feeds the argument: it defends steps 2–3 against the charge of invalidity, and so supports step 11.

People often read the knowability argument as a simple leap from ignorance to distinctness. The real argument concerns what even *complete* knowledge of an essence would contain — and that is exactly what the aspirin objection fails to touch.

checks.q: Which logical principle does the critic say breaks down in the knowability argument?
options: The law of non-contradiction
The principle of sufficient reason
The substitutivity of identicals, which fails in intentional contexts like knowing
Modus tollens
checks.explanation: The critic points out that one can know something about aspirin without knowing it about acetylsalicylic acid, though they are identical.

checks.q: What is the key notion in Klima's reply?
options: Whether the concepts involved are logically independent when fully grasped
Whether the substances are natural kinds
Whether aspirin is popular
Whether the concepts are expressed in Latin
checks.explanation: Fully grasped, aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid are not logically independent concepts; a lion's essence and its existence are.

checks.q: How does Klima rebut the charge that the reply begs the question?
options: By appealing to Aquinas's authority
By noting that knowing an essence gives a priori knowledge of what any member of the kind would be like, while whether any exists is known only a posteriori
By denying that aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid
By conceding the point
checks.explanation: This a priori / a posteriori pattern is independent evidence that knowledge of essence doesn't include knowledge of existence.

summary.heading: Do things really have essences?
summary.plain: Some critics deny that things have real natures at all, saying our categories are just human conventions. Feser admits this is true of man-made things like can openers, but argues that natural things — copper, oaks, polar bears — clearly have real natures that science discovers. And denying that anything has a real nature undermines itself, since it would have to apply to our own minds too.
summary.takeaway: The proof needs only some real, mind-independent essences, and these are guaranteed by the unity and lawfulness of nature, by science's own practice and results, and by the incoherence of denying that the mind itself has one.
summary.body:
Other critics target the essence side. For the Thomist, a thing's essence is its nature, that by which it is what it is, grasped when we identify its genus and specific difference. Some essences are clearly partly conventional: what counts as a carburetor or a can opener depends on our purposes. **Essentialism** is the thesis that at least some things, especially natural substances, have real, mind-independent essences. (Feser notes this is not the rationalist ‘essentialism’ Étienne Gilson criticized, which tried to read reality off abstract essences; Aquinas was an essentialist in Feser's sense and an ‘existentialist’ in Gilson's.)

Can essentialism be proved? Feser offers several considerations:

- **Aristotle's point** (*Physics* book 2): trying to prove that things have natures is absurd, not because it's doubtful but because it is more evident than any argument for or against it; only dubious philosophical assumptions make it seem doubtful.
- **Unity among things:** these oaks, these polar bears, these copper samples each share causal powers and properties exactly as we'd expect if they shared a real nature — a miracle if their grouping were mere convention.
- **Unity within things:** each oak or polar bear behaves uniformly and predictably over time, persists through superficial change, and has integrated parts — again what real natures would predict. That essences are sometimes hard to discover does not show they aren't there; no serious essentialist thinks natures can be read off from the armchair.
- **Scientific practice:** ‘new essentialist’ philosophers of science hold that science seeks the essential powers of things. Nancy Cartwright notes that physics studies idealized, interference-free conditions (frictionless surfaces, bodies free of other forces) and often takes a few contrived experiments — even one — to settle a law, which is just how one would look for natures.
- **Scientific results:** Brian Ellis argues that laws of nature require essences and that chemistry reveals discrete natural kinds of substance, each with its own properties, discovered rather than invented (Ellis himself does not extend this to biological kinds, though other essentialists do).
- **Incoherence of conventionalism** (Crawford Elder): if all essences are mind-dependent, so is the essence of the mind itself; but what depends on the mind presupposes the mind, so the mind would be both prior and posterior to itself. So at least one real essence — ours — cannot be denied. And since the conventionalist's arguments would apply to us as much as to anything, and we know they fail for us, why trust them elsewhere?

Finally, the proof needs only *some* real essences. Even if ‘dog’ were a conventional label for particles arranged a certain way, the particles and the minds applying the label would have non-conventional essences distinct from their existence — and the Thomistic reasoning goes through for them. Feser concludes that all the objections fail, leaving a fourth proof of God's existence.
summary.deepDive:
The most philosophically striking argument here is Crawford Elder's, so walk through it carefully. The conventionalist says that a thing's essence — what makes it what it is — depends on our minds: our ways of thinking, our linguistic habits. Apply this consistently to everything, including the mind itself. Then what makes the mind a mind depends on the mind's ways of thinking. But dependence brings priority. Whatever depends on the mind presupposes the mind; the mind must already be there, being what it is, for anything to depend on it. So the mind would have to be **prior** to its own essence (as the thing doing the classifying) and **posterior** to it (as a thing whose nature is produced by classifying). Nothing can be prior to itself. So at least one real, non-conventional essence — the essence of our own minds — cannot coherently be denied. Feser adds a supplement: the arguments for conventionalism would apply to us as much as to anything, and we know they fail for us, so why trust them elsewhere?

The other considerations are more everyday. **Unity among things**: every sample of copper conducts electricity, melts at the same temperature, and reacts in the same ways. If ‘copper’ were just a human grouping, this agreement would be a coincidence on a miraculous scale. **Unity within things**: an oak keeps growing as an oak, repairs itself, and has parts working together, through countless changes in size and shape. **Science's practice** (Cartwright): physicists isolate things under idealized, contrived conditions and often take one careful experiment to settle a law for all things of that kind. That makes sense only if they're uncovering universal natures. **Science's results** (Ellis): the periodic table isn't a convenient slicing of a continuum; chemical kinds are discrete and discovered.

Nuances Feser adds: artifacts like carburetors and can openers do have conventional essences. Discovering essences is often hard — no serious essentialist thinks it's done from the armchair. And Feser's ‘essentialism’ is not the rationalism Gilson criticized.

The decisive final point: the proof needs only **some** real essences. Suppose ‘dog’ were conventional, a label for particles arranged a certain way. The particles would still have real natures, and so would the mind doing the labeling, and each of those natures would be really distinct from its existence. The argument runs on them.

How this feeds the argument: it secures step 1's claim that things have essences to distinguish from their existence.

People often think hard cases of classification (where exactly one species ends and another begins) refute essentialism. But difficulty in *discovering* a boundary isn't evidence that there are no real natures at all.

checks.q: Which essences does Feser concede are conventional?
options: Chemical kinds
Biological species
The human mind
Artifacts like carburetors and can openers
checks.explanation: What makes something a can opener is fixed by our purposes. Feser defends real essences for natural substances.

checks.q: What is Crawford Elder's argument against thoroughgoing conventionalism?
options: Science discovers natural kinds
Things behave uniformly
If all essences were mind-dependent, the mind's own essence would be too, making the mind prior and posterior to itself
Aristotle said essences are obvious
checks.explanation: Mind-dependence implies the mind's priority; a mind whose essence depends on itself would be prior to itself — incoherent.

checks.q: Why would the proof survive even if the essence of a dog were conventional?
options: Because the particles and the mind applying the label would still have real essences distinct from their existence
Because dogs are necessary beings
Because conventions are real essences
Because the proof is only about human beings
checks.explanation: Feser says the proof needs only some real essences; the argument runs on particles and minds just as well as on dogs.

argument.name: The Thomistic Proof (from the real distinction between essence and existence)
argument.overview:
Feser's formal statement has 36 steps, which fall into six phases.

1. **Steps 1–11: the real distinction.** Three independent lines of argument show that, in the things we experience, essence and existence are really (not just conceptually) distinct: (a) we can know a thing's essence without knowing whether it exists (2–3); (b) the things of experience are contingent, not necessary (4–5); (c) there could be at most one thing whose essence is its existence, yet the things of experience come, or could come, in many (6–10).
2. **Steps 12–18: dependence here and now.** A thing with really distinct essence and existence cannot give itself existence, so it must receive it from a distinct cause — and since the distinction persists at every moment, it must receive it at every moment, including now.
3. **Steps 19–23: the first cause.** The cause is either another such thing or something whose essence is existence. A series of the former is hierarchical, so it cannot regress infinitely; its first member must be subsistent existence itself.
4. **Steps 24–27: uniqueness and universality.** There can be only one subsistent existence itself, so everything else has distinct essence and existence and therefore depends on it: it is the cause of everything other than itself.
5. **Steps 28–33: attributes.** It is necessary, uncaused, and purely actual, and so (by chapter 1's reasoning) immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient.
6. **Steps 34–36: conclusion.** Such a cause is what we mean by God; so God exists.

Notice two features. First, the whole argument turns on one pivot: **whatever merely *has* existence must receive it; only what *is* existence need not.** Second, the argument is about what sustains things **now**, not about a beginning in time.

stages.title: Stage 1a — The real distinction between essence and existence
stages.gist: Three arguments (knowability, contingency, uniqueness) show that in every thing we experience, what it is and that it is are really distinct aspects of reality.

stages.title: Stage 1b — Existence must be imparted here and now
stages.gist: Nothing can give itself existence, so each such thing depends on a distinct cause for its existence at every moment it exists.

stages.title: Stage 1c — The regress terminates in subsistent existence itself
stages.gist: The series of existence-imparting causes is hierarchical, so it needs a first member, which can only be something whose essence just is existence.

stages.title: Stage 2a — Unique cause of everything else
stages.gist: Since there can be only one thing whose essence is existence, everything else depends on it for existence.

stages.title: Stage 2b — The divine attributes
stages.gist: Subsistent existence itself is necessary, uncaused, and purely actual, and so has all the attributes that follow from pure actuality.

stages.title: Conclusion — God exists
stages.gist: A unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual cause of all that sustains everything in being is God.

steps.text: For each of the things we know from experience — stones, trees, dogs, people, and so on — we can distinguish its essence (what it is) from its existence (that it is).
steps.why: This much is simply the observation Feser opens with: knowing that a human is a rational animal is different from knowing that humans are really out there. The open question is only whether the distinction is real or merely verbal, like ‘bachelor’ vs. ‘unmarried man’.
steps.example: You know that a human being is a rational animal (what it is) and that there are human beings (that it is); you know what a unicorn is but not that there is one.
steps.challenge: Maybe this is only a difference in how we talk, like ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’.
steps.answer: Step 1 claims only that the distinction can be drawn. Whether it is real rather than verbal is exactly what steps 2–11 go on to argue.

steps.text: If the distinction were not real — a distinction in things themselves rather than just in how we think or speak — then knowing what a thing is would by itself tell us whether it exists.
steps.why: A thing's essence is part of its objective reality, and so is its existence if it has one. If these were the very same feature of reality, grasping the one would be grasping the other.
steps.example: If a lion's existence were the very same feature of reality as its lion-ness, then studying lion biology would be studying its existence, and the textbook alone would tell you that lions exist.
steps.challenge: Knowing X without knowing Y never shows X and Y are distinct — you can know aspirin without knowing it is acetylsalicylic acid.
steps.answer: Klima: that holds when a concept is incompletely grasped. Complete knowledge of aspirin reveals that it is acetylsalicylic acid, but no complete knowledge of an essence reveals the thing's existence.

steps.text: But knowing a thing's essence does not by itself tell us whether it exists.
steps.why: The lion/pterodactyl/unicorn test: a full description of their natures does not reveal which one exists, which is extinct, and which never existed. And denying a lion's existence is a false judgment, not a misconception of what a lion is — unlike denying that a lion is a cat.
steps.example: Given full descriptions of lions, pterodactyls, and unicorns, no one could say which exists, which is extinct, and which never existed.
steps.challenge: We never grasp essences completely, so existence might be in the part we haven't grasped.
steps.answer: Denying a thing's existence is a false judgment but not a misconception of what it is, unlike denying a genuine part of its essence (judging that a lion is not a cat). So existence doesn't behave like part of an essence.

steps.text: If the distinction were not real, the things we know from experience would exist necessarily rather than contingently.
steps.why: If existence belonged to a thing simply by virtue of what it is, it would exist by its very nature and could not fail to exist.
steps.example: If ‘exists’ belonged to lion-ness as ‘three-sided’ belongs to triangularity, a nonexistent lion would be as impossible as a four-sided triangle.
steps.challenge: A thing might exist by its nature and still be contingent in some weaker sense.
steps.answer: To exist by one's very nature just is to be unable not to exist; Feser says such a thing would not be contingent at all but necessary.

steps.text: But in fact these things exist only contingently, not necessarily.
steps.why: They come into being and pass away; lions might never have existed and may one day go extinct. Their need for causes and their vulnerability to destruction presuppose that existence is not part of what they are.
steps.example: Lions might never have evolved and may one day go extinct; Fido was born and will die.
steps.challenge: Contingency is just having a cause and a potential for nonexistence — no real distinction required.
steps.answer: Why would a thing need, or even be able to have, a cause of existence or a potential for nonexistence unless its existence were distinct from its essence? Those features presuppose the distinction.

steps.text: If there could be more than one thing whose essence is identical to its existence, they would have to be distinguished from one another either as species within a genus, or as members of a single species, or in some other way.
steps.why: Two things are two only if something differentiates them. The two standard ways are by a specific difference (as rationality marks off humans among animals) or by matter (as Socrates and Plato are distinct parcels of the same humanity); step 6 leaves room for any other way too.
steps.example: Humans differ from horses by a specific difference (rationality); Socrates differs from Plato by being made of different matter.
steps.challenge: Perhaps two such beings could just be two, with nothing at all distinguishing them.
steps.answer: Feser insists that for there to be two things there must be something by virtue of which they are distinct rather than one; step 6's ‘or in some other way’ covers every possible differentiator.

steps.text: But such things could not be distinguished in any of these ways.
steps.why: Any differentiating factor — a specific difference, a parcel of matter, or anything else — would make each one ‘existence itself PLUS something’, so neither would really be that which is simply existence itself.
steps.example: A would be existence itself plus a specific difference, or plus this parcel of matter — just as Socrates is humanity plus this matter, and so is not humanity itself.
steps.challenge: Why couldn't existence itself have some extra feature and still be existence itself?
steps.answer: Whatever has an added feature is ‘existence itself PLUS F’, not simply existence itself — just as a human is not animality itself but animality plus rationality.

steps.text: So there could not, even in principle, be more than one thing whose essence is identical to its existence.
steps.why: Follows from 6 and 7: every possible way of making two such things fails.
steps.example: However many candidates you imagine, each either collapses into the one existence itself or turns out to be ‘existence plus something’.

steps.text: So, for any of the things we know from experience, if its essence and existence were not really distinct, there could not be more than one of its kind.
steps.why: Follows from 8. If essence and existence are not really distinct, they are identical (there is no middle option of existence being a mere ‘part’ of the essence), and anything like that would be one of a kind.
steps.example: If a lion's essence and existence were identical, lion-ness would just be existence itself — and then there could be only one lion.
steps.challenge: Maybe a lion's existence is one part of its essence, without its essence simply being existence.
steps.answer: That middle option collapses: if the whole lion depends on its ‘existence part’, existence is its true essence — just as making the human essence depend on animality alone would make animality the true essence.

steps.text: But for each of the things we know from experience, there is, or at least could be, more than one of its kind.
steps.why: There are many stones, trees, dogs, and people; and even where a kind is down to its last member, there could be more.
steps.example: There are countless stones, trees, and dogs; even the last surviving member of an endangered species could have had others of its kind.
steps.challenge: What about a kind that has only one member?
steps.answer: Feser's wording covers this: there is, or could be, more than one. A class reduced to a single member still could have had more, so its member is not existence itself.

steps.text: So, for each of the things we know from experience, the distinction between its essence and its existence is a real distinction.
steps.why: Follows from 9 and 10 (modus tollens), and is independently supported by 2–3 and by 4–5. Three separate routes converge on the same conclusion.
steps.example: In Fido, being a dog and being real are two really different aspects of one thing, like a circle's radius and circumference.
steps.challenge: Each of the three supporting arguments can be doubted.
steps.answer: The conclusion is over-determined: knowability (2–3), contingency (4–5), and uniqueness (6–10) are independent routes, so rejecting one still leaves the other two.

steps.text: Anything whose essence is really distinct from its existence must have existence imparted to it either by itself or by some cause distinct from it.
steps.why: Its existence does not follow from its essence (as a circle's properties follow from its essence), so it must be conferred; and the only options are self or other.
steps.example: A circle's circumference follows from its essence and needs no further source; Fido's existence does not follow from ‘dog’, so it must come from somewhere.
steps.challenge: Why not treat a thing's existence as a brute fact with no source at all?
steps.answer: Essence and existence are distinct yet united, and their inseparability itself needs explaining; where distinct features always go together, as in a circle, there is always an explanation.

steps.text: If it imparted existence to itself, it would be the cause of itself.
steps.why: Imparting existence to oneself just is causing one's own existence.
steps.example: For Fido to impart existence to himself would simply be Fido causing Fido to exist.
steps.challenge: Couldn't a thing sustain itself, the way an organism maintains itself by eating?
steps.answer: Metabolism is an already existing organism acting on matter; Feser's point is that Fido cannot do anything at all unless he exists, so self-maintenance presupposes the existence in question.

steps.text: Nothing can be the cause of itself.
steps.why: To act — including to impart existence — a thing must already exist. A thing that must receive existence would therefore have to exist before it exists in order to cause itself to exist, which is incoherent.
steps.example: Like trying to lift yourself by your own bootstraps: there would have to be a you doing the lifting before there is a you.
steps.challenge: Some philosophers call God ‘self-caused’ (causa sui), so self-causation must be coherent after all.
steps.answer: The Thomistic God is not self-caused but uncaused. Causing requires already existing, so causing one's own existence would mean existing before existing.

steps.text: So it cannot impart existence to itself.
steps.why: Follows from 13 and 14.
steps.example: So Fido is not the source of his own existence.

steps.text: So anything whose essence is really distinct from its existence must have its existence imparted by some cause distinct from it.
steps.why: Follows from 12 and 15: of the two options, the first is ruled out.
steps.example: Fido's existence must come from something other than Fido.

steps.text: Because such a thing's essence and existence remain really distinct at every moment it exists, including right now, its existence must be imparted by a distinct cause at every moment it exists, including right now.
steps.why: The Fido point: the real distinction does not disappear once Fido has been conceived. At every instant his existence still doesn't follow from his essence and still can't be self-supplied, so at every instant something else must be supplying it — or he would blink out of existence.
steps.example: At noon today Fido's essence still doesn't include his existence, so at noon today something must be imparting existence to him — otherwise he would blink out.
steps.challenge: Once a thing exists it just keeps existing unless something destroys it; no continual cause is needed.
steps.answer: That treats existence as natural to the thing, which the real distinction denies. The distinction holds at every moment, so the need for a cause holds at every moment.

steps.text: So each of the things we know from experience has its existence imparted to it by a distinct cause at every moment it exists, including here and now.
steps.why: Apply 16 and 17 to the things of experience, which by 11 all have really distinct essence and existence.
steps.example: Every stone, tree, dog, and person is, at this very moment, receiving its existence from something distinct from it.

steps.text: This cause is either something whose own essence is distinct from its existence, or something whose essence and existence are identical — something that just is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: These two options are exhaustive; the ‘middle ground’ of existence being merely part of an essence was shown to collapse into the second option.
steps.example: Fido's cause C is either another receiver of existence, like Fido, or existence itself.
steps.challenge: Couldn't the cause be something that has existence as only one part of its essence?
steps.answer: No: the middle-ground option collapses into essence being existence (see step 9), so the two options are exhaustive.

steps.text: If the cause is something whose essence is distinct from its existence, then it too needs a distinct cause imparting existence to it at every moment it exists, including now.
steps.why: Steps 16–17 apply to anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, not just to the things we observe. So Fido's cause C needs B, and B needs A, all right now.
steps.example: If C is also a receiver of existence, then C needs B right now, just as Fido needs C right now.
steps.challenge: The cause might be a different sort of thing — a physical field or an angel — exempt from needing a cause.
steps.answer: Steps 16–17 apply to anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, whatever its nature; Feser explicitly includes immaterial things like angels and souls.

steps.text: The series of causes this generates is hierarchical, and a hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely but must have a first member.
steps.why: Each member imparts existence only insofar as it is simultaneously receiving existence from the one above it — its causal power is entirely derivative (instrumental). As chapter 1 argued, derivative causes without an underived source explain nothing, however many of them there are (the IOU point).
steps.example: As with chapter 1's hand, stick, and stone: the stick moves the stone only while the hand moves the stick. Likewise C gives Fido existence only while B gives C existence.
steps.challenge: Why not an infinite hierarchical series, with each member explained by the one above it (Hume)?
steps.answer: Each member is merely instrumental, so an infinite series of borrowers has no source — like infinitely many IOUs with no money behind them. Miller adds that the explanation cannot be completed without naming a first member.

steps.text: This first member can only be something whose essence and existence are identical — something that just is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: The first member must impart existence without having to receive it. Anything whose essence is distinct from its existence must receive it (16), so the first member cannot be like that; by 19 it must be subsistent existence itself.
steps.example: The first member is to existence what cash is to IOUs: it has existence not on loan but by its very nature.
steps.challenge: Why couldn't the first member be an ordinary thing that just happens to be uncaused?
steps.answer: Anything whose essence is distinct from its existence must receive existence (step 16), so it cannot be first. Only what is existence can give it without receiving it.

steps.text: So each of the things we know from experience has its existence imparted to it at every moment, including now, either directly or through intermediaries, by a cause whose essence and existence are identical — subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: Follows from 18 through 22.
steps.example: Right now Fido is being given existence, perhaps through intermediate causes, by subsistent existence itself.
steps.challenge: Doesn't this make ordinary causes like parents irrelevant?
steps.answer: No. The step says ‘directly or indirectly’: intermediate causes are real, but their causal power is derivative.

steps.text: Since there cannot be more than one thing whose essence is identical to its existence, this cause which is subsistent existence itself is unique.
steps.why: Follows from 8.
steps.example: Fido's series, a stone's series, and a star's series all terminate in one and the same subsistent existence itself.
steps.challenge: Maybe the first cause in Fido's series is different from the first cause in a stone's series.
steps.answer: Both would be things whose essence is existence, and step 8 shows there can be only one such thing, so every series terminates in the same cause.

steps.text: Since it is unique, everything else that exists must be something whose essence is distinct from its existence.
steps.why: Follows from 24 together with the exhaustiveness of the two categories (19): if only one thing can be of the second kind, everything else is of the first.
steps.example: Quarks, galaxies, angels (if any), and you all have an essence distinct from your existence.

steps.text: Anything whose essence is distinct from its existence has its existence imparted to it, directly or indirectly, by the cause which is subsistent existence itself.
steps.why: The reasoning of 16–23 applies to any such thing whatsoever — including immaterial things such as angels or souls, if they exist — not only to the things of experience.
steps.example: An angel or a disembodied soul, if such things exist, would depend on subsistent existence itself just as Fido does.
steps.challenge: Maybe some immaterial beings exist without depending on it.
steps.answer: Feser says the reasoning covers anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, including immaterial things like angels and disembodied souls.

steps.text: So this unique cause which is subsistent existence itself is the cause of everything other than itself.
steps.why: Follows from 25 and 26. Note that the claim about ‘everything’ (and so the whole universe) is a conclusion here, not a premise — which is why the fallacy-of-composition charge misses.
steps.example: Everything — including the matter things are made of and their causal powers — is being caused to exist by subsistent existence itself.
steps.challenge: This commits the fallacy of composition, reasoning from each thing needing a cause to everything needing one.
steps.answer: No: the claim about everything follows from uniqueness (24) plus step 26, not from a part-to-whole leap; the premises concern single things.

steps.text: Since anything without a real distinction between its essence and existence would exist necessarily rather than contingently, this unique cause exists necessarily.
steps.why: Draws on the principle behind step 4: what exists by its very essence cannot fail to exist. Subsistent existence itself is the limiting case — its essence is existence.
steps.example: Just as a triangle cannot lack three sides, what is existence itself cannot lack existence.
steps.challenge: Defining something as existing necessarily doesn't show that it exists.
steps.answer: Nothing is defined into existence here: steps 1–23 first show, from Fido, that such a cause exists; necessity is a feature of what has been proved.

steps.text: Whatever is subsistent existence itself neither needs, nor could have had, a cause of its own.
steps.why: A cause would have to impart existence to it; but it has nothing that receives existence — it is existence. This is why ‘What caused God?’ misfires: God is not an exception to a rule, but lacks the very feature (distinct essence and existence) that generates the need for a cause.
steps.example: There is nothing in subsistent existence itself waiting to receive existence, so there is nothing a cause could do for it.
steps.challenge: If everything has a cause, what caused God?
steps.answer: The premise was never that everything has a cause, only that whatever has distinct essence and existence does. God has no such distinction, so he not only needs no cause but could not have one.

steps.text: So this unique cause which is subsistent existence itself is uncaused.
steps.why: Follows from 29.
steps.example: It is the uncaused cause of all else.

steps.text: If subsistent existence itself had some potentiality for existence needing to be actualized, existence would have to be imparted to it by some cause.
steps.why: Essence stands to existence as potency to act: an essence distinct from its existence is a mere potential thing until existence actualizes it. Having such a potency would make it just another receiver of existence.
steps.example: Fido's essence is a potential dog until existence actualizes it. If subsistent existence itself had a potential for existence, it would likewise be waiting on something to actualize it.
steps.challenge: Why assume essence relates to existence as potency to act at all?
steps.answer: Because an essence taken by itself is only a possible thing, which becomes actual only when existence is imparted; this is Aquinas's point, which Feser adopts.

steps.text: So subsistent existence itself has no potential for existence needing actualization; it exists in a purely actual way.
steps.why: Follows from 30 and 31: since it is uncaused, it cannot have a potency that a cause would have to actualize. This is the bridge to chapter 1's purely actual actualizer — and since there can be only one purely actual thing, they are the same being.
steps.example: Nothing in it is ‘not yet’; it is existence without any unrealized capacity.
steps.challenge: It lacks a potential for existence, but why should it lack every other kind of potential too?
steps.answer: Any unactualized potential would need a cause to actualize it, but subsistent existence itself is uncaused (30); and chapter 1 shows that the ultimate source of actualization must be purely actual.

steps.text: Whatever is purely actual must be immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient.
steps.why: Established in chapter 1 (and developed in chapter 6): change, temporal succession, and matter all involve potentiality; perfection and goodness are a matter of actuality; the source of all actualization has all power; and by the principle of proportionate causality the cause of all things must contain their forms in the way an intellect does, and so knows all things.
steps.example: Change is the actualization of potential, so what has no potential cannot change: it is immutable.
steps.challenge: Pure actuality is an abstraction; it can't be intelligent, good, or personal.
steps.answer: Chapter 1 argues that goodness is a matter of actuality and, by proportionate causality, that the cause of all things must contain their forms as an intellect does; chapter 6 develops these points.

steps.text: So each of the things we experience has its existence imparted to it at every moment by a cause which is subsistent existence itself: one, necessary, the uncaused cause of everything else, purely actual, immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, intelligent, and omniscient.
steps.example: This single cause is what is keeping Fido, you, and the stars in being right now.

steps.text: For such a cause to exist is for God to exist.
steps.why: This is what classical theism means by ‘God’: not one more being among beings but the one who is existence itself, sustaining all things, with the attributes just listed. (Chapter 6 develops the divine attributes and why they belong to one and the same God.)
steps.example: ‘God’ in the classical tradition means exactly this: the one, necessary, purely actual, all-powerful, all-knowing, good source of all things.
steps.challenge: That's a philosopher's abstraction, not the God people worship.
steps.answer: The attributes listed are the ones monotheistic traditions ascribe to God; chapter 6 goes on to develop God's intellect, will, goodness, and love.

steps.text: So God exists.
steps.why: Follows from 34 and 35.
steps.example: God's existence follows from steps 34 and 35.

keyTerms.definition: A thing's nature: what it is, that by which it is the kind of thing it is. For the Thomist it is what we grasp when we identify a thing's genus and specific difference.
keyTerms.example: The essence of a human being is (traditionally) rational animality; the essence of a triangle is being a closed plane figure with three straight sides.
keyTerms.origin: Latin essentia, built from esse (‘to be’), used to render Greek ousia and Aristotle's to ti ên einai (‘the what-it-was-to-be’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Existence — essence answers ‘What is it?’, existence answers ‘Is there any?’

keyTerms.definition: The fact or act of a thing's being real — not what it is, but that it is. For the Thomist it is not a property or accident, since a thing must exist before it can have properties. To ‘exist’ is to have existence — or, in the unique case of God, to be it.
keyTerms.example: Lions and unicorns have well-defined essences, but only lions have existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin esse, the infinitive ‘to be’ used as a noun; Aquinas also speaks of the actus essendi, the ‘act of being’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Property or accident — existence is not one more feature alongside a thing's others, but what makes a thing with features real at all.

keyTerms.definition: A distinction that reflects a difference in mind-independent reality itself, not merely in the way we think or speak. It may or may not involve separability. Items so distinguished are said to be ‘really distinct’.
keyTerms.example: A dog and its leg are really distinct (and separable); a circle's radius and circumference are really distinct (but inseparable).
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic distinctio realis, from res (‘thing’): a distinction that holds on the side of the thing itself.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Separability — a real distinction does not require that the two items could ever exist apart.

keyTerms.definition: A distinction that exists only in our words or concepts, with nothing in the thing itself corresponding to it.
keyTerms.example: ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’: one reality, two phrases.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic distinctio rationis, ‘distinction of reason’ — one drawn by the mind.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Real distinction — a conceptual distinction is only in our words or thoughts; a real one is in the thing.

keyTerms.definition: Existing, but able not to exist; having existence not by one's own nature. The noun is ‘contingency’.
keyTerms.example: Lions exist but might never have evolved and could go extinct.
keyTerms.origin: Latin contingere, ‘to touch, befall, happen’ — what merely happens to be.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Temporary or caused-in-the-past — a contingent thing need not have a beginning; it is contingent because it could fail to exist.

keyTerms.definition: Unable, even in principle, not to exist — existing by virtue of what one is. The noun is ‘necessity’; something that exists this way is a ‘necessary being’.
keyTerms.example: Only something whose essence is existence itself would exist necessarily in this sense.
keyTerms.origin: Latin necesse, ‘unavoidable’ (literally ‘not yielding’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical necessity of a proposition — here ‘necessary’ describes a being that cannot fail to exist, not a truth of logic.

keyTerms.definition: In traditional logic and metaphysics (not modern biology), the more general class under which a kind falls.
keyTerms.example: Animal is the genus of human being.
keyTerms.origin: Latin genus (‘birth, kind, race’), rendering Greek genos; a basic term of Aristotle's logic.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The biological rank ‘genus’ — Feser uses the broad logical sense (animal is a genus), not modern taxonomy.

keyTerms.definition: In the traditional sense, the more specific class within a genus, marked off by a specific difference.
keyTerms.example: Human being is a species of animal.
keyTerms.origin: Latin species (‘appearance, kind’), rendering Greek eidos.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Biological species — in the traditional sense, human being is a species of the genus animal regardless of taxonomic rankings.

keyTerms.definition: The feature that distinguishes one species from others within the same genus.
keyTerms.example: Rationality distinguishes humans from other animals.
keyTerms.origin: Latin differentia specifica, from Aristotle's diaphora — the difference that makes a species.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Accidental difference — a specific difference marks off a kind (rationality), not an individual's incidental traits (fur color).

keyTerms.definition: The way members of the same species differ from one another: by being this parcel of matter rather than that one. Other differences (fur color, brain wiring) presuppose distinct matter.
keyTerms.example: Socrates is humanity plus this matter; Plato is humanity plus that matter — which is why neither is humanity itself.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian–Thomistic doctrine that matter is the ‘principle of individuation’ (principium individuationis) for members of a material species.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Specific difference — matter distinguishes individuals within one species; a specific difference distinguishes one species from another.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's term for that whose essence just is existence: not one existing thing among others, but existence itself, subsisting on its own. It need not and could not receive existence from anything. To ‘subsist’ is to exist in one's own right rather than as a feature of something else.
keyTerms.example: The terminus of the Thomistic proof; the one being that does not have existence but is existence.
keyTerms.origin: Aquinas's Latin phrase, literally ‘subsisting being itself’ (On Being and Essence, ch. 4, and elsewhere).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The sum of all existing things (pantheism) — it is not the totality of beings but the unique source of their existence, distinct from them.

keyTerms.definition: Causing an essence that is distinct from its existence to actually exist — adding existence to it, as it were.
keyTerms.example: Something must be imparting existence to Fido's essence right now for Fido to exist right now.
keyTerms.origin: Feser's phrasing for what scholastics call giving or communicating esse to an essence.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Generation — imparting existence here means sustaining a thing in being now, not producing a new thing from pre-existing materials.

keyTerms.definition: The causal activity by which a thing is kept in existence from moment to moment rather than lapsing into nothing — as opposed to generation, which brings a thing into being from pre-existing materials. To ‘conserve’ a thing is to keep it in being.
keyTerms.example: Fido's parents generated him; what conserves him (and them, and their matter) in being now is a different question.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conservare, ‘to keep, preserve’; scholastic conservatio in esse, ‘preservation in being’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conservation of energy — the physical law describes quantities within existing systems; metaphysical conservation keeps the systems in being.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member causes only insofar as it is simultaneously being caused by a prior member, so that all but the first are merely instrumental. Such a series must have a first member. Also called an ‘essentially ordered’ series.
keyTerms.example: C imparts existence to Fido only while B imparts existence to C, and B only while A imparts it to B.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic series per se ordinata, ‘series ordered through itself’ (essentially ordered).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Merely simultaneous causes — simultaneity is typical, but the defining mark is that each member's causal power is derived from the one before it.

keyTerms.definition: A series of causes extended through time in which each member, once it exists, can act independently of earlier members. Such a series could in principle regress infinitely. Also called an ‘accidentally ordered’ series.
keyTerms.example: Fido from his parents, they from theirs, back through the generations.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic series per accidens ordinata, ‘series ordered incidentally’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Hierarchical series — in a linear series each member can act once it exists, even if earlier members are gone.

keyTerms.definition: A cause whose causal power is entirely derived from something else in the very act of causing.
keyTerms.example: Every existence-imparting cause whose own essence is distinct from its existence is instrumental; it passes on existence it is itself receiving.
keyTerms.origin: Latin instrumentum, ‘tool’ — like a stick moved by a hand.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A weak or unimportant cause — ‘instrumental’ means its power is borrowed in the very act of causing, not that it is small.

keyTerms.definition: Not the earliest cause in time, but the primary cause: one that causes without needing, in the act of causing, to be caused — the source on which every member of a hierarchical series depends.
keyTerms.example: Subsistent existence itself imparts existence without receiving it.
keyTerms.origin: Latin prima causa; Aristotle's notion of a first principle on which others depend.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The earliest cause in time — here ‘first’ means primary in the order of dependence.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's point that in a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence, essence is to existence as potency is to act: the essence alone is a merely potential thing; existence actualizes it. The pair is also called ‘potency’ and ‘act’; to ‘actualize’ is to make a potential actual.
keyTerms.example: Fido's essence by itself is a potential dog; with existence imparted, there is an actual dog.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle's dynamis and energeia (Latin potentia and actus); Aquinas applied the pair to essence and existence.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Logical possibility vs. reality — potency is a real capacity in a thing, not merely something not self-contradictory.

keyTerms.definition: Actuality with no admixture of potentiality. Subsistent existence itself must be purely actual, since it has no potential for existence needing actualization. A thing with this character is called ‘purely actual’ (actus purus, ‘pure act’).
keyTerms.example: The same being reached by the Aristotelian proof as the purely actual actualizer.
keyTerms.origin: Latin actus purus, ‘pure act’, Aquinas's description of God.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Maximal busyness or activity — it means having no unactualized potential at all, not frantic doing.

keyTerms.definition: Existence as expressed by the existential quantifier (‘there is an x such that x is F’) — a second-order predicate of concepts, saying a concept has instances. Associated with Frege.
keyTerms.example: ‘Cats exist’ = something falls under the concept cat.
keyTerms.origin: Anthony Kenny's label (Aquinas on Being, 2002) for the Fregean, quantificational notion of existence.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Individual existence — specific existence is about a concept's having instances, not about an individual's still being around.

keyTerms.definition: Existence as something true of an individual — what a thing has while it lasts and loses when destroyed. Corresponds to Frege's Wirklichkeit.
keyTerms.example: The Great Pyramid still has it; the Library of Alexandria lost it.
keyTerms.origin: Kenny's label; corresponds to Gottlob Frege's Wirklichkeit (‘actuality’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence — Kenny treats a thing's existing as just its going on being what it is; the Thomist says the two are distinct though inseparable.

keyTerms.definition: Knasas's point that we grasp the subject of an existential statement without already presupposing that it exists or doesn't, so ‘Martians do not exist’ is not self-contradictory even if existence is predicated of things.
keyTerms.example: ‘Martians do not exist’ = Martians, which of themselves are neutral as to existence, are not in fact real.
keyTerms.origin: John F. X. Knasas's reply to the Fregean argument against existence as a first-level predicate.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Grasping something as nonexistent — neutral means neither affirming nor denying existence in grasping the subject.

keyTerms.definition: The logical rule that co-referring terms can be swapped without changing truth value — which fails in contexts of knowing or believing.
keyTerms.example: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, but I may know aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does.
keyTerms.origin: Tied to Leibniz's principle that identicals can be swapped salva veritate (‘with truth preserved’); its failure in belief contexts was studied by Frege and Quine.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Indiscernibility of identicals — that holds of things themselves; substitutivity concerns swapping words in sentences, which can fail in ‘knows that’ contexts.

keyTerms.definition: Two concepts are logically independent when fully grasping one does not bring knowledge of the other. Klima uses this to show why the lion case differs from the aspirin case.
keyTerms.example: Fully grasping aspirin's chemical essence brings knowledge that it is acetylsalicylic acid; fully grasping a lion's essence never brings knowledge that lions exist.
keyTerms.origin: Gyula Klima's key notion in his reply to the ‘merely conceptual distinction’ objection.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mere difference of concepts — two concepts can differ (aspirin / acetylsalicylic acid) without being logically independent once fully grasped.

keyTerms.definition: The thesis that at least some things, especially natural substances, have real, mind-independent essences — not to be confused with the rationalist ‘essentialism’ Gilson criticized. Someone who holds it is an ‘essentialist’.
keyTerms.example: Copper, oaks, and polar bears have natures discovered, not invented, by us.
keyTerms.origin: From ‘essence’; defended in contemporary form by David Oderberg (Real Essentialism) and Feser.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Gilson's target ‘essentialism’ — a rationalist attempt to read reality off abstract essences, which Feser's essentialism does not involve.

keyTerms.definition: The view that all essences are products of human concepts, language, or purposes. Feser (following Crawford Elder) argues it is incoherent when applied to the mind itself. Essences of this sort are called ‘conventional’, and a defender of the view is a ‘conventionalist’.
keyTerms.example: Artifacts like can openers have conventional essences; the conventionalist says everything does.
keyTerms.origin: Latin conventio, ‘agreement’ — essences as products of our agreements, concepts, or language.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Nominalism — nominalism denies real universals generally; conventionalism specifically says what fixes a thing's essence is our way of classifying.

keyTerms.definition: Wrongly inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do. Feser argues part-to-whole inferences are not always fallacious and that the Thomistic proof doesn't rely on one anyway.
keyTerms.example: Each brick weighs a pound, so the wall weighs a pound (fallacious); each Lego brick is red, so the wall is red (valid).
keyTerms.origin: A traditional informal fallacy catalogued since Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Fallacy of division — inferring that parts have a property because the whole does (the reverse direction).

keyTerms.term: De Ente et Essentia (On Being and Essence)
keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's early treatise, chapter 4 of which is the classic source of the reasoning behind the Thomistic proof and of the phrase ‘subsistent existence itself’.
keyTerms.example: Feser cites it when introducing ipsum esse subsistens.
