keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘On Being and Essence’; an early work of Aquinas, written in the 1250s.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Five Ways of the Summa Theologiae — the Thomistic proof in this chapter is the De Ente argument, not one of the Five Ways.

keyTerms.definition: In its Aristotelian form (chapter 1), the principle that any potential that is actualized is actualized by something already actual. In this chapter's form: whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence requires a cause of its existence.
keyTerms.example: Fido's existence, not being part of his essence, must be supplied here and now by something other than Fido.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic principium causalitatis; rooted in Aristotle's analysis of change.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Everything has a cause’ — the principle applies only to what has potential or has essence distinct from existence, not to absolutely everything.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in some way in its total cause — formally, eminently, or virtually. Feser uses it (from chapter 1) to show the cause of all things must have intellect and omniscience.
keyTerms.example: Since the forms or patterns of all things exist in their effects, they must pre-exist in the cause of all things in the way ideas exist in an intellect.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic principle; Aquinas and later Descartes use versions of it.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Causes resemble their effects’ — the PPC does not require a copy of the effect in the cause, only that the cause somehow contains what it gives.

keyTerms.definition: The doctrine that God has no parts of any kind — physical or metaphysical — including no distinction between essence and existence. The adjective is ‘simple’ (meaning non-composite, without parts).
keyTerms.example: Subsistent existence itself does not ‘have’ existence added to a nature; its nature simply is existence.
keyTerms.origin: Classical theism (Augustine, Anselm, Maimonides, Aquinas); Chapter 2's ‘absolutely simple’ One.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simple-mindedness or being easy to understand — simplicity here means lacking composition, not being uncomplicated to grasp.

keyTerms.definition: Composition not of physical pieces but of principles that together make up a thing, such as form and matter, or essence and existence.
keyTerms.example: Chapter 2 lists essence and existence among the metaphysical parts whose union needs a cause; chapter 4 develops that case.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotelian–scholastic metaphysics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Physical parts — you cannot cut a dog's essence away from its existence the way you can remove a leg.

keyTerms.definition: A feature that exists in a substance rather than on its own, such as a color, size, or location. For the Thomist, existence is not an accident, since a thing must already exist to have accidents.
keyTerms.example: Fido's brown fur is an accident; Fido's existence is not one more such feature.
keyTerms.origin: Latin accidens, ‘what befalls’ (Aristotle's symbebêkos).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A chance event (‘an accident’) — in metaphysics it means a feature inhering in a substance.

keyTerms.definition: The symbol and logical device (‘there is at least one x such that…’) by which modern logic expresses existence claims.
keyTerms.example: ‘Cats exist’ becomes ‘there is at least one x such that x is a cat.’
keyTerms.origin: Developed by Frege and later logicians; written ∃.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Thomistic act of existence — the quantifier records that something falls under a concept; the Thomist asks what makes that so.

keyTerms.definition: A predicate that applies to concepts rather than to objects. On the Fregean view, existence is such a predicate: it says of a concept that it has instances.
keyTerms.example: ‘Is instantiated’ is said of the concept horse, not of any particular horse.
keyTerms.origin: Frege's distinction between first-level and second-level concepts.
keyTerms.confuseWith: First-order predicate — ‘is brown’ applies to Fido himself; ‘is instantiated’ applies to the concept dog.

keyTerms.definition: Frege's term for actuality or reality in the sense of an individual thing's being actual — the notion Kenny calls ‘individual existence’.
keyTerms.example: The Great Pyramid still has Wirklichkeit; the Library of Alexandria no longer does.
keyTerms.origin: German, ‘actuality, reality’ (from wirken, ‘to act, work’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Frege's quantificational ‘existence’ — Wirklichkeit concerns individuals, not concepts' having instances.

keyTerms.definition: A statement denying that something exists, such as ‘Martians do not exist’. Fregeans argue these would be self-contradictory if existence were predicated of objects.
keyTerms.example: ‘Unicorns do not exist’ seems to be about unicorns — but there are none for it to be about.
keyTerms.origin: A classic puzzle in philosophy of language (Plato's Sophist, Meinong, Russell, Frege).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A self-contradiction — Knasas argues that, rightly understood, negative existentials are not contradictory even on the Thomist view.

keyTerms.definition: A context involving a mental attitude — knowing, believing, wanting — in which swapping co-referring terms can change a sentence's truth value.
keyTerms.example: ‘I know aspirin relieves pain’ can be true while ‘I know acetylsalicylic acid relieves pain’ is false.
keyTerms.origin: From the scholastic and Brentanian notion of intentionality (the mind's being directed at objects).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Intentional in the sense of ‘on purpose’ — here it means ‘about something’, as thoughts are.

keyTerms.definition: A priori knowledge is had independently of experience; a posteriori knowledge depends on experience. Klima notes that knowing an essence gives a priori knowledge of what any member of the kind would be like, but whether any member exists is known only a posteriori.
keyTerms.example: From triangle's essence you know a priori any triangle's angles sum to 180°; whether a triangle is drawn on this board you learn by looking.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘from what is earlier’ / ‘from what is later’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Necessary / contingent — a priori and a posteriori concern how we know; necessary and contingent concern how things are.

keyTerms.definition: Assuming, in an argument's premises, the very conclusion at issue. Feser and Klima rebut the charge by giving independent reasons for the disputed premise.
keyTerms.example: The critic says ‘you just assume complete knowledge of essence wouldn't reveal existence’; Klima answers with the a priori/a posteriori pattern.
keyTerms.origin: Latin petitio principii, ‘assuming the starting point’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: ‘Raising the question’ — in logic, begging the question means circular reasoning, not prompting a further question.

keyTerms.definition: A grouping of things in nature that reflects a real, shared nature rather than human convenience.
keyTerms.example: Copper, oak trees, and polar bears; Ellis argues each chemical substance is a natural kind.
keyTerms.origin: Term from 19th-century philosophy of science (Whewell, Mill); central to modern essentialism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Artifact kind — can openers and carburetors are grouped by our purposes, not by a shared nature.

keyTerms.definition: A school in philosophy of science holding that science discovers the essences and essential causal powers of things, and that laws of nature are grounded in them.
keyTerms.example: Brian Ellis argues laws of nature need essences; Nancy Cartwright argues experimental physics is a search for natures.
keyTerms.origin: Contemporary philosophy of science (Ellis, Scientific Essentialism, 2001).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Armchair rationalism — the new essentialists hold that essences are discovered through empirical science, not deduced a priori.

keyTerms.definition: Describing how a thing would behave under conditions that never fully obtain, with interfering factors removed.
keyTerms.example: Frictionless surfaces; Newton's law of gravity describing bodies with no other forces acting on them.
keyTerms.origin: Standard term in philosophy of science; highlighted by Nancy Cartwright.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Falsification or fudge — idealizations isolate a thing's real powers; they are not errors.

keyTerms.definition: Something is mind-dependent if its being what it is depends on our thinking or language; mind-independent if it would be what it is whether or not anyone thought about it.
keyTerms.example: What makes something a can opener is mind-dependent; lion biology is mind-independent.
keyTerms.origin: Standard terminology in debates over realism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Mental vs. physical — a mind-independent thing can be immaterial, and something physical can have a mind-dependent classification.

keyTerms.definition: One thing is temporally prior if it comes earlier in time; ontologically prior if the other depends on it for its being, whether or not it comes earlier.
keyTerms.example: Elder's argument: what is mind-dependent presupposes the mind, so the mind is ontologically prior to it.
keyTerms.origin: Aristotle's senses of ‘prior’ (Categories 12; Metaphysics V).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Earlier in time — a sustaining cause is prior to what it sustains even when they exist simultaneously.

keyTerms.definition: The mainstream conception of God in Western philosophy and theology: God as one, simple, immutable, eternal, purely actual, and subsistent existence itself — not one being among others.
keyTerms.example: Aquinas, Maimonides, and Avicenna are classical theists.
keyTerms.origin: Term used in contemporary philosophy of religion for the view of Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, and others.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Theistic personalism — the view of God as a very great person or being among beings, which Feser rejects.

keyTerms.definition: A thing's ceasing to exist entirely — not being transformed into something else, but lapsing into nothing.
keyTerms.example: Without a conserving cause, Fido would ‘blink out’ — be annihilated — not decay into dust.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ad nihil, ‘to nothing’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Destruction by corruption — when a dog dies, its matter persists in new forms; annihilation leaves nothing.

keyTerms.definition: A concept or kind's having an actual instance — something falling under it.
keyTerms.example: The concept unicorn is not instantiated; the concept lion is.
keyTerms.origin: Latin instantia; modern logic's term for a concept's being satisfied.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The act of existence — instantiation is the fact that something falls under a concept; the Thomist asks what makes that fact obtain.

keyTerms.definition: Miller's analysis of explanations of the form ‘A is caused to G by B insofar as B is caused to G by C insofar as…’: such a sentence can only be completed by naming a first member.
keyTerms.example: Put ‘Fido’ for A and ‘exist’ for G: however many intermediate causes you add, the explanation needs a final M that is subsistent existence itself.
keyTerms.origin: Barry Miller, ‘Necessarily Terminating Causal Series and the Contingency Argument’ (Mind, 1982).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A temporal regress — Miller's point concerns the logical form of explanation by derived causality, not a series stretching into the past.

keyTerms.definition: Étienne Gilson's name for Aquinas's emphasis on the act of existence and on knowing real existents through experience, which he contrasted with rationalist ‘essentialism’.
keyTerms.example: Feser says Aquinas was an ‘existentialist’ in Gilson's sense and an essentialist in Feser's sense — no conflict.
keyTerms.origin: Étienne Gilson, 20th-century Thomist historian of philosophy.
keyTerms.confuseWith: 20th-century existentialism (Sartre, Heidegger) — Gilson's usage has nothing to do with ‘existence precedes essence’.

keyTerms.definition: A substance without matter, such as an angel or a disembodied soul (if there are such). Feser notes the argument applies to them too, since their essence is still distinct from their existence.
keyTerms.example: Even an angel, lacking matter, would have existence imparted by subsistent existence itself.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic substantia separata, ‘separated substance’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Subsistent existence itself — being immaterial is not enough to be God; only something whose essence is existence is uncaused.

keyTerms.definition: Being all-powerful: able to bring about anything that is intrinsically possible. ‘Omnipotent’ is the adjective. For Feser, what is purely actual is the source of all actualization and so is omnipotent.
keyTerms.example: The purely actual cause can produce any possible thing, but ‘making a square circle’ isn't a task at all, so it's no limit on omnipotence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) + potens (‘powerful’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ability to do the logically impossible — omnipotence concerns whatever can possibly be, not contradictions.

keyTerms.definition: Knowing all things; ‘omniscient’ is the adjective. Feser derives it (from chapter 1) from the fact that the cause of all things contains, in the way an intellect does, the forms of everything it causes.
keyTerms.example: Since everything other than subsistent existence itself is caused by it, it knows everything that exists.
keyTerms.origin: Latin omnis (‘all’) + scientia (‘knowledge’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Prediction from data — God's knowledge isn't inferred from evidence but belongs to him as the cause of all things.

keyTerms.definition: Changelessness; ‘immutable’ is the adjective. What is purely actual cannot change, since change is the actualization of a potential and it has none.
keyTerms.example: Subsistent existence itself does not grow, learn, or become anything it wasn't already.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- (‘not’) + mutabilis (‘changeable’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Inertness or lifelessness — immutability is fullness of actuality, not a static lack of activity.

keyTerms.definition: Existence without beginning, end, or succession of moments; ‘eternal’ is the adjective. Since time involves change, what is purely actual and immutable is outside time altogether.
keyTerms.example: Subsistent existence itself does not live through one moment after another; it sustains every moment.
keyTerms.origin: Latin aeternitas; Boethius defined eternity as the complete, simultaneous possession of unending life.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Everlastingness — lasting through endless time. The classical notion of eternity is timelessness.

keyTerms.definition: Being without matter and without a body; ‘immaterial’ and ‘incorporeal’ are the adjectives. Matter involves potentiality, so what is purely actual cannot be material or bodily.
keyTerms.example: Subsistent existence itself has no parts, location, or mass.
keyTerms.origin: Latin in- + materia (‘stuff’); in- + corpus (‘body’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Being made of some subtle stuff like gas or energy — immaterial means no matter at all.

keyTerms.definition: Lacking nothing; ‘perfect’ is the adjective. In the Aristotelian-Thomistic sense, a thing is perfect to the extent it is actual, so what is purely actual lacks no perfection.
keyTerms.example: Every deficiency is some unrealized potential; pure act has none.
keyTerms.origin: Latin perfectus, ‘thoroughly made, complete’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Moral flawlessness alone — perfection here means completeness of being, of which moral goodness is one aspect.

keyTerms.definition: Being wholly good, without defect. For the Thomist, goodness is a matter of actuality and badness is a privation (a lack), so what is purely actual is fully good.
keyTerms.example: Blindness is bad because it is the lack of sight an animal should have; pure act lacks nothing.
keyTerms.origin: The scholastic view that evil is a privation of good (privatio boni), from Augustine.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Obeying moral rules — God's goodness is fullness of being, not compliance with duties imposed from outside.

keyTerms.definition: The power of grasping forms, concepts, or natures in an abstract way; ‘intelligent’ is the adjective. By the principle of proportionate causality, the cause of all things must contain their forms as an intellect does, so it is intelligent.
keyTerms.example: The patterns realized in every dog, star, and atom pre-exist in their cause not as physical copies but as ideas.
keyTerms.origin: Latin intellectus, from intellegere, ‘to understand’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A brain or step-by-step reasoning — the divine intellect has no brain and does not work things out one step at a time.

keyTerms.definition: The claim that there can be only one God. Feser shows this by showing there can be at most one thing whose essence is existence (and, in chapter 1, at most one purely actual thing).
keyTerms.example: Any would-be second God would have to be ‘existence itself plus something’, and so would not be existence itself.
keyTerms.origin: Classical theism; Latin unicus, ‘one and only’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A mere fact that happens to hold — God's uniqueness could not have been otherwise.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which each member depends on a prior member, with no first member. Feser argues that a hierarchical series cannot regress infinitely, though a linear series could.
keyTerms.example: Fido ← C ← B ← A ← … with no source would be an infinite regress of borrowers of existence.
keyTerms.origin: Latin regressus, ‘a going back’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An infinite past — that is a linear regress in time, which the Thomistic proof does not rule out.

keyTerms.definition: Bringing a new thing into being out of pre-existing materials, by causes that act on those materials.
keyTerms.example: Fido's parents generated Fido; they are not what keeps him in being now.
keyTerms.origin: Latin generare, ‘to beget’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conservation — keeping a thing and its materials in existence at every moment.

keyTerms.definition: The valid pattern of reasoning: if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P.
keyTerms.example: If a lion's essence were identical with its existence, there could be only one lion; there are many lions; so its essence is not identical with its existence (steps 9–11).
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘the mode that removes’ (it removes the ‘if’ part by denying the ‘then’ part).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Denying the antecedent — ‘if P then Q; not P; so not Q’ — which is invalid.

keyTerms.definition: Refuting a supposition by showing that it leads to an absurdity or contradiction.
keyTerms.example: Suppose there were two things whose essence is existence; each would then be existence itself plus something, which contradicts the supposition.
keyTerms.origin: Latin, ‘reduction to the absurd’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Ridicule — a reductio is a rigorous logical argument, not mockery.

keyTerms.definition: The view that there are no real natures or universals shared by many things — only individual things and the names or concepts we apply to them.
keyTerms.example: A nominalist says ‘copper’ is just our label for similar lumps, not a real common nature.
keyTerms.origin: Latin nomen, ‘name’; associated with William of Ockham.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conventionalism about essences — the two are closely related, but conventionalism says specifically that our classifying fixes what a thing's essence is.

keyTerms.definition: The view that God and the universe (or nature) are identical.
keyTerms.example: A pantheist says the cosmos is God; the Thomist says the cosmos depends on God for its existence.
keyTerms.origin: Greek pan (‘all’) + theos (‘god’).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Divine conservation — God's keeping all things in being does not make them identical to God.

keyTerms.definition: A modern conception of God as a very great person, one being among others, with attributes distinct from his essence, typically rejecting divine simplicity. Feser opposes it to classical theism.
keyTerms.example: Feser counts Alvin Plantinga's criticism of divine simplicity as an instance of this view.
keyTerms.origin: Term associated with Brian Davies; Feser also calls it ‘neo-theism’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Classical theism, on which God is subsistent existence itself rather than a being among beings.

keyTerms.definition: Aquinas's five famous arguments for God's existence in the Summa Theologiae: from motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, and order.
keyTerms.example: Feser's Aristotelian proof is related to the First Way; his Thomistic proof comes from On Being and Essence instead.
keyTerms.origin: Latin quinque viae, Summa Theologiae I, question 2, article 3.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The De Ente argument — the Thomistic proof of this chapter is not one of the Five Ways.

keyTerms.definition: An argument that the universe began to exist and therefore has a cause. Unlike the Thomistic proof, it depends on the universe having a beginning.
keyTerms.example: Arguments that use Big Bang cosmology to show a first moment of time are kalām-style arguments.
keyTerms.origin: Arabic kalām (‘speech’), the name for medieval Islamic dialectical theology (for example, al-Ghazali).
keyTerms.confuseWith: The Thomistic proof, which concerns what sustains things now and is compatible with an eternal universe.

keyTerms.definition: A hypothesized collection of many universes. Feser notes that even an eternal multiverse would leave the Thomistic proof untouched.
keyTerms.example: A multiverse, having a definite nature and many members, would be a receiver of existence, not existence itself.
keyTerms.origin: Modern cosmology and speculative physics.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Subsistent existence itself — a multiverse is a collection of things whose essence is distinct from their existence.

keyTerms.definition: An argument meant to establish its conclusion with certainty, by deduction from evident premises, rather than to show it merely probable.
keyTerms.example: Feser presents the Thomistic proof as a demonstration, not as a hypothesis awaiting more data.
keyTerms.origin: Latin demonstratio, translating Aristotle's apodeixis.
keyTerms.confuseWith: An empirical hypothesis, which stays open to confirmation or refutation by future observations.

keyTerms.definition: Invoking God to fill a current gap in scientific explanation — a gap future science might close.
keyTerms.example: ‘Science can't yet explain X, so God did it’ is god-of-the-gaps reasoning; the Thomistic proof instead asks why anything exists at all.
keyTerms.origin: Phrase popularized in 20th-century debates (Dietrich Bonhoeffer, C. A. Coulson).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Metaphysical explanation — the Thomistic proof starts from what science presupposes (existing things), not from what science hasn't yet explained.

keyTerms.definition: A thing that exists in its own right — a dog, a stone, a person — as opposed to features (accidents) that exist in it.
keyTerms.example: Fido is a substance; his brown color is an accident of Fido.
keyTerms.origin: Latin substantia, ‘what stands under’, translating Aristotle's ousia.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A chemical ‘substance’ or stuff — in metaphysics a substance is an individual thing with its own nature.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle's analysis of material things: matter is the potential to be something; form is what makes it actually the kind of thing it is. Chapter 2 treats their union as a composition needing a cause.
keyTerms.example: A statue's bronze is its matter and its shape its form; a dog's matter is organized by the form of a dog.
keyTerms.origin: Greek hylē (‘matter’) and morphē (‘form’) — hence ‘hylemorphism’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Essence and existence — form and matter together make up a material thing's essence; existence is what makes the whole essence actual.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that there is an explanation for why anything exists and has the features it has; the engine of chapter 5's rationalist proof.
keyTerms.example: Asking why the universe exists rather than nothing, and refusing to accept ‘there's no reason’ as an answer.
keyTerms.origin: Named by Leibniz.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The principle of causality — the PSR concerns explanation in general; the PC concerns causes of actualization or existence.

keyTerms.definition: Any argument from the existence, change, or causal dependence of things in the world to a first or ultimate cause.
keyTerms.example: The Aristotelian, Neoplatonic, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs are all cosmological arguments in the broad sense.
keyTerms.origin: Greek kosmos (‘ordered world’); the label was popularized by Kant.
keyTerms.confuseWith: The kalām argument — only one kind of cosmological argument relies on a beginning of the universe.

keyTerms.definition: The feature of quantum mechanics (on standard interpretations) whereby individual outcomes are not fixed by prior conditions, only their probabilities.
keyTerms.example: When a particular radioactive atom decays is not predictable, though the decay has causal antecedents.
keyTerms.origin: 20th-century physics (Heisenberg, Bohr).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Uncaused events — indeterministic is not the same as uncaused; a cause need only make its effect intelligible (chapter 1).

keyTerms.definition: Hume's claim that, because we can conceive of something beginning to exist without a cause, the principle of causality is not necessarily true.
keyTerms.example: Imagining a coffee cup popping into existence without picturing any cause of it.
keyTerms.origin: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Conceiving of something as uncaused — Feser (chapter 1) argues that conceiving of a thing without also conceiving its cause is not conceiving it as having none.

keyTerms.definition: Reasoning about God's existence and nature from premises available to anyone through reason and experience, without appeal to revelation.
keyTerms.example: Feser's five proofs are exercises in natural theology.
keyTerms.origin: From the ancient division (Varro, Augustine) of theology into natural, civil, and mythical.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Revealed theology, which relies on Scripture or divine revelation.

keyTerms.definition: The view that science is the only genuine, or only reliable, source of knowledge.
keyTerms.example: Someone who says ‘if physics can't measure it, it isn't real’ is expressing scientism.
keyTerms.origin: 20th-century term, usually critical.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Science itself — one can value science fully while denying that it is the only kind of knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: In philosophy, the tendency to derive knowledge of reality from reason and concepts alone; in Gilson's sense, the attempt to read reality off abstract essences.
keyTerms.example: Gilson criticized rationalist ‘essentialism’; Feser's chapter 5 is called the ‘rationalist proof’ because it uses the PSR, associated with rationalist philosophers like Leibniz.
keyTerms.origin: Latin ratio, ‘reason’; the 17th-century tradition of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Simply being rational — rationalism is a specific view about the sources of knowledge.

keyTerms.definition: A general regularity in how things behave. Brian Ellis and other new essentialists hold that laws are grounded in the essences and causal powers of things.
keyTerms.example: Copper conducts electricity because of what copper is; the ‘law’ describes that.
keyTerms.origin: Early modern natural philosophy (Descartes, Newton).
keyTerms.confuseWith: A cause of existence — a law describes how things with certain natures behave; it does not make anything exist.

keyTerms.definition: Newton's first law: a body continues at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a force.
keyTerms.example: A puck gliding across frictionless ice keeps going without a push.
keyTerms.origin: Latin iners, ‘idle’; Newton's Principia (1687).
keyTerms.confuseWith: Persistence in existence — inertia concerns the motion of bodies that already exist, not why bodies exist at all.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that has no cause of its own. Subsistent existence itself is the uncaused cause of the existence of everything else.
keyTerms.example: It imparts existence to all things without receiving existence from anything.
keyTerms.origin: Scholastic phrase, parallel to Aristotle's ‘unmoved mover’.
keyTerms.confuseWith: Self-caused (causa sui) — the Thomistic God does not cause himself; he has no cause at all.

keyTerms.definition: A misconception wrongly denies something that belongs to a thing's essence; an incomplete conception merely fails to include it. Feser uses the contrast to show that existence is not part of an essence.
keyTerms.example: Thinking a lion isn't a cat misconceives lions; not yet knowing it's a cat is incomplete; thinking lions are extinct is neither — just false.
keyTerms.origin: Feser, drawing on David Oderberg's Real Essentialism.
keyTerms.confuseWith: A false judgment — wrongly thinking a thing doesn't exist is false but does not misconceive what it is.

distinctions.name: Essence vs. existence

left.label: Essence (what it is)
left.desc: The nature a thing has — the answer to ‘What is it?’ Fully describable without settling whether any such thing is real (lions, pterodactyls, unicorns).

right.label: Existence (that it is)
right.desc: The fact or act of being real — the answer to ‘Is there any?’ Known only by experience (a posteriori) in the case of the things around us, never read off the essence.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The whole proof rests on this contrast. If existence were part of what things are, they would need no cause of their being; because it isn't, they must receive existence from outside.

distinctions.name: Real distinction vs. merely conceptual (verbal) distinction

left.label: Merely conceptual
left.desc: Two ways of thinking or speaking about one and the same reality, like ‘bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’, or (the critic claims) ‘aspirin’ and ‘acetylsalicylic acid’.

right.label: Real
right.desc: Two aspects that differ in mind-independent reality, whether or not they can be separated.

distinctions.whyItMatters: If essence and existence differed only in our concepts, a thing's existence might be ‘built into’ it after all, and no cause of existence would be required. Feser's three arguments and Klima's reply to the aspirin objection defend reality here.

distinctions.name: Distinct-and-separable vs. distinct-but-inseparable

left.label: Separable real distinction
left.desc: Things that can exist apart: two dogs; a dog and its leg.

right.label: Inseparable real distinction
right.desc: Aspects that can never occur apart yet are not the same: a circle's radius and circumference; triangularity and trilaterality; a thing's essence and its existence.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Kenny's objection assumes that real distinction requires separability. Showing that it doesn't disarms him — and also shows why ‘they're inseparable’ doesn't explain why essence and existence are united.

distinctions.name: Incomplete conception vs. misconception

left.label: Incomplete conception
left.desc: Missing part of a thing's essence without denying it: knowing a lion is an animal but not yet that it is a cat.

right.label: Misconception
right.desc: Denying something that belongs to the essence: judging that a lion is not a cat.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Denying that lions exist is a false judgment but not a misconception of what a lion is. That shows existence is not part of a lion's essence, answering the charge that we just haven't grasped the essence completely.

distinctions.name: Linear (generating) series vs. hierarchical (conserving) series

left.label: Linear / per accidens
left.desc: Causes spread out in time, generating new things from pre-existing materials; each member can act independently once it exists (Fido's ancestry). Could in principle be infinite.

right.label: Hierarchical / per se
right.desc: Simultaneous causes, each imparting existence only insofar as it is right now receiving existence from a prior one. All but the first are instrumental; must have a first member.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Hume's ‘why need there be a first cause?’ and the ‘what about an eternal universe?’ objection both target linear series. The Thomistic proof is entirely about the hierarchical series of conservation.

distinctions.name: Having existence vs. being existence

left.label: Having existence (esse receptum)
left.desc: A thing whose essence is distinct from its existence: it is a potential that has been actualized, needs a cause, can be many, is contingent.

right.label: Being existence (ipsum esse subsistens)
right.desc: That whose essence just is existence: needs and could have no cause, is unique, necessary, purely actual.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is why the proof's first cause is not an ad hoc exception to a causal rule: the rule applies only to what has existence, and the first cause is what is existence. And it is why there is no middle ground: existence as a ‘part’ of an essence collapses into essence being existence.

distinctions.name: Specific existence vs. individual existence (Kenny)

left.label: Specific existence
left.desc: ‘There is an x such that x is F’ — a concept's having instances; a second-order predicate of concepts (Frege).

right.label: Individual existence
right.desc: What an individual has while it lasts and loses when destroyed (Great Pyramid vs. Library of Alexandria); Frege's Wirklichkeit.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Kenny argues the real distinction fails on either reading. The Thomist replies that Kenny assumes separability, assumes these are the only respectable notions of existence, and ignores the further question of what makes a concept be instantiated at all — which is the Thomist's act of existence.

distinctions.name: First in time vs. first in the order of dependence

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest cause in a sequence stretching back into the past — the cause a ‘beginning of the universe’ argument is after.

right.label: Primary (ontologically first)
right.desc: The cause on which every other member depends right now for its causal power — even if (per impossibile) the series were infinite.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The Thomistic proof's ‘first cause’ is primary, not temporally first. That is why it is compatible with an eternal universe or multiverse.

illustrations.title: Lions, pterodactyls, and unicorns
illustrations.body:
Describe three creatures in full biological detail to someone who has never heard of them. Then tell him: one of these is alive today, one is extinct, one never existed — which is which? No amount of study of the descriptions will tell him. The essences are fully on the table, but existence is not among the items listed.

Use it to show that **what a thing is** leaves open **whether it is**. Then add the follow-up: denying that lions exist would be a mistake about the world, not a misunderstanding of what a lion is.

illustrations.title: Bachelors and unmarried men
illustrations.body: ‘Bachelor’ and ‘unmarried man’ are two expressions for exactly one reality — nothing in any bachelor answers to the difference in wording. Feser uses this as the model of a *merely verbal* distinction, to sharpen the question: is essence vs. existence like this, or does it mark something in things themselves?

illustrations.title: The circle's radius and circumference
illustrations.body:
Every circle has a radius and a circumference, and you will never find one without the other. Yet they are obviously not the same thing — one is 2π times the other. They are **really distinct but inseparable**, and both follow from the essence of a circle. The same goes for having three angles and having three sides.

This example does double duty: it shows that a real distinction need not mean separability (answering Kenny), and it shows what essence and existence *lack* — existence does not follow from a lion's essence the way the circumference follows from the circle's.

illustrations.title: Fido blinking out
illustrations.body:
Fido's parents explain how he got started. But right now, this instant, Fido's existence is still not part of what a dog is, and Fido cannot be supplying it to himself (he would have to exist already in order to do anything). So something must be imparting existence to him now — otherwise he would simply blink out, no more real than before he was conceived.

Use Fido to shift the listener's imagination from **how things began** to **what keeps them in being**.

illustrations.title: An infinite stack of IOUs
illustrations.body: An IOU is only worth something if, somewhere, it is backed by real money. Pile up IOUs that point to other IOUs, even infinitely many, and you still have no money. A chain of causes each of which only *passes on* existence it is itself receiving is like that: however long, it yields no real dog unless it is backed by something that has existence not on loan but by nature — subsistent existence itself.

illustrations.title: Socrates is not humanity
illustrations.body: Socrates and Plato are both fully human, yet they are two. What makes them two is that each is humanity *plus* a distinct parcel of matter — which is exactly why neither of them *is* humanity itself. Now try to make two things that are each *existence itself*: whatever you add to distinguish them (a specific difference, a parcel of matter, anything) makes each ‘existence itself plus something’, which is no longer existence itself. So there can be only one.

illustrations.title: Red Lego wall vs. heavy brick wall
illustrations.body: Each brick weighs a pound; the wall doesn't. But each Lego brick is red; the wall is red. Some part-to-whole inferences fail and some succeed, so ‘fallacy of composition’ is not a magic word. And in any case the Thomistic proof never needs the inference: one dog is enough to get to subsistent existence itself.

illustrations.title: Aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid
illustrations.body: Aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, yet a person with a hazy grasp of aspirin can know it relieves pain without knowing it is acetylsalicylic acid. The critic says the lion's essence and existence might be like that: one reality, two concepts. Klima's reply: if you grasped aspirin's chemical essence *completely*, you couldn't miss that it is acetylsalicylic acid. But no complete grasp of what a lion is would ever tell you that lions exist. The concepts of aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid are not logically independent; the concepts of a lion and a lion's existence are.

illustrations.title: A recipe is not a dinner
illustrations.body: A recipe tells you exactly what a dish is — ingredients, proportions, method. You can own a thousand recipes and still be hungry: none of them contains a meal. A recipe is a *potential* dinner; something else must make it actual. An essence is like the recipe; existence is the meal being real. (Unlike a recipe, of course, an essence is not an object on its own — it only ever exists as the essence of an existing thing; the analogy is about the gap between specification and reality.)

illustrations.title: The picture on a screen
illustrations.body: An image on a monitor is there only while the signal is continuously being sent; cut the signal and the picture doesn't linger, it vanishes. Compare a statue, which stays put after the sculptor leaves. The Thomistic claim is that, with respect to *existence itself*, everything is like the screen image rather than the statue: its being is continuously received. Use this to explain conservation — but add that the ‘signal source’ in the proof, unlike any transmitter, is not itself receiving power from anything further.

objections.title: We never grasp essences completely
objections.whoRaises: A careful critic of the first argument for the real distinction
objections.objection: The knowability argument says we can know a thing's essence without knowing it exists. But we almost never know the *complete* essence of a natural thing. For all we know, existence is part of the essence we haven't yet grasped — so our failure to read existence off the essence proves nothing.
objections.reply:
Feser points to a revealing disanalogy between genuine parts of an essence and existence.

1. If you know a lion is an animal but not that it is a cat, your idea of a lion is *incomplete* but not *wrong*.
2. If you judge that a lion is *not* a cat, you have *misconceived* what a lion is.
3. But if you judge that lions *don't exist* — thinking them extinct like pterodactyls or fictional like unicorns — you have made a false judgment about the world without misconceiving what a lion is.
4. If existence were part of the lion's essence, denying it would be a misconception on a par with denying that lions are cats. It isn't. So existence is not part of the essence, however incompletely we grasp the rest.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘maybe existence is part of the essence in some way that denying it wouldn't count as misconceiving,’ ask what that could mean. The test for whether a feature belongs to an essence is precisely whether denying it distorts your idea of what the thing is. By that test existence fails every time for the things of experience. Add Klima's point: knowing an essence tells you a priori what any member of the kind would have to be like, but whether any member exists is always learned a posteriori.

objections.title: Contingency is explained by causes, not a real distinction
objections.whoRaises: A critic of the second (contingency) argument
objections.objection: We don't need any metaphysical distinction to explain why a lion is contingent. It is contingent because it needs a cause (earlier lions) and has potentialities for nonexistence (predators, starvation, disease). Causes and vulnerabilities do all the work.
objections.reply:
This misses the point. The question is *why* the lion needs — or even *can have* — a cause of its existence, and *why* it has any potential for nonexistence at all.

1. If existence were simply part of what a lion is, the lion would have it by nature, so nothing else would need to supply it.
2. And nothing in its nature could give it a potential to lose existence.
3. So the lion's dependence on causes and its liability to perish are *evidence* of the real distinction, not alternatives to it. The objection explains the symptoms while ignoring what makes them possible.
objections.pushback: If pressed — ‘why not just take dependence and fragility as brute facts?’ — point out that this abandons explanation at the exact point where an explanation is available. The real distinction tells you *why* anything could be caused or destroyed at all; treating that as brute is a refusal to ask the question, not an answer to it.

objections.title: Existence could be one part of an essence (the ‘middle ground’)
objections.whoRaises: Discussed by Peter Weigel; a natural move for anyone resisting the uniqueness argument
objections.objection: Why assume only two options — essence distinct from existence, or essence identical to existence? Maybe some things have existence as *one component* of their essence, alongside other components. Then their essence and existence wouldn't be distinct, yet their essence wouldn't simply *be* existence, and the uniqueness argument wouldn't apply to them.
objections.reply:
Feser argues the suggestion collapses.

1. Take the human essence, rational animality, with parts rationality and animality. Suppose existence were a third part.
2. Then the existence of the whole human being would depend on that one part — which is as implausible as the whole human essence depending on animality alone.
3. If someone insisted that the whole really did depend on animality alone, he would in effect be making animality the *true* essence.
4. By parity, making the whole thing depend on its ‘existence part’ makes existence the true essence.
5. So we are back to a thing whose essence just is existence — exactly what the objector wanted to avoid. There is no middle ground.
objections.pushback: If the objector says existence could be a part without the whole depending on it, ask what existence is doing there, then. A ‘component’ that doesn't account for the whole's existing doesn't make the essence and existence non-distinct at all — the thing would still need existence supplied from outside. Either existence carries the whole (and is the real essence) or it doesn't (and the real distinction stands).

objections.title: Essence and existence are simply inseparable — no cause needed
objections.whoRaises: A critic trying to stop the argument after the real distinction is granted
objections.objection: Fine, essence and existence are really distinct. But you yourself say they're inseparable, like a circle's radius and circumference. Inseparable things just go together. Why should their union need an external cause?
objections.reply:
Inseparability is not an explanation; it is what needs explaining.

1. Radius and circumference are inseparable *because* both follow from the essence of a circle. Anything with that essence has both.
2. But existence does not follow from the essence of a lion, pterodactyl, or unicorn: if it did, knowing the essence would reveal the existence, and such things would be necessary rather than things that come and go.
3. The only thing whose existence would follow from its essence is something whose essence *is* existence — and there can be only one such thing, whereas stones, dogs, and people come in many.
4. Nor can the thing supply existence to itself, since it would have to exist already to do so.
5. So the union of essence and existence in such a thing must be accounted for by a cause outside it.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘the union is just a brute fact,’ note that in every other case of inseparable-but-distinct features (radius/circumference, three angles/three sides) we do have an explanation. Treating this case alone as brute is special pleading — and it is the one case where the explanation leads somewhere the critic doesn't want to go.

objections.title: Even if there is a first cause, it needn't be God
objections.whoRaises: Common among critics of all first-cause arguments
objections.objection: Grant a first cause of existence. Why call it God? It could be some impersonal force, or a quantum vacuum, or the multiverse.
objections.reply:
Feser says it is no good to allege this glibly, because Stage 2 gives reasons the first cause must be divine.

1. The first cause must be something whose essence is existence itself — otherwise it would need existence imparted and wouldn't be first.
2. There can be only one such thing, so it is unique and the cause of everything else.
3. It exists necessarily and is uncaused.
4. It is purely actual (no potential for existence waiting to be actualized), so it has chapter 1's attributes: immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good, and — by proportionate causality — intelligent and omniscient.
5. A quantum vacuum or multiverse has a definite nature, parts, potentialities, and could be otherwise; its essence is distinct from its existence, so it is among the things that need a cause, not the cause. Detailed defense of the attributes comes in chapter 6.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘pure actuality and subsistent existence are just abstractions, not a personal God,’ point to the intellect argument (proportionate causality) and to chapter 6. The point to hold on to here is that the first cause cannot be anything with the kinds of features that make a thing physical or plural — those features are exactly what make something a receiver of existence.

objections.title: The argument assumes the universe had a beginning
objections.whoRaises: Popular critics; people who confuse the argument with the kalām argument
objections.objection: Science can't rule out an eternal universe or an eternal multiverse. If the universe had no beginning, there's no need for a first cause to get it started.
objections.reply:
The argument has nothing to do with a beginning in time.

1. It does not trace causes back into the past to a first moment.
2. It traces Fido's existence *here and now* down to what is sustaining it at this instant.
3. Even if the universe or a multiverse has always existed, each thing in it at each moment has an essence distinct from its existence and so needs existence imparted now.
4. So an eternal universe would not change the outcome in the slightest. (Aquinas himself thought philosophy could not prove the universe had a beginning.)
objections.pushback: If the skeptic says ‘but causes precede effects,’ point to the hierarchical examples: the causes in such a series operate simultaneously with their effects — C imparts existence to Fido only while B imparts it to C. Temporal priority is irrelevant; dependence is what matters.

objections.title: ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’
objections.whoRaises: Russell, Dawkins, and countless popular critics
objections.objection: The argument says everything needs a cause, then arbitrarily exempts God. If everything needs a cause, God does too; if something can exist uncaused, why not the universe?
objections.reply:
The argument never says everything has a cause.

1. Its actual premise is narrower: whatever has an essence *really distinct from its existence* needs a cause of its existence.
2. God is not an exception carved out of a universal rule. In him there is no such distinction — his essence is existence — so he not only needs no cause; he *could not* have one, because there is nothing in him that receives existence.
3. This is not a modern dodge invented to answer the objection; it was the point of the Thomistic tradition from the start.
4. As for the universe: it has an essence distinct from its existence (it is made of such things, is one thing among possible alternatives, and so on), so it falls under the principle. Feser calls the ‘What caused God?’ retort utterly incompetent — it misses the argument's point entirely.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘you're just defining God into existence as uncaused,’ reply that nothing is being defined into existence: the argument first shows, from Fido, that there must be a cause whose essence is existence; only then does it note what follows about that cause. Uncausedness is a conclusion, not a stipulation.

objections.title: Hume and quantum mechanics undermine the causal principle
objections.objection: Hume showed we can conceive of something coming into being without a cause, and quantum mechanics shows events happen without causes. So why accept that something with distinct essence and existence needs a cause?
objections.reply:
Feser refers back to chapter 1: these objections are no better here than against the Aristotelian proof.

1. Conceiving of something without *at the same time* conceiving of its cause is not conceiving of it as *having no* cause, and does not show it could exist uncaused (chapter 1's reply to Hume).
2. Causality does not require determinism: a cause need only make its effect intelligible, and indeterministic quantum transitions still have causal antecedents. Moreover, physics abstracts from much of reality, so its failure to assign a cause doesn't show there isn't one (chapter 1's reply on quantum mechanics).
3. And here the causal principle is even more tightly grounded: a thing whose existence isn't in its essence, and which cannot give itself existence, must get it from something else. The alternative isn't a surprising discovery but an incoherence — existence coming from nowhere to an essence that is by itself merely potential.
objections.pushback: If pressed on quantum vacuums, note that a vacuum state is a physical something with a definite structure and governed by laws — an essence distinct from its existence — so it needs existence imparted as much as Fido does.

objections.title: Why need there be a first cause? (Hume's infinite-series objection)
objections.objection: If every member of a causal series is explained by an earlier member, then even in an infinite series each thing has its explanation. Nothing is left unexplained, so there's no need for a first cause.
objections.reply:
Feser grants Hume's point for **linear** series but denies its relevance.

1. The Thomistic series is **hierarchical**: every cause other than the first is merely instrumental, with no causal power of its own. Infinite extension changes nothing; something outside the series must impart power to all its members — ‘first’ in the sense of that on which all depend.
2. The series Hume rightly allows to be infinite is one of things *generated in time* from pre-existing materials (Fido from his parents, and so on).
3. But the Thomistic question is what **conserves** Fido — and his parents, and the matter and powers involved — in existence at each moment. Even an infinite line of dogs would need each dog conserved at every moment.
4. An infinite chain of conserving causes that merely pass on existence yields no real dog, just as an infinite chain of IOUs yields no real money.
5. Barry Miller's logical point: an explanation of the form ‘A is caused to G by B insofar as B is caused to G by C insofar as…’ can only be completed by naming a first member M. The only non-arbitrary M is subsistent existence itself.
objections.pushback: If the Humean says ‘but each member *is* explained by the one above it,’ answer: in a hierarchical series each member is only *conditionally* explained — explained on the assumption that the one above it is actually giving it existence. An infinite chain of conditional explanations never discharges the condition. That is the IOU point in logical dress.

objections.title: The fallacy of composition
objections.whoRaises: A standard textbook objection to cosmological arguments (associated with Russell and others)
objections.objection: Each thing in the universe may need a cause, but it doesn't follow that the universe as a whole does — just as each brick weighing a pound doesn't mean the wall weighs a pound.
objections.reply:
Two replies.

1. **Part-to-whole reasoning isn't always fallacious.** If every Lego brick in a wall is red, the wall is red. What shows a material thing needs a cause is its real distinction of essence and existence; the space-time universe is made of such things and has its own essence distinct from its existence, so it too needs a cause.
2. **More importantly, the proof doesn't reason from parts to whole.** It can start from a single thing — Fido, one stone — and show that it needs a conserving cause that is subsistent existence itself. The claim that this cause causes the whole universe is a *consequence* (via uniqueness, steps 24–27), not a premise.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘then you still haven't shown the universe needs a cause,’ point out that the universe either is or isn't something whose essence is existence. It can't be: there can be only one such thing, it must be purely actual and without parts, and the universe is manifestly composite and changing. So it is among the things that receive existence.

objections.title: Kenny's objection: no sense of ‘existence’ makes the real distinction work
objections.objection: There are two notions of existence. **Specific existence** (‘there is an x such that x is F’) is a second-order predicate of concepts; on that reading we can know what God is without knowing if there is one, just as with unicorns — so God's essence and existence are as distinct as anything's — and saying God's essence *is* specific existence would be gibberish (‘God's essence is *there is an x such that…*’). **Individual existence** (what the Great Pyramid still has and the Library of Alexandria lost) is just a thing's going on being what it is; so if in God existence equals essence because God goes on being God, then Fido's existence equals his essence too, since he goes on being a dog. Either way the Thomistic contrast between God and creatures collapses.
objections.reply:
Following Gyula Klima, Feser finds several problems.

1. **Separability assumed.** Kenny says that if a real distinction means we can have one without the other, Fido's essence and existence aren't really distinct. But real distinction does not entail separability (radius and circumference), and assuming it does begs the question. Fido's being what he is need not be identical to his individual existence even if you never get one without the other — and the three arguments show they are not identical.
2. **Only two respectable notions assumed.** The standard reason for restricting existence to the quantifier is that, if existence were a first-level predicate, ‘Martians do not exist’ would say that some existing Martians lack existence — a contradiction. But (John Knasas) that follows only if we grasp *Martian* as already applying to something existent. We don't: the subjects of existential statements are grasped existence-neutrally, so the statement means Martians, neutral in themselves, are not in fact real.
3. **Specific existence leaves something out.** If ‘cats exist’ means something falls under the concept *cat*, we can still ask what makes it the case that something does. The answer — an act of existence that actualizes an otherwise merely potential essence — is what the Thomist means.
4. (Existence, so understood, is not a property or accident, since a thing must exist to have properties. That this fits neither Frege's categories nor the property/accident scheme only shows those categories are too narrow.)
objections.pushback: If a Fregean insists that existence *just is* instantiation, ask what grounds the instantiation. ‘There is an x that is a cat’ is true because of something about reality — a real cat is actually there. The quantifier records that fact; it doesn't explain it. The Thomistic act of existence is a proposed account of what the quantifier is tracking.

objections.title: Only a conceptual distinction (the aspirin objection)
objections.whoRaises: Critics appealing to the failure of substitutivity in intentional contexts (discussed by Gyula Klima)
objections.objection: From ‘I can know X without knowing Y’ you can't infer ‘X is distinct from Y’. I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does, though they are the same stuff. Likewise, knowing a lion's essence without knowing its existence shows only that the *concepts* differ, not the realities.
objections.reply:
Klima's reply turns on **logical independence** of concepts.

1. Some concept pairs are logically independent: knowing all about aspirin doesn't tell me it's now less popular than acetaminophen. No surprise there.
2. With a vague grasp of aspirin (a chemical sold for pain), I might not know it's acetylsalicylic acid. But with *complete* knowledge of aspirin's chemical essence, I couldn't fail to know it. The fully grasped concepts are not independent.
3. If a lion's essence were identical to its existence, a complete grasp of the essence should likewise bring knowledge of its existence. It never does — for lions, stones, trees, or anything we experience.
4. **Not question-begging:** we have independent reason. Knowing a kind's essence, I know a priori what any member that does, did, will, or could exist would be like; but whether any member actually exists I can only learn a posteriori. And judging that aspirin isn't acetylsalicylic acid misconceives aspirin, while judging aspirin doesn't exist doesn't misconceive it at all.
objections.pushback: If the critic says ‘maybe complete knowledge of a lion's essence *would* reveal its existence — we've just never had it,’ answer that the a priori/a posteriori pattern holds for essences we *do* know well (triangles, water's chemistry): knowing what they are fixes what any instance must be like, never whether there is an instance. There is no sign that more knowledge of the same kind would change the pattern.

objections.title: Things don't really have essences (conventionalism)
objections.whoRaises: Nominalists, conventionalists, some empiricists and philosophers of language
objections.objection: Essences are human conventions — the way we choose to sort things, like ‘carburetor’ or ‘can opener.’ If there are no real essences, there's no real distinction between a thing's essence and its existence, and the argument never gets started.
objections.reply:
Feser grants that artifacts have conventional essences, but offers several reasons to accept real essences for natural things.

1. **Aristotle:** trying to prove that things have natures is absurd, because it is more obvious than any premise for or against it; only dubious assumptions make it seem doubtful.
2. **Unity across things:** oaks, polar bears, and copper samples share causal powers exactly as real common natures would predict — a miracle if the grouping were mere convention.
3. **Unity within things:** each thing acts in regular, characteristic ways, persists through superficial change, and has integrated parts. Difficulty in discovering essences doesn't show they aren't there.
4. **Science's practice:** as Nancy Cartwright notes, physics isolates things under idealized, contrived conditions and often needs only a few experiments — the way you look for natures.
5. **Science's results:** Brian Ellis argues laws require essences and chemistry reveals discrete, discovered natural kinds.
6. **Incoherence:** (Crawford Elder) if all essences were mind-dependent, so would be the mind's own essence, making the mind prior and posterior to itself. And arguments for conventionalism would apply to us as well — where we know they fail.
7. **Enough is enough:** the proof needs only *some* real essences. Even if ‘dog’ were conventional, the underlying particles and the mind applying the label have real essences, distinct from their existence.
objections.pushback: If the conventionalist says ‘particles are just mathematical structures, no essences,’ ask whether the structure is real and whether it could have failed to exist. If it is real and contingent, there is a *what* and a *that*, and the argument proceeds.

objections.title: Conservation laws make a sustaining cause unnecessary
objections.objection: Physics already explains persistence: mass-energy is conserved, and objects continue in their states unless acted upon. Things don't need anything to keep them in existence; persistence is the default.
objections.reply:
This confuses a description of *how* existing things behave with an explanation of *why* there is anything behaving at all.

1. Conservation laws say that, given a physical system, certain quantities stay constant. They presuppose an existing system with an essence (a definite nature governed by laws).
2. The Thomistic question is why that system — and the laws' holding of it — is real at this instant, given that its essence doesn't include existence.
3. Treating persistence as a ‘default’ assumes that existence belongs to physical things by nature — which is exactly what the arguments for the real distinction deny (physical things are knowable without their existence being known, contingent, and many).
4. Chapter 1 already showed that the physics of inertia doesn't conflict with the Aristotelian principle of causality; the same holds here.
objections.pushback: If the skeptic says ‘matter-energy is the necessary being,’ ask: is matter-energy something of which there could be more or less, which is structured in various ways, and which physics describes as having definite, contingent properties? Then it isn't existence itself; it's one more thing that has existence.

objections.title: ‘Existence itself’ is an empty abstraction
objections.whoRaises: Analytic philosophers; skeptics who think ‘Being itself’ is word-magic (course addition)
objections.objection: ‘Existence’ isn't a thing — it's a feature things have or the fact that a concept is instantiated. Talking of ‘subsistent existence itself’ is like talking of subsistent redness itself: a grammatical illusion turning an abstract noun into an entity.
objections.reply:
The reasoning of the proof, not grammar, forces the conclusion.

1. The argument doesn't start by positing ‘existence itself’. It shows that Fido needs existence imparted now by something, and that any imparter that itself merely *has* existence would need an imparter too.
2. The series must end in something that doesn't receive existence; such a thing cannot have an essence distinct from its existence; and the middle option collapses — so its essence *is* existence.
3. Redness is a poor comparison: redness is always the redness *of* some material thing and needs a subject. Existence is what makes any subject real at all; something whose essence is existence is not a feature of something else but the source of every subject's being.
4. Kenny-style worries that ‘existence’ can only mean quantification were answered above: the quantifier records that something is real but doesn't say what makes it real.
objections.pushback: If the skeptic says ‘I still can't picture it,’ agree: you can't picture it, because pictures are of things with limits and parts. Ask them instead to follow the logic: what could impart existence without receiving it, other than something whose nature is to exist?

misconceptions.myth: The Thomistic proof argues that the universe had a beginning and God started it.
misconceptions.correction: It concerns what imparts existence to things here and now. It is fully compatible with an eternal universe or multiverse.

misconceptions.myth: The argument's premise is ‘everything has a cause,’ with God as an arbitrary exception.
misconceptions.correction: The premise is that whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence needs a cause. God lacks that distinction, so he neither needs nor could have a cause.

misconceptions.myth: A ‘real distinction’ between essence and existence means they are two separable things, as if a lion's essence could float around without existing.
misconceptions.correction: They are inseparable in any real thing, like a circle's radius and circumference — yet really distinct. Real distinction need not mean separability.

misconceptions.myth: Saying essence and existence are distinct just means we have two different words or concepts.
misconceptions.correction: Feser argues it is a real distinction in things themselves: shown by knowability (with Klima's reply to the aspirin objection), by contingency, and by the uniqueness of anything whose essence is existence.

misconceptions.myth: The first cause is ‘first’ in the sense of earliest.
misconceptions.correction: It is first in the order of dependence: the cause on which every other cause in a hierarchical series depends, right now, for the existence it passes on.

misconceptions.myth: The argument needs to reason from the parts of the universe to the universe as a whole.
misconceptions.correction: It can begin from a single thing like Fido. That God causes the whole universe is a consequence of uniqueness, not a premise.

misconceptions.myth: ‘Subsistent existence itself’ is just the biggest or oldest existing thing.
misconceptions.correction: It is not one existing thing among others at all, but that whose very essence is existence — which is why it is unique, uncaused, and purely actual.

misconceptions.myth: The Thomistic proof reaches a different God from the Aristotelian proof.
misconceptions.correction: Essence relates to existence as potency to act, so subsistent existence itself is purely actual; since there can be only one purely actual being, the two proofs arrive at the same God from different starting points.

misconceptions.myth: If essences are hard to discover, essentialism must be false.
misconceptions.correction: Essentialism claims essences are real, not easy to know. Science's hard-won discoveries of natural kinds support rather than undercut it.

misconceptions.myth: Parents or physical processes are all a thing needs to exist.
misconceptions.correction: They explain how a thing comes to be from pre-existing materials (a linear series), not what keeps it — and its matter and powers — in existence at each instant (a hierarchical series of conservation).

misconceptions.myth: The uniqueness argument is circular because it assumes God exists in order to show ordinary things have distinct essence and existence.
misconceptions.correction: It is conditional: if there is anything whose essence is existence, there can be only one. That holds whether or not such a thing exists, so using it in Stage 1 assumes nothing about God.

misconceptions.myth: Essentialists think the natures of things can be read off from the armchair or everyday experience.
misconceptions.correction: Feser says no serious essentialist believes this; natures are often hard to discover and are uncovered by science. The claim is only that they are there.

misconceptions.myth: The argument only applies to physical things, so immaterial beings like angels could be uncaused.
misconceptions.correction: Feser says the reasoning applies to anything whose essence is distinct from its existence, including immaterial things like angels or souls. Being immaterial doesn't make something existence itself.

explain.tweet: What a thing is ≠ that it is. A lion's nature doesn't include its existing, so it can't give itself being—it must receive it, right now. A chain of receivers explains nothing; it must end in what IS existence itself: one, necessary, uncaused. That's God. #Aquinas
explain.elevator: Everything around us has a *what* and a *that*. You can know exactly what a lion is without knowing whether lions exist — so existence isn't part of a lion's nature. It must get existence from something else, not just once but at every moment. If that source merely has existence too, it needs a source as well. The chain must end in something whose very nature is to exist — and there can be only one such thing. That's what we call God.
explain.twoMinute:
Here's the core idea. Think of anything — a dog, a tree, you. There are two different things you can know about it. One is *what* it is: its nature, its essence. The other is *that* it is: the fact that it actually exists. These really are different. I can describe a lion, a pterodactyl, and a unicorn in full detail, and you still couldn't tell me which one is alive today, which is extinct, and which never existed. Knowing what something is doesn't tell you whether it is.

So for ordinary things, existence isn't part of the package of what they are. That means they don't exist on their own steam. And they can't give themselves existence either — you'd have to already exist to do anything, including giving yourself existence. So whatever has existence without *being* existence has to be receiving it from something else.

And not just in the past. Your parents explain how you got started, but right now, this second, your existence still isn't built into your nature. So something must be keeping you in being right now.

Now suppose that something is also the kind of thing that merely *has* existence. Then it needs a source too, right now, and so on. That's a chain of borrowers passing along something none of them owns — like an infinite stack of IOUs with no money behind it. The chain has to end in something that doesn't borrow existence at all, something whose very essence *is* to exist. Aquinas calls it subsistent existence itself.

And there can only be one of those. To have two, you'd need something to tell them apart — but anything added to ‘existence itself’ makes it ‘existence itself plus something,’ which is no longer existence itself. So it's unique, which means everything else depends on it. It can't fail to exist, it has no cause, and it has no unrealized potential. Which means it's changeless, timeless, immaterial, all-powerful, and — as the book argues — intelligent and good. That's not a being among beings. That's what classical theism has always meant by God.

Notice what I didn't say: I never said the universe had a beginning, and I never said ‘everything has a cause.’ Only what *has* existence needs a cause. What *is* existence doesn't — and couldn't.
explain.eli12:
Imagine you have a drawing of a dragon. You know exactly what it looks like — wings, scales, fire. But knowing what a dragon *is* doesn't make one real. Being *real* is something extra.

That's true of everything: dogs, trees, even you. What you are is one thing; being real is another. So where does your ‘being real’ come from? Not from yourself — you'd have to already be real to give yourself anything.

So something else has to keep you real, right now, like a lamp keeps a room lit. If that something also just *borrows* its realness, it needs a source too. But you can't have an endless line of borrowers and nobody who actually has the thing. There has to be something that doesn't borrow realness at all — something whose whole nature is *being real*.

And there can only be one of those, because anything you added to tell two of them apart would make them ‘being real plus something.’ That one source of everyone's existence is what people mean by God.
