explain.keyAnalogy: The IOU analogy (Feser's own). A thing whose essence is distinct from its existence is like an IOU: it ‘has’ value only because something else backs it. An existence-imparting cause that itself merely has existence is just another IOU pointing to another. However long the chain — even infinite — it produces no real money unless it is backed by actual cash, something that has value not on loan but in itself. Subsistent existence itself is the ‘cash’: it doesn't have existence on credit; it is existence. Use it after the listener has accepted that a dog can't supply its own existence, and then ask: ‘How many IOUs do you need before you get a dollar?’ Close by noting the analogy's limit: the backing isn't just the first in a line of IOUs but something of a completely different kind.

persuade.coreInsight:
The click comes when a listener sees that **having existence** and **being existence** are different, and that anything which merely *has* existence is, right now, *receiving* it. Once that is grasped, the rest is almost automatic: receivers can't be the ultimate source; a chain of receivers explains nothing; the source must be what *is* existence; and there can be only one such thing.

It usually fails to click for two reasons. First, people hear ‘first cause’ and picture the *earliest* domino, so they think of the Big Bang and an eternal universe, and the argument seems to rest on disputed cosmology. Second, they take existence for granted as the default state of things — ‘stuff just exists, and it takes something to *destroy* it.’ The lion/unicorn contrast and the question ‘what makes a dog real right now, given that ‘dog’ doesn't include ‘real’?’ are the tools for dislodging that assumption.

audiences.startingPoint: Assumes physical stuff simply exists, that persistence is the default (conservation laws), and that ‘first cause’ means the Big Bang.
audiences.approach: Separate the argument cleanly from cosmology at the outset: it works even for an eternal multiverse. Then make the point about physics' own method: laws describe what existing systems do; they presuppose the systems. Use the lion/pterodactyl/unicorn test with a scientific twist — a complete physical description of a particle type doesn't tell you whether any exist; you must look. Present the real distinction as a claim about the logic of scientific knowledge (natures a priori, existence a posteriori). Only then bring in the conservation question and the hierarchical series.
audiences.openingQuestion: If you had the complete physics of a particle that was predicted but not yet detected, could the equations alone tell you whether it exists?
audiences.avoid: Don't lean on the Big Bang, and don't treat ‘God’ as an explanation competing with physics for the same job.

audiences.startingPoint: Believes existence is just instantiation (the existential quantifier) and that ‘existence is not a predicate’ settles the matter.
audiences.approach: Engage Kenny's objection directly and respectfully. Grant that the quantifier captures something. Then press the grounding question: what makes it true that something falls under the concept *cat*? Use Knasas's existence-neutral grasp to defuse the ‘Martians’ argument, and Klima's point that real distinction need not mean separability. Frame the Thomistic act of existence as a proposal about what the quantifier is tracking.
audiences.openingQuestion: When ‘there is an x such that x is a cat’ is true, is it true because of the concept, or because of something about the world?
audiences.avoid: Don't dismiss Frege or treat Kenny as a straw man; don't say ‘existence is a property’ — the Thomist denies that too.

audiences.who: Churchgoing believer who has never heard the argument
audiences.startingPoint: Believes God created the world, but pictures creation as a past event and God as a very great being among beings.
audiences.approach: Show that on this argument creation is ongoing: God is not the one who lit the fuse long ago but the one who keeps everything in being now. Introduce ‘subsistent existence itself’ as a way of understanding why God is not one more thing in the universe. Connect with ‘in him we live and move and have our being’-type intuitions without leaning on Scripture as a premise.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God stopped thinking about you for one second, what do you suppose would happen to you?
audiences.avoid: Don't let the believer treat the argument as a mere restatement of faith; insist that each step stands on reason.

audiences.startingPoint: Expects ‘Everything has a cause, so God’ and has ‘What caused God?’ ready.
audiences.approach: Pre-empt the caricature immediately: the premise is that only things whose essence is distinct from their existence need a cause. Walk through why a dog is such a thing and why a being whose essence is existence couldn't have a cause. Then let them see that ‘What caused God?’ is like asking what makes a triangle's three sides three-sided — it misunderstands what is being claimed.
audiences.openingQuestion: Would you agree that knowing what a unicorn is doesn't tell you whether there are any?
audiences.avoid: Don't get defensive or rhetorical; don't concede ‘everything has a cause’ as the premise, even for simplicity.

audiences.startingPoint: Open-minded, suspects metaphysics is word games, but willing to follow an argument.
audiences.approach: Use the whiteboard sequence. Emphasize that each step is independently checkable and that three separate arguments converge on the real distinction. Invite them to find the weakest step, then address it honestly. Show the payoff: the same conclusion as the Aristotelian and Neoplatonic proofs from a different starting point.
audiences.openingQuestion: What's the difference between knowing what something is and knowing that it is?
audiences.avoid: Don't rush to the attributes or to ‘God’; let them feel the force of the uniqueness argument first.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So this is another ‘first cause’ argument? Everything has a cause, so there's a first cause, so God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: No — and that's the most common misreading. The argument never says everything has a cause. It says that anything whose existence isn't part of what it is needs a cause for its existence.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: ‘Existence isn't part of what it is’ — what does that even mean?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Try this. I describe three animals to you in complete detail: a lion, a pterodactyl, a unicorn. One is alive, one is extinct, one never existed. Can you tell which from the descriptions?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Obviously not. I'd have to check the world.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Right. So knowing what a thing is doesn't give you that it is. If a lion's existence were just part of its nature, knowing its nature would tell you it exists. It doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe I just don't know the lion's nature completely. Existence could be in the part I'm missing.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Here's the test. If you thought a lion wasn't a cat, you'd have a wrong idea of what a lion is. If you thought lions were extinct, you'd be wrong about the world — but your idea of a lion would be fine. So existence isn't one of the features that make up what a lion is.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, suppose essence and existence are different. So what?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then a lion doesn't exist by its own nature. And it can't give itself existence — to do anything you already have to exist. So its existence has to come from something else.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sure: its parents. Evolution. No God required.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Parents explain how a lion got started. But right now, this second, the lion's existence still isn't part of its nature. What's supplying it now? Not the parents — they may be dead. Not the lion itself.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Why does it need supplying? Things just keep existing unless something destroys them.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That's assuming existence is the default for a lion — that it belongs to lions by nature. But we just saw it doesn't. Physics tells you how existing things behave; it doesn't tell you why there's anything there to behave.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, say something is keeping it in existence. Why not an infinite regress of such things?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because each link would only be passing on existence it's itself receiving at that very moment. It's like an infinite stack of IOUs — you never get a dollar unless something is backed by actual cash. The chain has to end in something that doesn't receive existence at all.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And what would that be?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Something whose very nature is to exist — not something that has existence, but existence itself. Aquinas calls it subsistent existence itself.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Why not several of those? A committee of necessary beings?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: What would make two of them two? Some extra feature, or some bit of matter. But then each would be ‘existence itself plus something’ — and so not existence itself. There can only be one.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what caused *it*?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Nothing could. The need for a cause came from having an essence that isn't existence. This has no such gap. It's not an exception to the rule; the rule doesn't apply.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even granting all that, why call it God? Maybe it's the universe, or the laws of physics.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The universe has a definite nature, parts, and could have been otherwise — so it's something that has existence, not existence itself. And existence itself has no unrealized potential, which means it's changeless, timeless, immaterial, and unlimited in power. That's exactly the classical idea of God — and the same being the argument from change reaches.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I'm not convinced yet, but I admit it's not the argument I thought it was.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That's a fair start. If you want to attack it, the place to push is the real distinction — and there are three separate arguments for it. Pick the one you think is weakest and we'll look at it.

socratic: Can you tell me what a unicorn is? Does knowing that tell you whether there are any?
If you thought lions were extinct, would you have misunderstood what a lion is, or just be wrong about the world?
Could something that exists by its very nature ever go out of existence?
What would a thing have to do in order to give itself existence? Could it do that without already existing?
Your parents explain how you began. What explains your existing at this very second?
If each link in a chain only passes along what it receives, what would the chain pass along if nothing at the top had it to begin with?
What makes two things of the same kind two rather than one?
If we tried to have two things that were each ‘existence itself’, what would distinguish them — and would they still be existence itself?
Why might something whose nature is existence not need a cause, even if everything else does?
If something has no potential waiting to be realized, could it change? Could it be made of parts or of matter?
Is ‘a circle's radius’ the same thing as ‘its circumference’? Can you have one without the other? What does that tell you about whether ‘distinct’ means ‘separable’?
When you learned that dodos are extinct, did your idea of what a dodo is change, or only your belief about whether there are any?
If you borrowed a book from a friend who borrowed it from someone else, and so on forever, would there ever be a book to borrow unless someone actually owned it?

traps.trap: Presenting the argument as ‘everything has a cause, so God,’ which invites ‘What caused God?’
traps.fix: State the premise precisely from the start: whatever has an essence really distinct from its existence needs a cause of its existence.

traps.trap: Framing it as an argument about the beginning of the universe or the Big Bang.
traps.fix: Say explicitly that it concerns what keeps things in being now and would work even if the universe were eternal.

traps.trap: Describing the real distinction as if essence and existence were separable things, so the listener pictures ‘essences waiting in a warehouse.’
traps.fix: Use the radius/circumference example: really distinct, never apart. Essences don't exist on their own.

traps.trap: Skipping the uniqueness argument, so the listener imagines many necessary beings or a physical necessary being.
traps.fix: Walk through ‘existence itself plus F’ carefully; it is what rules out rivals and makes subsistent existence the cause of everything else.

traps.trap: Leaping from ‘first cause’ to the God of a particular religion without the attribute derivation.
traps.fix: Show the bridge: essence is to existence as potency to act, so subsistent existence is pure act, and pure act has the classical attributes (chapter 1, developed in chapter 6).

traps.trap: Answering Kenny-style or Fregean objections by insisting that existence is a property.
traps.fix: The Thomist denies existence is a property or accident; it is the act by which a thing is real at all. Press the grounding question instead.

traps.trap: Getting lost in jargon (esse, ipsum esse subsistens, per se series) before the listener has the basic intuition.
traps.fix: Start with the lion/unicorn test and Fido right now; introduce the technical terms only as labels for what the listener already sees.

connections.note: The introduction's framework — demonstrations from evident starting points, not probabilistic hypotheses or God-of-the-gaps reasoning — applies here: the starting point (things have an essence and exist) is as evident as anything could be.

The Thomistic proof reuses chapter 1's machinery at every crucial joint: the hierarchical (per se) series and why it can't regress infinitely; the instrumental character of its intermediate members; the replies to Hume, quantum mechanics, and ‘What caused God?’. Above all, essence relates to existence as potency to act, so subsistent existence itself is pure actuality — the very same unique being as the Aristotelian proof's purely actual actualizer, with all the attributes derived there.

Chapter 2 already listed essence and existence among the ‘metaphysical parts’ whose combination needs a cause, and argued that the first cause must be absolutely simple. Chapter 4 takes that particular composition and develops it in depth. Its uniqueness argument (any differentiator makes it ‘existence itself plus F’) closely parallels chapter 2's argument that there can be only one absolutely simple One, and subsistent existence itself — with no distinction of essence and existence — is that simple One.

Chapter 3 argues from abstract objects (universals, propositions, possibilities) to a divine intellect. The Thomistic proof's appeal to real essences and to proportionate causality (for intellect and omniscience) complements it: the essences of things, understood in the divine intellect, are what God gives existence to.

The rationalist proof reaches a necessary being via the principle of sufficient reason. The Thomistic proof supplies a metaphysical account of what necessity is — a being whose essence is its existence — and of why contingent things are contingent: their essence is distinct from their existence.

Stage 2 compresses the derivation of the divine attributes; chapter 6 develops them at length, and the idea of God as subsistent existence itself undergirds divine simplicity, unity, and immutability there.
Chapter 6's treatment of God's knowledge, will, goodness, and relation to creation (conservation and concurrence) builds on the claim here that God imparts existence to all things at every moment.

Chapter 7 answers general objections to natural theology — including charges about the principle of causality, ‘What caused God?’, and the move from first cause to God — that are briefly flagged in this chapter's ‘objections rebutted’ section.

Later objections in chapter 7 lean on this chapter's picture of God. Against scientism: no physical description tells us what imparts existence to physical things. Against the ‘one god further’ jibe: subsistent existence itself is not one more being alongside Zeus and Thor, but the unique source of all beings. And the replies on evil and divine hiddenness presuppose the purely actual, fully good cause established here.

In a capstone synthesis, the Thomistic proof is the deepest of the five convergent routes: change (ch1), composition (ch2), and contingency (ch5) are all, at bottom, cases of things that have existence without being existence.

quiz.q: According to Feser, what two distinct things do we know about the stones, trees, dogs, and people we encounter?
options: Their causes and their effects
Their matter and their form
What they are and that they are
Their properties and their relations
quiz.explanation: The chapter opens by distinguishing a thing's essence (what it is) from its existence (that it is). Matter and form are chapter 1–2 concepts, not the contrast this proof turns on.

quiz.q: What is the point of the lion / pterodactyl / unicorn thought experiment?
options: Knowing a thing's essence doesn't tell you whether it exists, so its existence is really distinct from its essence
Extinction proves that all living things are contingent
Unicorns show that some essences are merely conventional
We never know the essence of any animal completely
quiz.explanation: Someone given full descriptions of the three couldn't say which exists, which is extinct, and which never existed. If existence were the same feature of reality as essence, knowing the essence would reveal it. Contingency is the second, separate argument.

quiz.q: A critic says we never grasp essences completely, so existence might be hidden in the part we haven't grasped. How does Feser reply?
options: He admits the argument is only probable
He argues that we actually do grasp every essence completely
He says only God knows essences, so the objection is irrelevant
He notes that denying a thing's existence is a false judgment but not a misconception of what it is, unlike denying a genuine part of its essence
quiz.explanation: Judging that a lion is not a cat misconceives a lion; judging that lions don't exist doesn't. So existence doesn't behave like a part of the essence, however incomplete our grasp. Feser doesn't claim complete knowledge of essences.

quiz.q: Why does the contingency of lions show that their essence and existence are really distinct?
options: Because lions have causes, and causes are always distinct from their effects
Because if existence weren't distinct from their essence, lions would exist by their very nature and so exist necessarily
Because contingent things are material, and matter is distinct from form
Because there are many lions
quiz.explanation: Something that has existence simply by being what it is could not fail to exist. Lions can fail to exist, so existence isn't part of what they are. ‘There are many lions’ belongs to the third argument, from uniqueness.

quiz.q: An objector says contingency is fully explained by a thing's having a cause and a potential for nonexistence. What is Feser's response?
options: He agrees and drops the contingency argument
The real question is why the thing would need, or even could have, a cause and a potential for nonexistence if its existence weren't distinct from its essence
He appeals to quantum mechanics to show causes are unnecessary
He argues that potentialities are mere illusions
quiz.explanation: Causal dependence and fragility are symptoms of the real distinction; they presuppose it rather than replace it. If existence were part of a lion's nature, nothing would need to supply it and nothing could take it away.

quiz.q: Why can't two things that are each ‘existence itself’ be distinguished the way two species of a genus are?
options: Because existence is not a genus in modern biology
Because specific differences only apply to animals
Because they would have to be material
Because each would then be existence itself PLUS its specific difference, and so would not be existence itself
quiz.explanation: Just as a human is animality plus rationality (and so not animality itself), any differentiated ‘existence itself’ would be existence plus something. Feser explicitly uses genus and species in the traditional logical sense, not the biological one.

quiz.q: According to the chapter, what makes Socrates and Plato two different members of the same species?
options: Their association with different parcels of matter
Different specific differences
Different essences
The fact that one exists necessarily and the other contingently
quiz.explanation: Members of a species are individuated by matter; other differences (brain wiring, and so on) presuppose different matter. They share the same essence, humanity, so ‘different essences’ is wrong.

quiz.q: What does the third (uniqueness) argument conclude about stones, trees, and dogs?
options: They exist necessarily
Each is unique
Since there is or could be more than one of each kind, their essence and existence must be really distinct
Each is existence itself plus a parcel of matter
quiz.explanation: Anything whose essence is identical with its existence would be one of a kind. The things of experience come, or could come, in many, so they are not like that. Option D misreads the reductio: ‘existence itself plus matter’ was shown to be incoherent.

quiz.q: An objector proposes a ‘middle ground’: existence might be one part of a thing's essence. How does Feser answer?
options: Existence can't be a part because all parts are material
He concedes the middle ground but calls it irrelevant
He denies that rational animality has any parts
If the whole thing depended on its ‘existence part’, existence would be its true essence — collapsing back into essence being existence
quiz.explanation: Compare making the whole human essence depend on animality alone: that would make animality the true essence. Likewise, an existence ‘component’ on which the whole depends just is the essence. So there is no third option.

quiz.q: What does the example of a circle's radius and circumference illustrate?
options: That a thing's essence and existence can exist apart
That a real distinction need not involve separability
That geometrical essences are conventional
That existence follows from essence
quiz.explanation: Radius and circumference are really distinct (one is 2π times the other) but never found apart. Essence and existence are likewise really distinct but inseparable. The example also shows what existence lacks: unlike the circumference, it does not follow from the essence.

quiz.q: Why can't the inseparability of a lion's essence and existence explain why they are united?
options: Because they are actually separable
Because only geometrical figures have inseparable features
Because inseparability itself needs explaining; for a circle it's explained by properties following from the essence, but a lion's existence doesn't follow from its essence
Because existence is a property like any other
quiz.explanation: Feser says pointing to inseparability just raises the question why they are inseparable. Existence can't follow from a lion's essence (or knowing the essence would reveal it, and lions would be necessary), so the union must come from outside. The Thomist denies that existence is a property.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, can't a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence impart existence to itself?
options: To do anything it must already exist, so it would have to exist before it exists
Because it lacks sufficient energy
Because God forbids self-causation
Because it would violate the conservation of energy
quiz.explanation: Acting presupposes existing. A thing that has to receive existence would have to exist already in order to confer it on itself — incoherent. The point is metaphysical, not physical.

quiz.q: What is the main lesson of the Fido example?
options: Fido needs a cause imparting existence to him here and now, at every moment, not just a cause in the past
Fido's conception requires parents
Dogs have immaterial souls
The evolutionary history of dogs requires a designer
quiz.explanation: Everything said about the real distinction holds at every moment of Fido's life, so something must be imparting existence to him now; otherwise he would ‘blink out’. His parents explain only his beginning.

quiz.q: What makes the series ‘Fido ← C ← B ← A’ a hierarchical series, according to Feser?
options: Merely that all the causes operate at the same time
That it stretches back into the distant past
That none of its members can act independently: each imparts existence only insofar as it is itself receiving existence from the one before it
That every member is a material object
quiz.explanation: Feser says simultaneity is a feature but the more fundamental point is dependence: C gives existence to Fido only while B gives existence to C. A series stretching into the past is a linear series.

quiz.q: Why must the first member of the series be something whose essence is existence itself?
options: Because it must be the earliest cause in time
Because anything whose essence is distinct from its existence must receive existence, so it couldn't cause without being caused
Because it must be the largest thing in the universe
Because the universe must have had a beginning
quiz.explanation: The first cause must impart existence without deriving it. Anything with a real distinction between essence and existence has to derive it. ‘First’ means primary, not earliest.

quiz.q: What does Aquinas call the cause the Thomistic proof arrives at?
options: The Unmoved Mover
The One
The Demiurge
Subsistent existence itself (ipsum esse subsistens)
quiz.explanation: Feser cites Aquinas's On Being and Essence for the phrase. ‘Unmoved Mover’ is Aristotle's (chapter 1); ‘the One’ is Plotinus's (chapter 2).

quiz.q: How does Feser show that the Thomistic proof and the Aristotelian proof reach the same God?
options: Both begin from the fact of change
Both require that the universe had a beginning
Essence is to existence as potency is to act, so subsistent existence itself is purely actual — and there can be only one purely actual being
Both rely on the principle of sufficient reason
quiz.explanation: Fido's essence alone is a merely potential dog; existence actualizes it. What just is existence has no such potency, so it is pure act. Chapter 1 showed there can be only one purely actual thing. The PSR is the rationalist proof's engine (chapter 5).

quiz.q: How does Feser respond to the charge that the Thomistic proof assumes the universe had a beginning?
options: He argues that the universe did begin
He relies on the Big Bang
He concedes the point but says it doesn't matter
The argument traces existence to a cause here and now, and would work even if the universe or a multiverse had always existed
quiz.explanation: The chain of causes does not run back into the past but ‘down’ to what sustains things now. Nothing in the argument depends on a beginning.

quiz.q: Why does ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ miss the Thomistic proof?
options: Because God is an exception granted by faith
Because the premise is only that things whose essence is distinct from their existence need a cause, and in God there is no such distinction
Because God caused himself
Because the series of causes is infinite
quiz.explanation: God is not an arbitrary exception to a universal rule; the rule was never universal. Self-causation is exactly what the argument rules out as incoherent.

quiz.q: Hume says that in an infinite causal series every member is explained by an earlier one, so no first cause is needed. What is the best reply on Feser's behalf?
options: That holds for linear series of things generated in time, but the Thomistic series is hierarchical and concerns conservation; an infinite chain of derived existence is like an infinite chain of IOUs with no money
No infinite series of any kind is possible
Hume is right, so the Thomistic proof must be abandoned
Hume's objection concerns only quantum events
quiz.explanation: Feser agrees with Hume about linear series. But every member of a hierarchical series is instrumental, so infinite extension leaves the whole series without the existence it passes along. Barry Miller adds that the explanation can only be completed by naming a first member.

quiz.q: On the fallacy-of-composition charge, what is Feser's second and more important reply?
options: Part-to-whole reasoning is sometimes valid, as with a wall made of red Lego bricks
The universe as a whole weighs as much as its parts
The universe is just one very large brick
The proof doesn't reason from parts to whole at all: it can start from one thing like Fido, and its claim about the whole universe is a consequence, not a premise
quiz.explanation: Option A is Feser's first reply, and it's correct but not the more important one. The deeper point is that no premise concerns the universe as a whole; ‘cause of everything’ follows from uniqueness.

quiz.q: Which correctly describes Kenny's two notions of existence?
options: Specific existence is what the existential quantifier expresses (a concept's having instances); individual existence is what an individual has while it lasts and loses when destroyed
Specific existence belongs to biological species; individual existence belongs only to persons
Specific existence is necessary existence; individual existence is contingent existence
Specific existence is God's existence; individual existence is creatures' existence
quiz.explanation: Kenny's examples: ‘there is an x such that x is F’ (specific), and the Great Pyramid still existing while the Library of Alexandria doesn't (individual). The other options invent contrasts Kenny doesn't draw.

quiz.q: What is Klima's answer to the objection that the lion case is just like aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid (one reality, two concepts)?
options: Substitutivity of identicals always holds, even in intentional contexts
Aspirin and acetylsalicylic acid are actually distinct substances

A complete grasp of aspirin's essence would reveal that it is acetylsalicylic acid, since the concepts aren't logically independent; but no complete grasp of a lion's essence would reveal that it exists
The aspirin example shows that all essences are conventional
quiz.explanation: The failure of substitutivity with a vague concept of aspirin disappears with a full concept. The lion case is different: essence and existence stay independent however fully the essence is grasped. Klima grants that substitutivity fails in intentional contexts.

quiz.q: What is Crawford Elder's argument against the view that all essences are conventional?
options: Science has discovered natural kinds in chemistry
If all essences were mind-dependent, the mind's own essence would be too, making the mind both prior and posterior to itself
Aristotle said it is absurd to try to prove that things have natures
Artifacts like can openers have conventional essences
quiz.explanation: Mind-dependent things presuppose the mind; so a mind whose essence is mind-dependent would presuppose itself. The other options are real points in the chapter (Ellis, Aristotle, the artifact concession) but not Elder's.

quiz.q: Which step of the formal argument asserts that each kind of thing we experience has, or could have, more than one member?
options: Step 3
Step 5
Step 10
Step 17
quiz.explanation: Step 10 is the plurality premise; combined with step 9 (anything whose essence is existence would be unique) it yields step 11. Step 3 is the knowability premise, step 5 the contingency premise, step 17 the here-and-now premise.

quiz.q: Which step secures that Fido cannot be keeping himself in existence?
options: Step 14: nothing can be the cause of itself
Step 21: a hierarchical series must have a first member
Step 24: the cause which is subsistent existence itself is unique
Step 33: whatever is purely actual has the divine attributes
quiz.explanation: Steps 13–15 rule out self-imparted existence, and step 14 is the key premise: a thing would have to exist before it exists to cause itself. Step 21 concerns the chain of other causes, not self-causation.

quiz.q: Which group of steps establishes that subsistent existence itself is the cause of everything other than itself?
options: Steps 1–3
Steps 24–27
Steps 28–30
Steps 31–33
quiz.explanation: Steps 24–27 run: unique (24), so everything else has distinct essence and existence (25), all such things depend on it (26), so it causes everything else (27). Steps 28–30 give necessity and uncausedness; 31–33 pure actuality and the attributes.

quiz.q: Step 21 claims that a hierarchical series of causes cannot regress infinitely. Where does Feser establish this?
options: In chapter 5's discussion of the principle of sufficient reason
In chapter 1's analysis of hierarchical (per se) causal series
In chapter 3's argument from abstract objects
In Hume's analysis of causation
quiz.explanation: Feser explicitly refers back to chapter 1, where he argued that in a hierarchical series all causes but the first are merely instrumental, so there must be a first cause. Hume is the source of an objection, not of the premise.

quiz.q: A student says: ‘My parents caused me, their parents caused them, and so on forever — so there's no need for God.’ Which distinction does this objection ignore?
options: Essence vs. accident
Genus vs. species
Linear generation vs. hierarchical conservation
A priori vs. a posteriori knowledge
quiz.explanation: The student describes a linear series of generation in time, which Feser grants could be infinite. The Thomistic question is what conserves the student (and the parents, and their matter) in being right now — a hierarchical series.

quiz.q: Kenny writes that if a real distinction between A and B means we can have one without the other, then Fido's essence and existence are not really distinct. Which distinction does this reasoning overlook?
options: Separable real distinctions vs. inseparable real distinctions
Specific vs. individual existence
Genus vs. species
Linear vs. hierarchical causal series
quiz.explanation: Klima and Feser reply that real distinction does not entail separability — a circle's radius and circumference are really distinct but inseparable — so assuming otherwise begs the question against the Thomist.

quiz.q: What would Feser reply to someone who proposes that the universe itself is the thing whose essence is existence?
options: He would agree, as long as the universe is eternal
He would say the universe is too large to be a cause
He would say the Big Bang proves the universe began, so it can't be necessary

There can be only one thing whose essence is existence, and it must be purely actual and unmixed with anything added; the universe is composite, changing, and made of things whose essence is distinct from their existence
quiz.explanation: The universe has an essence distinct from its existence (Feser says so explicitly in answering the composition charge). Only something with nothing added to existence itself can be uncaused. Appeals to the Big Bang are irrelevant to this argument.

quiz.q: Why is the ‘first’ in ‘first cause’ not a matter of time?
options: Because time did not exist before creation
Because Aquinas held that the universe certainly had no beginning
Because the argument assumes the universe is eternal
Because the first cause is the one on which every member of the series depends for its causal power here and now, even if the series were infinite
quiz.explanation: Feser says that even an infinite hierarchical series of purely instrumental causes would need a cause outside it — ‘first’ in the sense that every member depends on it. The argument neither assumes nor denies a beginning.

quiz.q: Someone says: ‘Water is H2O by nature, so surely water's existence follows from its essence.’ How would Feser respond?
options: Knowing water's essence tells you what any water would be like, but whether any water exists is learned only by experience — so existence doesn't follow from essence
Agree: chemical essences are the one exception to the real distinction
Say that water's essence is merely a convention
Say that chemistry has no bearing on metaphysics
quiz.explanation: This is Klima's a priori / a posteriori point: an essence fixes the attributes of any possible instance, not whether there is one. Feser treats chemical kinds as real essences, so options B and C misread him.

quiz.q: Why does Feser say that the claim ‘subsistent existence itself causes the whole universe’ is a consequence of the argument rather than a premise?
options: Because he wants to avoid discussing the Big Bang
Because the universe has no essence
Because it follows from uniqueness plus the dependence of everything whose essence is distinct from its existence, while the argument itself can start from one single thing
Because Hume proved that wholes never need causes
quiz.explanation: The proof starts from any individual — Fido, a stone — and reaches subsistent existence itself. Only later, via uniqueness (steps 24–27), does it follow that everything else depends on it. That is why the fallacy-of-composition charge misses.

quiz.q: What is John Knasas's point about ‘Martians do not exist’?
options: Existence is a property like color, so negative existentials are about properties
Negative existential statements are always false
‘Martians do not exist’ is really a statement about the word ‘Martian’
We grasp the subjects of existential statements in an existence-neutral way, so denying existence of Martians is not self-contradictory
quiz.explanation: The Fregean worry assumes that grasping ‘Martians’ already means grasping existing Martians. Knasas says the grasp is neutral, so the statement means Martians, neutral in themselves, are not real. The Thomist denies that existence is a property (option A).

quiz.q: A friend says: ‘A circle's radius and circumference are inseparable, so they are just two descriptions of one thing — and so are essence and existence.’ What is the best reply?
options: Agree: inseparable features are always identical
Point out that radius and circumference are inseparable yet really distinct (one is 2π times the other), so inseparability doesn't show identity
Deny that a circle's radius and circumference are inseparable
Say that essence and existence are separable after all
quiz.explanation: Feser, following Oderberg, uses exactly this example to show that real distinction does not require separability. Essence and existence are inseparable in any real thing but still really distinct.

quiz.q: In the knowability argument, why does it matter that what a thing is belongs to its objective reality?
options: It blocks the reply that essence is just our concept: if both a thing's essence and its existence belong to its mind-independent reality, their identity would mean knowing one gives you the other
It shows that essences are conventional
It proves that unicorns exist
It shows that existence is a property
quiz.explanation: Feser notes that lion biology would be the same whether or not anyone studied it, and that existence is also part of a real thing's reality. So if they were the same feature of reality, grasping the essence would be grasping the existence.

quiz.q: The argument that there can be only one thing whose essence is existence is used twice. What jobs does it do?
options: It is used only in Stage 2, to prove uniqueness
It is used only to answer Kenny
In Stage 1 it shows that ordinary things, which come in many, have really distinct essence and existence; in Stage 2 it shows the first cause is unique and so the cause of everything else
It shows that there are many gods, one for each kind
quiz.explanation: Steps 6–11 use it to establish the real distinction; steps 24–27 use it (via step 8) for uniqueness and universal causality.

quiz.q: What would Feser reply to the suggestion that there might be two necessary beings — one good, one evil?
options: He would accept it, since the argument cannot decide
He would say the evil one must be weaker
He would appeal to Scripture
Two things whose essence is existence would need something to differentiate them, making each ‘existence itself plus F’ — so there can be only one
quiz.explanation: Any differentiating feature — a specific difference, matter, or anything else — would destroy the candidate's being existence itself. Also, a being whose essence is existence is purely actual and so fully good (chapter 1).

quiz.q: Why must subsistent existence itself be purely actual?
options: Because it is extremely active
Because essence relates to existence as potency to act, and what just is existence has no potency for existence awaiting actualization
Because it is material
Because it started the universe
quiz.explanation: If it had a potential for existence needing actualization, it would be one more thing that receives existence from a cause (steps 31–32). ‘Purely actual’ means no unactualized potential, not busyness.

quiz.q: Which thinker's analysis of the logical form of necessarily terminating causal explanations does Feser cite against Hume?
options: Barry Miller
Anthony Kenny
Crawford Elder
Nancy Cartwright
quiz.explanation: Miller shows that ‘A is caused to G by B insofar as B is caused to G by C insofar as…’ can only be completed by naming a first member. Kenny is a critic; Elder and Cartwright appear in the essentialism section.

quiz.q: What point does Nancy Cartwright make that Feser uses to support essentialism?
options: Science has proven that all kinds are conventional
Physics relies on vast numbers of repeated everyday observations
Physicists study things under contrived, idealized conditions and often treat one good experiment as enough — just how one looks for natures
Laws of nature describe only laboratory objects that don't exist in the wild
quiz.explanation: The regularities physics seeks are rarely observable in ordinary circumstances, and a few controlled experiments settle them — which makes sense only if science is uncovering universal natures. Option B is the naive picture of induction she rejects.

quiz.q: Why, according to Feser, is Hume's ‘why need there be a first cause?’ objection even more obviously irrelevant once we attend to essence and existence?
options: Because Hume denied all causation
Because hierarchical series are always finite in time
Because the Thomistic proof requires a beginning of the universe
Because the infinite series Hume allows concerns generation in time, whereas the Thomistic question is what conserves each member — and its matter and powers — in existence at every moment
quiz.explanation: Even if every dog came from an earlier dog forever, each dog's existence is distinct from its essence, so each needs conserving now. The Thomistic proof does not require a beginning (option C).

quiz.q: A conventionalist says that ‘dog’ is only a label we apply to particles arranged a certain way. Why doesn't this stop the Thomistic proof?
options: It does stop it, since the proof depends on dogs having real essences
The particles and the mind applying the label still have real essences distinct from their existence, so the argument runs on them
Particles have no essences at all
Dogs are the only things with real essences
quiz.explanation: Feser says the proof needs only some real essences. Even on the conventionalist's picture, the particles have non-conventional natures, and so does the human mind (Elder's point).

shortAnswer.q: Distinguish essence from existence, and explain the difference between a real distinction and a merely conceptual one. Why does the Thomistic proof need the distinction to be real?
shortAnswer.model:
A thing's **essence** is what it is — its nature (a human is a rational animal). Its **existence** is the fact that it is — that there really is such a thing. A **merely conceptual** (or verbal) distinction is one we draw in words or thought with nothing in reality answering to it, like ‘bachelor’ vs. ‘unmarried man’. A **real** distinction marks a difference in things themselves, though not necessarily separability (radius and circumference).

The proof needs a real distinction because if a thing's existence were really the same as its essence, it would exist by its very nature and need no cause of its existence. Only if existence is really something other than what a thing is does the question arise of where its existence comes from.
rubric: Defines essence as what a thing is and existence as that it is, with an example
Defines merely conceptual distinction with an example like bachelor/unmarried man
Notes a real distinction need not mean separability
Explains that without a real distinction there would be no need for a cause of existence

shortAnswer.q: Lay out Feser's three arguments for the real distinction between essence and existence, and one objection with its reply.
shortAnswer.model:
1. **Knowability:** we can know what lions, pterodactyls, and unicorns are without knowing which exist. Since essence and existence are both part of a thing's objective reality, if they were identical knowing one would give the other.
2. **Contingency:** the things of experience could fail to exist. If existence were not distinct from their essence, they would exist by nature, necessarily.
3. **Uniqueness:** anything whose essence is identical with its existence would be one of a kind (any differentiator makes it ‘existence itself plus F’). Stones, dogs, and people come in many, so their essence and existence are distinct.

**Objection and reply:** ‘We never grasp essences completely.’ But denying a lion's existence isn't misconceiving what a lion is, whereas denying it's a cat is; so existence isn't part of the essence. (Alternatives: the contingency objection — cause and potential for nonexistence presuppose the distinction; the middle-ground objection — an existence ‘part’ on which the whole depends becomes the real essence.)
rubric: States the knowability argument with an example
States the contingency argument
States the uniqueness argument and the plurality premise
Gives at least one objection and Feser's reply accurately

shortAnswer.q: Explain why there can be at most one thing whose essence is identical with its existence.
shortAnswer.model: For two such things, A and B, to be two, something must differentiate them. Things are differentiated either (a) as species within a genus, by a **specific difference** (humans are animality plus rationality), or (b) as members of one species, by distinct **matter** (Socrates is humanity plus this matter), or (c) in some other way. But in each case, the differentiator is something *added*: A would be existence itself plus its difference, and B existence itself plus its difference. Then neither would be simply existence itself, just as Socrates is not humanity itself. So there is no sense in the idea of two things whose essence is existence: such a thing, if there is one, is unique. And there is no middle option where existence is merely one part of an essence, since that collapses into existence being the essence.
rubric: States that plurality requires a differentiating factor
Explains the genus/species (specific difference) route and why it fails
Explains the matter route and why it fails
Generalizes: any differentiator yields ‘existence itself plus F’

shortAnswer.q: Why must a thing whose essence is distinct from its existence have a cause of its existence here and now, and not just in the past?
shortAnswer.model:
Its existence does not **follow from** its essence (unlike a circle's properties), since otherwise knowing the essence would reveal existence and the thing would be necessary. It cannot **impart existence to itself**, since to do anything it must already exist — it would have to exist before it exists. So existence must be imparted by **something else**.

And this is true at **every moment**: the real distinction does not disappear once the thing has come into being. Right now, Fido's existence still isn't part of what he is and still can't be self-supplied, so right now something must be imparting it. Without that, he would ‘blink out’, no more existent than before his conception. Self-causation is as incoherent at an instant as over a stretch of time. His parents explain only his coming to be, not his continuing to be.
rubric: Explains that existence doesn't follow from essence
Explains why self-causation of existence is incoherent
Explains that the distinction persists at every moment (Fido)
Distinguishes generation (parents) from conservation

shortAnswer.q: Why can't the series of existence-imparting causes regress infinitely, and why must its first member be subsistent existence itself rather than just any uncaused thing?
shortAnswer.model:
The series is **hierarchical**: C imparts existence to Fido only insofar as B is imparting existence to C, and so on. Each member other than the first is merely **instrumental** — it passes on existence it is itself receiving. As chapter 1 argued, such a series without a primary cause explains nothing, however long it is: an infinite chain of IOUs never produces real money. So there must be a cause that imparts existence **without receiving it**.

That cause cannot be something whose essence is distinct from its existence, because anything like that must receive existence. Nor is there a middle option (existence as a mere part of the essence). So the first member must be something whose essence just is existence — subsistent existence itself. Barry Miller's point reinforces this: the explanation must stop with a first term M, and the only non-arbitrary stopping point is one that needs no cause of existence.
rubric: Identifies the series as hierarchical and explains why
Explains why a hierarchical series needs a primary cause (instrumental causes; IOUs)
Argues that any cause with distinct essence and existence would need existence imparted
Concludes that the first member's essence must be existence

shortAnswer.q: How does Stage 2 derive the divine attributes, and how does this connect the Thomistic proof to chapters 1 and 2?
shortAnswer.model:
Stage 2 argues: (1) there can be only one thing whose essence is existence, so it is **unique**; (2) the two categories — distinct vs. identical essence and existence — are exhaustive, so everything else is of the first kind and depends on it: it is the **cause of everything else**; (3) since its essence is existence, it cannot fail to exist — **necessary** — and neither needs nor could have a cause — **uncaused**; (4) since essence relates to existence as potency to act, what just is existence has no potency for existence to be actualized: it is **purely actual**.

**Chapter 1:** there can be only one purely actual being, so the Thomistic and Aristotelian proofs reach the same God; and pure actuality entails immutability, eternity, immateriality, incorporeality, perfection, omnipotence, and goodness, while proportionate causality adds intellect and omniscience. **Chapter 2:** essence/existence is a kind of metaphysical composition, and subsistent existence itself — with no such composition — is the absolutely simple One; the uniqueness argument parallels chapter 2's argument that there can be only one simple cause.
rubric: Derives uniqueness and universal causality
Derives necessity and uncausedness
Explains essence/existence as potency/act and the move to pure actuality
Links to chapter 1 (one purely actual being; attributes; proportionate causality)
Links to chapter 2 (composition; simplicity; parallel uniqueness argument)

shortAnswer.q: Answer the objection ‘If everything has a cause, what caused God?’ as it applies to the Thomistic proof.
shortAnswer.model: The argument never claims that everything has a cause. Its premise is that whatever has an essence **really distinct from its existence** requires a cause of its existence. God is not an arbitrary exception to a universal rule, because the rule was never universal. In subsistent existence itself there is no distinction between essence and existence, so nothing in it receives existence; it therefore not only needs no cause but **could not** have one. Feser stresses that this is not a recent evasion but what the Thomistic tradition always meant. Moreover, uncausedness is a conclusion reached after the argument has shown, from something like Fido, that such a cause must exist; nothing is being ‘defined into existence’.
rubric: Rejects ‘everything has a cause’ as the premise
States the actual premise precisely
Explains why subsistent existence itself could not have a cause
Notes this is not ad hoc / not a definitional trick

shortAnswer.q: State Hume's ‘why need there be a first cause?’ objection and give Feser's full reply, including Barry Miller's point.
shortAnswer.model:
**Hume:** if every member of a series is explained by an earlier one, then even an infinite series leaves no member unexplained, so no first cause is needed.

**Reply:** (1) True of **linear** series, but the Thomistic series is **hierarchical**: every non-first member is instrumental and has no causal power of its own, so even an infinite series needs a cause outside it that is ‘first’ in the sense that all depend on it. (2) The series Hume allows is one of things **generated in time** from pre-existing materials (Fido's ancestry). The Thomistic proof asks what **conserves** Fido, his parents, and their matter and powers in being at each moment. Even an infinite line of dogs needs each dog conserved. (3) An infinite chain of conserving causes that merely pass on existence produces no dog, as infinite IOUs produce no money. (4) **Barry Miller:** an explanation of the form ‘A is caused to G by B insofar as B is caused to G by C insofar as…’ can only be completed by naming a first member M; with ‘exist’ as G, the only non-arbitrary M is subsistent existence itself.
rubric: States Hume's objection fairly
Distinguishes linear from hierarchical series and conservation from generation
Uses the instrumental-cause / IOU point
Explains Barry Miller's logical-form point

shortAnswer.q: Explain Kenny's objection to the real distinction and the Thomist's reply.
shortAnswer.model:
**Kenny** distinguishes **specific existence** (the existential quantifier: ‘there is an x such that x is F’, a second-order predicate of concepts) from **individual existence** (what the Great Pyramid has and the Library of Alexandria lost). On the first, God's essence and existence are as distinct as anything's (we can know what God is without knowing whether there is one), and identifying them would be nonsense. On the second, existing is just a thing's going on being what it is — true of Fido as much as of God — so the contrast collapses.

**Reply (Klima, Knasas, Feser):** (1) Kenny assumes a real distinction means separability, which begs the question; radius and circumference show otherwise. (2) He assumes his two notions are the only respectable ones, relying on the Fregean worry that ‘Martians do not exist’ would be contradictory if existence were predicated of things. Knasas: the subjects of such statements are grasped existence-neutrally, so no contradiction. (3) Specific existence leaves open what makes it the case that something falls under a concept — and that is the Thomistic act of existence actualizing an essence. (Existence so understood is not a property or accident.)
rubric: Explains specific vs. individual existence with examples
States Kenny's dilemma for the Thomist
Gives the separability reply
Gives the Knasas existence-neutral reply to the Martians argument
Gives the ‘what makes the quantifier true?’ point

shortAnswer.q: Explain the objection that the essence/existence distinction is merely conceptual (the aspirin case) and Klima's reply, including his answer to the charge of begging the question.
shortAnswer.model:
**Objection:** substitutivity of identicals fails in intentional contexts. I can know aspirin relieves pain without knowing acetylsalicylic acid does, though they are one substance. Similarly, knowing a lion's essence without knowing its existence shows only that the concepts differ, not that reality contains two aspects.

**Klima:** what matters is whether the concepts are **logically independent**. With a vague notion of aspirin I might not know it's acetylsalicylic acid, but with complete knowledge of its chemical essence I couldn't miss it. If a lion's essence were identical with its existence, complete knowledge of the essence would likewise yield knowledge of its existence — but for no thing of experience does it.

**Begging the question?** No: there's independent reason. Knowing an essence, I know a priori what any member of the kind that exists, existed, will exist, or could exist would be like; but whether any member actually exists I learn only a posteriori. Also, judging aspirin is not acetylsalicylic acid misconceives aspirin, while judging aspirin doesn't exist doesn't.
rubric: States the substitutivity/aspirin objection accurately
Explains logical independence and the complete-knowledge contrast
Rebuts the circularity charge with the a priori/a posteriori point
Uses the misconception contrast

shortAnswer.q: How does Feser defend the claim that things really have essences, and why does the proof need only some real essences?
shortAnswer.model:
Feser grants that artifacts (carburetors, can openers) have conventional essences, but defends **essentialism** for natural substances: (1) **Aristotle:** it is absurd to try to prove things have natures, since it's more evident than any argument about it. (2) **Unity among things:** members of natural kinds share causal powers as real common natures would predict. (3) **Unity within things:** each behaves characteristically, persists through superficial change, has integrated parts; difficulty in discovering essences doesn't show they are absent. (4) **Scientific practice** (Cartwright): physics studies idealized conditions and settles laws with a few contrived experiments — how one looks for natures. (5) **Scientific results** (Ellis): laws need essences; chemistry shows discrete natural kinds. (6) **Incoherence** (Elder): if all essences were mind-dependent, the mind's own essence would be, making the mind prior and posterior to itself; and conventionalist arguments fail for us, so why trust them elsewhere?

The proof needs only **some** real essences: even if ‘dog’ were conventional, particles and minds would have real essences distinct from their existence, and the argument runs on them.
rubric: Concedes artifact essences are conventional
Gives at least three of Feser's considerations accurately
Explains Elder's incoherence argument
Explains why only some real essences are needed

shortAnswer.q: Explain why a real distinction does not require separability, and show how this point undermines Kenny's objection.
shortAnswer.model:
Some real distinctions involve separability (two dogs; a dog and its leg), but not all. A circle's **radius** and **circumference** are really distinct — the circumference is 2π times the radius, so they aren't the same thing — yet in a circle neither ever occurs without the other. **Triangularity** and **trilaterality** are likewise distinct but inseparable. Essence and existence are like this: there is no essence floating around without existence or vice versa, yet they are really distinct.

Kenny argues that if a real distinction between A and B means we can have one without the other, Fido's essence and existence can't be really distinct. But that simply assumes real distinction entails separability, which begs the question against the Thomist (Klima). Fido's being what he is need not be identical to his individual existence, even though you never get one without the other — and the three arguments for the real distinction show they aren't identical.
rubric: Distinguishes separable from inseparable real distinctions with an example
Explains why radius and circumference are really distinct
States Kenny's separability assumption
Explains why assuming separability begs the question

shortAnswer.q: Explain the fallacy-of-composition objection and both parts of Feser's reply.
shortAnswer.model:
**Objection:** each brick in a wall may weigh a pound without the wall weighing a pound; so even if each thing in the universe needs a cause, the universe as a whole may not.

**Reply 1:** part-to-whole reasoning isn't always fallacious. If every brick in a Lego wall is red, the wall is red. Whether the inference works depends on the property. What makes a material thing need a cause is its real distinction between essence and existence; the space-time universe, made of such things and with its own essence distinct from its existence, needs a cause too.

**Reply 2 (more important):** the Thomistic proof doesn't reason from parts to whole at all. It can start from one individual — Fido, a stone — and show it needs a conserving cause that is subsistent existence itself. The claim that this cause causes the entire universe is a *consequence*, derived from uniqueness (steps 24–27), not a premise.
rubric: States the objection with the brick example
Gives the Lego counterexample and explains why the universe case is legitimate
Explains that the proof starts from a single thing
Notes that the universe claim is a consequence via uniqueness

shortAnswer.q: A science-minded friend says: ‘Physics already explains why things keep existing — conservation laws and inertia. No sustaining cause needed.’ Respond using the chapter.
shortAnswer.model:
Conservation laws and inertia describe how **existing** physical systems behave: given a system, certain quantities stay constant, bodies continue in their states. They presuppose that the system is there, with a definite nature governed by laws. The Thomistic question is different: **why is the system real at this instant at all**, given that nothing in its essence includes existence?

To treat persistence as a ‘default’ is to assume existence belongs to physical things by nature — exactly what the arguments for the real distinction deny: physical kinds can be fully described without our knowing whether they exist (a predicted particle's equations don't tell you it's there), they are contingent, and they come in many. So each still needs existence imparted now. Even the matter and causal powers that physics studies need conserving. Chapter 1 already showed that inertia doesn't conflict with the Aristotelian causal principle, and chapter 7 argues physics is silent on questions like this.
rubric: Distinguishes describing behavior of existing things from explaining their existence
Links the ‘default persistence’ assumption to denying the real distinction
Applies at least one argument for the real distinction to physical things
Mentions conservation (vs. generation) or the matter-and-powers point

shortAnswer.q: State the ‘middle ground’ objection to the uniqueness argument and reconstruct Feser's reply.
shortAnswer.model:
**Objection (discussed by Peter Weigel):** perhaps a thing's essence and existence are not distinct, not because its essence *is* existence, but because existence is one *part* of its essence alongside others. Then it would not be subsistent existence itself, and the uniqueness argument wouldn't apply.

**Reply:** Take the human essence, rational animality, with parts rationality and animality, and imagine existence as a third part. Then the existence of the whole human would depend on that single part. That is as implausible as the whole human essence depending on animality alone — and if someone insisted it did, he would be treating animality as the true essence. Likewise, if the whole thing depends on its ‘existence part’, existence is the true essence. So we are back to a thing whose essence just is existence. There is no middle ground: either essence is really distinct from existence, or essence is existence.
rubric: States the objection accurately
Uses the rational-animality comparison
Shows why the whole depending on one part makes that part the true essence
Concludes there is no third option

shortAnswer.q: Explain the objection that contingency can be accounted for without a real distinction, and Feser's reply. Why does the reply matter for the argument's overall strategy?
shortAnswer.model:
**Objection:** a lion is contingent simply because it needs a cause (earlier lions) and has potentialities for nonexistence (it can be killed, starve, catch disease). These facts explain contingency without positing any real distinction between essence and existence.

**Reply:** this misses the point. We need to know **why** the lion needs — or even could have — a cause of its existence, and **why** it has any potential for nonexistence. If existence were simply part of what a lion is, it would have existence by its nature: nothing else would need to supply it, and nothing in it could open the door to nonexistence. So dependence and fragility presuppose the real distinction rather than replacing it.

**Why it matters:** the argument's strategy is to find the deepest explanation of why things depend on causes. The objection stops at symptoms; the real distinction explains them, and it is precisely what drives the later steps (12–18) to a cause of existence here and now.
rubric: States the objection with the cause/potentiality examples
Gives Feser's ‘why would it need or could it have a cause?’ reply
Explains why existence-by-nature would rule out causes and fragility
Connects the point to the argument's later steps

flashcards.front: Essence
flashcards.back: What a thing is — its nature (e.g., rational animal for a human).

flashcards.front: Existence
flashcards.back: That a thing is — the fact or act of its being real. For the Thomist, not a property or accident.

flashcards.front: Real distinction vs. merely conceptual distinction
flashcards.back: Real: a difference in things themselves (may be inseparable). Conceptual/verbal: a difference only in words or thought (bachelor vs. unmarried man).

flashcards.front: Three arguments for the real distinction
flashcards.back: 1) Knowability: essence can be known without knowing existence. 2) Contingency: otherwise things would be necessary. 3) Uniqueness: what has essence = existence would be one of a kind, but things of experience are many.

flashcards.front: Lion, pterodactyl, unicorn
flashcards.back: Full knowledge of their natures won't tell you which exists, which is extinct, which never existed — so existence isn't part of essence.

flashcards.front: Incomplete conception vs. misconception
flashcards.back: Not knowing a lion is a cat = incomplete. Judging it is not a cat = misconception. Judging lions don't exist = false, but not a misconception — so existence isn't in the essence.

flashcards.front: Reply to ‘contingency = having causes and potential for nonexistence’
flashcards.back: Why would a thing need or could it have a cause, or a potential for nonexistence, unless its existence were distinct from its essence? Those presuppose the distinction.

flashcards.front: Why only one thing whose essence is existence?
flashcards.back: Any differentiator (specific difference, matter, anything) would make each ‘existence itself PLUS F’ — so not existence itself.

flashcards.front: How are species in a genus differentiated?
flashcards.back: By a specific difference (rationality marks off humans among animals).

flashcards.front: How are members of a species differentiated?
flashcards.back: By distinct parcels of matter (Socrates = humanity + this matter).

flashcards.front: The ‘middle ground’ objection (Weigel)
flashcards.back: Existence as one part of an essence. Reply: if the whole depends on that part, existence is the true essence — collapsing into essence = existence.

flashcards.front: Real distinction without separability
flashcards.back: A circle's radius and circumference; triangularity and trilaterality. Really distinct, never apart. So too essence and existence.

flashcards.front: Why ‘they're inseparable’ doesn't explain the union of essence and existence
flashcards.back: Inseparability needs explaining. For a circle, properties follow from the essence; a lion's existence does not follow from its essence.

flashcards.front: Why nothing can impart existence to itself
flashcards.back: To do anything it must already exist; it would have to exist before it exists.

flashcards.front: The Fido point
flashcards.back: Right now Fido's existence still isn't part of his essence and can't be self-supplied, so something must impart it now — or he'd blink out.

flashcards.front: Generation vs. conservation
flashcards.back: Generation: bringing a thing into being from pre-existing materials (parents). Conservation: keeping a thing (and its matter and powers) in being at each moment.

flashcards.front: Why the series Fido ← C ← B ← A is hierarchical
flashcards.back: Not just simultaneity: none can act independently; each imparts existence only while receiving it.

flashcards.front: Why the first cause must be subsistent existence itself
flashcards.back: It must impart existence without receiving it; anything with distinct essence and existence must receive it.

flashcards.front: Subsistent existence itself (ipsum esse subsistens)
flashcards.back: Aquinas's term (De Ente et Essentia, ch. 4) for that whose essence just is existence: not one existing thing among others.

flashcards.front: Stage 2: four immediate results
flashcards.back: Unique; cause of everything else; necessary; uncaused.

flashcards.front: Why the two categories are exhaustive
flashcards.back: A thing's essence is either really distinct from its existence or identical with it (no middle ground). Since only one can be the latter, all else is the former.

flashcards.front: Essence : existence :: ? : ?
flashcards.back: Potency : act. Fido's essence alone is a merely potential dog; existence actualizes it.

flashcards.front: Why subsistent existence itself is purely actual
flashcards.back: A potential for existence needing actualization would make it one more receiver of existence.

flashcards.front: Link to the Aristotelian proof
flashcards.back: Only one purely actual thing is possible, so the purely actual actualizer and subsistent existence itself are the same God.

flashcards.front: Attributes that follow (via ch. 1)
flashcards.back: Immutable, eternal, immaterial, incorporeal, perfect, omnipotent, fully good; plus intelligent and omniscient (by proportionate causality).

flashcards.front: Does the proof assume the universe had a beginning?
flashcards.back: No. It traces existence to its source here and now; it works even for an eternal universe or multiverse.

flashcards.front: Why ‘What caused God?’ misfires
flashcards.back: The premise is that whatever has essence distinct from existence needs a cause. God has no such distinction, so he needs no cause and could not have one.

flashcards.front: Hume: why need a first cause?
flashcards.back: True for linear series; but this series is hierarchical (instrumental causes) and concerns conservation, not generation.

flashcards.front: The IOU analogy
flashcards.back: Infinitely many IOUs never give you real money unless backed by cash; infinitely many borrowers of existence never give you a real dog unless backed by subsistent existence.

flashcards.front: Barry Miller's point
flashcards.back: ‘A is caused to G by B insofar as B is caused to G by C insofar as…’ can only be completed by naming a first member M.

flashcards.front: Fallacy of composition — two replies
flashcards.back: 1) Part-to-whole reasoning is sometimes valid (red Lego wall). 2) The proof doesn't need it: one dog suffices; ‘cause of the universe’ is a consequence.

flashcards.front: Kenny: specific vs. individual existence
flashcards.back: Specific: ‘there is an x such that x is F’ (Frege; concepts). Individual: what the Great Pyramid still has and the Library of Alexandria lost (Wirklichkeit).

flashcards.back: Complete knowledge of aspirin's essence would reveal it's acetylsalicylic acid (not logically independent); complete knowledge of a lion's essence would never reveal its existence.
