flashcards.front: Why the proof needs only some real essences
flashcards.back: Even if ‘dog’ were conventional, particles and minds have real essences distinct from their existence.

flashcards.front: What does step 2 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: If essence and existence weren't really distinct, knowing a thing's essence would tell you whether it exists — because both belong to its objective reality.

flashcards.front: What does step 4 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Without a real distinction, things would exist necessarily — they'd have existence by their very nature.

flashcards.front: What do steps 6–7 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Two things whose essence is existence would have to differ as species, as members of a species, or some other way — but any differentiator makes each ‘existence itself plus F’.

flashcards.front: What does step 9 claim?
flashcards.back: If a thing of experience lacked a real distinction between essence and existence, there could be only one of its kind.

flashcards.front: What does step 12 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: A thing with really distinct essence and existence gets existence either from itself or from a distinct cause — its existence doesn't follow from its essence.

flashcards.front: What does step 14 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Nothing can cause itself — it would have to exist before it exists.

flashcards.front: What does step 17 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: Since the real distinction persists at every moment, existence must be imparted at every moment, including now (the Fido point).

flashcards.front: What does step 19 claim?
flashcards.back: The cause is either something whose essence is distinct from its existence, or something whose essence is existence — no third option.

flashcards.front: What does step 21 claim, and where is it defended?
flashcards.back: The series is hierarchical, so it cannot regress infinitely and must have a first member — defended in chapter 1.

flashcards.front: What does step 22 claim, and why?
flashcards.back: The first member must be subsistent existence itself — it must give existence without receiving it.

flashcards.front: What does step 25 claim?
flashcards.back: Since subsistent existence itself is unique, everything else has an essence distinct from its existence.

flashcards.front: What does step 28 claim?
flashcards.back: Subsistent existence itself exists necessarily — what lacks a real distinction exists by its very essence.

flashcards.front: What does step 29 claim?
flashcards.back: Subsistent existence itself neither needs nor could have a cause — nothing in it receives existence.

flashcards.front: What does step 31 claim?
flashcards.back: If subsistent existence itself had a potential for existence needing actualization, a cause would have to impart existence to it.

flashcards.front: What does step 35 claim?
flashcards.back: For such a cause (unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual, etc.) to exist is for God to exist.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘A first cause needn't be God.’ → Reply
flashcards.back: Stage 2 shows it is unique, necessary, uncaused, purely actual, and so has the divine attributes.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Maybe the universe had no beginning.’ → Reply
flashcards.back: Irrelevant: the argument concerns what sustains things now; it works for an eternal universe or multiverse.

flashcards.front: Objection: Hume or quantum mechanics undermine causality. → Reply
flashcards.back: As in chapter 1: conceiving without a cause ≠ conceiving as uncaused; causation needn't be deterministic.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Your reply to the aspirin case begs the question.’ → Reply
flashcards.back: Independent reason: essence gives a priori knowledge of what any instance would be like; existence is known only a posteriori.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Things have no real essences.’ → Reply (short)
flashcards.back: Obvious (Aristotle); unity among and within things; science's practice and results; conventionalism is self-refuting (Elder); and only some real essences are needed.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘The universe is the necessary being.’ → Reply
flashcards.back: The universe is composite, changing, and made of things with distinct essence and existence; only one thing can be existence itself.

flashcards.front: Objection: ‘Conservation laws make a sustainer unnecessary.’ → Reply
flashcards.back: Laws describe existing systems; they don't explain why the systems exist at all.

flashcards.front: Great Pyramid vs. Library of Alexandria
flashcards.back: Kenny's example of individual existence: the Pyramid still has it; the Library lost it when destroyed.

flashcards.front: Triangularity vs. trilaterality
flashcards.back: Having three angles vs. having three sides — really distinct, never apart; both follow from the essence of a triangle.

flashcards.front: Carburetors and can openers
flashcards.back: Feser's examples of things whose essences are conventional, fixed by our purposes — unlike natural substances.

flashcards.front: Two kinds of unity supporting essentialism
flashcards.back: Unity among things (members of a kind share powers) and unity within things (characteristic behavior, persistence, integrated parts).

flashcards.front: Ellis's point
flashcards.back: Laws of nature need essences; chemistry reveals discrete natural kinds, discovered not invented (he doesn't extend this to biology).

flashcards.front: Why existence is not a property or accident (Thomist view)
flashcards.back: A thing must already exist to have properties or accidents at all.

flashcards.front: Does the argument apply to angels or souls?
flashcards.back: Yes — immaterial things too would have essence distinct from existence and so need existence imparted.

flashcards.front: Why is subsistent existence itself not one being among others?
flashcards.back: Others have existence added to an essence; it is existence itself, the source of all beings' existence.

flashcards.front: Is ‘What caused God?’ answered by an ad hoc exception?
flashcards.back: No — the Thomistic tradition always held that the need for a cause arises from distinct essence and existence, which God lacks.

flashcards.front: What does ‘blink out’ mean in the Fido example?
flashcards.back: Be annihilated — lapse into nothing if nothing were imparting existence to him at that moment.

teachBack:
**Your challenge:** explain the Thomistic proof out loud, in under **six minutes**, to a smart friend who has never studied philosophy and who suspects ‘first cause’ arguments are about the Big Bang.

**Constraints:**
- You may not use the phrases ‘everything has a cause’ or ‘the universe had a beginning’ except to reject them.
- You must use the lion/pterodactyl/unicorn test and the Fido-right-now example.
- You must explain in plain words why there can be only one thing whose essence is existence.
- You may use at most three technical terms, and must define each the moment you use it (suggested: essence, existence, subsistent existence itself).
- End by saying how this connects to the argument from change (pure actuality) in one sentence.

**Then have your friend (or an imagined skeptic) ask three questions:** ‘What caused God?’, ‘Why not an infinite regress?’, and ‘Isn't essence vs. existence just two words for one thing?’ Answer each in under 45 seconds.

**Check yourself:**
1. Did you say what the premise actually is (only what has essence distinct from existence needs a cause)?
2. Did you make the point about **here and now** clearly enough that your friend could restate it?
3. Could your friend explain, in their own words, why two ‘existence-itselfs’ are impossible?
4. Did you distinguish ‘first’ as primary from ‘first’ as earliest?
5. Did you use the radius/circumference example when asked about the real distinction, and the aspirin reply if pressed?

If any answer is no, reread the relevant summary section and try again tomorrow with a different listener.
videoPrompt: Audience: thoughtful adults new to philosophy, including skeptics. Explain Feser's Thomistic proof (Chapter 4 of Five Proofs of the Existence of God). Emphasize, in order: (1) essence (what a thing is) versus existence (that it is), using the lion, pterodactyl, and unicorn test; (2) why the distinction is real — contingency, and why only one thing could have existence as its essence; (3) real distinction without separability (a circle's radius and circumference); (4) nothing can give itself existence, so Fido needs a cause of existence right now; (5) the chain of such causes must end in ‘subsistent existence itself’ (the IOU analogy); (6) how uniqueness, necessity, pure actuality, and the divine attributes follow. Correct two misconceptions: the argument is not about the universe's beginning, and it never claims ‘everything has a cause.’ Briefly cover Hume, Kenny, and the aspirin objection. Tone: clear, calm, intellectually serious, never preachy.

readingGuide.beforeYouRead:
This chapter tries to prove that God exists by starting from the most ordinary fact there is: things exist. Look at any dog, tree, or person, and you can ask two separate questions about it — *what is it?* and *is it real?* Feser, following the medieval thinker Thomas Aquinas, argues that these two questions have genuinely different answers. What a thing is (its ‘essence’) does not include the fact that it is real (its ‘existence’). A perfect description of a unicorn doesn't make one exist.

From there the chapter asks: if being real isn't part of what a dog is, where does the dog's being real come from — not just when it was born, but right now? Feser argues that nothing can give itself existence, so everything like the dog must be receiving existence from something else at every moment. And a chain of things that merely pass existence along can't be the whole story. It has to end in something whose very nature is simply to exist — something that doesn't *have* existence but *is* existence. Feser argues there can be only one such thing, and that it has the features traditionally ascribed to God.

Why care? Because this argument is often misunderstood. It is not about the Big Bang or whether the universe had a beginning, and it does not rest on the claim that ‘everything has a cause’ — so the famous retort ‘Then what caused God?’ doesn't touch it. Understanding it will change how you hear most debates about God.

What will you be asked to accept? Mainly three things: that what a thing is and that it is are really different; that nothing can cause itself; and that a chain of causes which only pass on what they receive can't go on forever without a source. Each is argued for, not assumed.

The hard parts are the stretch on why there can be only one thing whose nature is existence (pages 120–122) and the replies to the philosophers Kenny and Klima near the end (pages 135–140), which use some technical logic. Don't worry if those pages feel dense on a first reading. The module's summaries and deep dives unpack every one of them slowly, and you can come back to them.

knowFirst.plain: What a thing is — its nature. The essence of a triangle is being a three-sided closed figure.
The fact that a thing is actually real, not just describable. Unicorns have an essence but no existence.
A difference that is in the things themselves, not just in our words. It doesn't have to mean the two could be pulled apart.
Real, but able not to be real. Lions are contingent: there might never have been any.
A potentiality is a capacity to be something; actuality is actually being it. Aquinas says a thing's essence is like a capacity to be real, and existence is that capacity being realized.
Keeping something in existence moment by moment, as opposed to making it in the first place.
A chain of causes acting at once, where each can act only because the one before it is acting on it right now — like a hand moving a stick that moves a stone.
A cause that only passes along power it is receiving at that moment, like the stick in the hand–stick–stone example.
Aquinas's name for the one thing whose very nature is to exist — which doesn't receive existence from anything, and which he identifies with God.

questionsToHold: What exactly is the difference between knowing what something is and knowing that it exists — and is that difference in the thing or only in my head?
Why can't something give itself existence?
Why does Feser keep saying ‘here and now’? What changes if we think about what keeps things in existence now rather than how they started?
Why couldn't there be two things whose nature is simply to exist?
Is God an exception to the rule that things need causes, or does the rule simply not apply to him — and what's the difference?
How does this chapter's conclusion connect to the purely actual ‘unmoved mover’ of chapter 1?
Which step would a skeptic most want to attack, and what is Feser's reply there?

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 1 — essence vs. existence and the first reason
map.what: Feser introduces the difference between what a thing is and that it is, asks whether it is real or merely verbal (bachelor/unmarried man), and gives the first reason: you can know what lions, pterodactyls, and unicorns are without knowing which exist. He answers the worry that we never fully know essences.
map.tip: Slow down on the lion/cat paragraph (incomplete conception vs. misconception); it comes back later in the chapter. The rest reads easily.

map.what: Things that could fail to exist can't have existence built into their nature. Feser answers the objection that having causes and being perishable explain contingency on their own.
map.tip: Short and clear. Make sure you see why ‘it has a cause’ presupposes the distinction rather than replacing it.

map.section: Stage 1 — the third reason: there could be only one thing whose essence is existence
map.what: The uniqueness argument: two things whose essence is existence would have to differ as species do or as individuals do, and either way each would be ‘existence itself plus something’. Since ordinary things come in many, their essence and existence are distinct. Then the ‘middle ground’ (existence as part of an essence) is rejected.
map.tip: The hardest pages in Stage 1. Read them twice, keeping the ‘PLUS’ idea in mind. The genus/species terms are used in the old logical sense, not the biology-class sense.

map.section: Stage 1 — real distinction without separability; how essence and existence are joined
map.what: Distinct doesn't mean separable (a circle's radius and circumference). Then: existence can't follow from a lion's essence, the way a circle's properties follow from its essence, and nothing can give itself existence.
map.tip: The quotation about the circle is from another philosopher (Oderberg); focus on the point, not the wording. The ‘would have to exist before it exists’ sentence is the key line.

map.section: Stage 1 — Fido here and now; the regress; subsistent existence itself
map.what: Fido needs a cause of existence at every moment, not just at conception, or he'd ‘blink out’. The chain of such causes is hierarchical, so it must end in something whose essence is existence itself.
map.tip: This is the heart of the chapter; read it slowly. If ‘hierarchical causal series’ is unclear, review chapter 1's hand–stick–stone example first.

map.section: Informal statement of the argument: Stage 2
map.what: Why subsistent existence itself is God: it is unique, the cause of everything else, necessary, uncaused, and purely actual, and so the same being as chapter 1's purely actual cause, with all its attributes.
map.tip: The list of attributes relies on chapter 1. On a first read, focus on the potency–act link (essence as a potential, existence as its actualization).

map.section: A more formal statement of the argument
map.what: The whole proof in 36 numbered steps.
map.tip: Don't memorize it. Read it alongside this module's step-by-step argument section, and group the steps into six phases (1–11, 12–18, 19–23, 24–27, 28–33, 34–36).

map.what: Quick replies: the first cause must be divine (Stage 2); the argument doesn't assume a beginning of the universe; it never says ‘everything has a cause’, so ‘What caused God?’ misses; Hume and quantum objections were answered in chapter 1.
map.tip: Easy and important. These are the objections you'll hear most, so learn these replies well.

map.section: Why need there be a first cause?
map.what: Hume's objection that an infinite chain leaves nothing unexplained. Feser's reply distinguishes chains stretching back in time from chains of present dependence, and uses the IOU analogy and Barry Miller's point about the logical form of explanations.
map.tip: Miller's bracketed formula looks scary; read it as ‘A exists because of B, insofar as B exists because of C, insofar as…’ and notice that the sentence can't be finished without a first term.

map.section: Why need there be a first cause? (continued) — the fallacy of composition
map.what: The charge that reasoning from parts to the whole universe is fallacious. Feser replies that some such reasoning is valid (the red Lego wall), and that his argument doesn't need it anyway: one dog is enough.
map.tip: Straightforward. Note the difference between a premise and a consequence.

map.what: Anthony Kenny's two senses of ‘existence’ and his argument that the real distinction fails on both. Replies drawing on Klima and Knasas: real distinction doesn't require separability; negative existential statements aren't contradictory; ‘there is an x such that…’ leaves open what makes it true.
map.tip: The most technical pages. First read for the three replies only; skip the footnotes. Return after reading this module's deep dive on Kenny.

map.section: A real distinction or merely conceptual distinction?
map.what: The aspirin/acetylsalicylic acid objection and Klima's reply using logical independence of concepts and the a priori / a posteriori contrast.
map.tip: Work through the aspirin example slowly with a pen. The key test: would complete knowledge close the gap?

map.what: Against the view that all essences are human conventions: Aristotle's point, the unity of things, scientific practice (Cartwright) and results (Ellis), Elder's incoherence argument, and the point that the proof needs only some real essences.
map.tip: The long quotation from Ellis can be skimmed. Slow down on Elder's argument (the mind prior and posterior to itself) and on the chapter's final paragraph.

afterReading: Without looking, explain in three sentences the difference between essence and existence, and give Feser's three reasons for thinking the difference is real.
Explain to an imaginary friend why Fido needs a cause of his existence right now, not just at his conception.
